0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy: The Book of Leviticus
0.overview:
Leviticus is the book most Christians skip and most preachers fear. Its pages drip with blood, smoke, and the minute regulation of altars, animals, and ailments. Yet to neglect Leviticus is to neglect the very heart of the gospel, for here, more than anywhere in the Old Testament, we learn how a sinful people may dwell with a holy God. The whole book answers a single question raised at the end of Exodus: when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle so that even Moses could not enter (Exod 40:35), how shall mortal, defiled creatures come near? Leviticus is God's gracious answer — a manual of access, written in the language of sacrifice.

The dominating word is holy. It appears more often in Leviticus than in any other book of the Bible. As R.C. Sproul never tired of insisting, holiness is not merely one of God's attributes among many; it is the very burning core of his being. The seraphim do not cry "Love, love, love" or "Mercy, mercy, mercy," but "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3). Leviticus exists to brand that threefold cry upon the conscience of a redeemed people: "You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy" (19:2).

But Leviticus is not legalism. It stands inside grace. Israel is already redeemed; the blood of the Passover lamb has already been shed; the people have already been brought out of Egypt and into covenant at Sinai. Everything in Leviticus is for a people God has already claimed as his own. The sacrifices do not purchase God's love — they are the appointed means by which an already-loved people may live in the presence of the One who loves them. Grace precedes law, as it always does.

Above all, Leviticus is about Jesus. Every offering, every priest, every drop of blood, every Day of Atonement points beyond itself to the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. The book of Hebrews is the inspired commentary on Leviticus, and its message is that all these shadows have found their substance in Christ. To read Leviticus rightly is to be brought, again and again, to the foot of the cross and to whisper with adoring wonder, "It is finished." Holy, holy, holy — and yet, in Christ, the holy God has made a way for us to come home.

1.title: The Burnt Offering: Wholly the Lord's
1.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.<sup>3</sup>"If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD.<sup>4</sup>He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.<sup>5</sup>Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>6</sup>Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces,<sup>7</sup>and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire.<sup>8</sup>And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar;<sup>9</sup>but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish,<sup>11</sup>and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>12</sup>And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar,<sup>13</sup>but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>"If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar.<sup>16</sup>He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes.<sup>17</sup>He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
1.overview:
Leviticus opens not with a command but with a calling: "The LORD called Moses." The same God whose glory had just filled the tabernacle now speaks from within it, and his first word to a redeemed people is about worship — how to draw near. The very first offering described is the burnt offering, the 'olah, the offering that ascends. It is the only sacrifice in which the entire animal, apart from the skin, is consumed upon the altar. Nothing is held back; nothing is eaten by priest or worshipper. It goes up entirely to God in smoke.

Gordon Wenham observes that the burnt offering is fundamentally an offering of total self-dedication. The worshipper is saying, in the language of fire, "All that I am I give to you." The key gesture is in verse 4: the worshipper lays his hand upon the head of the animal. This is the language of identification and substitution. As the hand presses down, the worshipper's guilt is symbolically transferred; what happens to the animal happens, by representation, to the man. The innocent dies in place of the guilty.

Sinclair Ferguson reminds us that the phrase "a pleasing aroma to the LORD" is not crude anthropomorphism but covenant language: the sacrifice is acceptable, it satisfies, it brings delight to the heart of God. And here the gospel breaks through, for Paul takes this very phrase and applies it to Christ: "Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2).

The burnt offering is Christ our whole burnt offering — the one who held nothing back, who gave himself entirely to the Father on our behalf, who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7). Where our consecration is always partial, hesitant, hedged with reservations, his was total. He ascended in the flame of the Father's will and rose as the fragrance that makes us, in him, acceptable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-2: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting — and the first word about offerings is a permission: When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD.

Verses 3-9: The burnt offering from the herd: the hand laid on its head so that it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him, the worshipper killing it himself, and the whole of it burned as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

Verses 10-13: The same, from the flock, with the identical result.

Verses 14-17: And from birds — two turtledoves or two young pigeons — again a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Leviticus Is For

Exodus ended with the glory so filling the tabernacle that Moses was not able to enter (Ex. 40:35). Leviticus opens with the problem that creates: God has moved in, and nobody can go near him. This book is not a legal appendix but a sustained answer to one question — how do sinful people live next door to a holy God without being destroyed?

The Hand on the Head

Verse 4 holds the logic of the whole system. A man presses his hand on a living animal and identifies himself with it; the animal is killed and he is not. The verse states what the transaction achieves — accepted for him, atonement for him. The acceptance is transferred.

The Ascending Offering

Olah comes from the verb to go up: all of it goes up in smoke, none eaten by the priest, none returned to the worshipper. It is the only sacrifice entirely consumed — which is why Paul reaches for it at the cross: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2). The whole of it given, nothing held back, and the smell of it acceptable to God.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The worshipper kills the animal himself — then he shall kill the bull before the LORD — and the priests handle the blood afterwards. Nobody in Israel was permitted to be sentimental about what sin costs, because everyone who dealt with it did the killing personally.

Now: Three tiers — bull, sheep, bird — and the same closing sentence every time. Nothing in the outcome is scaled down for the poor man; his offering is not a lesser atonement or a partial acceptance, and Scripture refuses to describe it in weaker terms. With the bird the priest even does the killing, and the small indignities of a small offering are handled discreetly.

Follow that provision to where it ends up. When Mary and Joseph came to present their firstborn they brought a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24) — the offering of the poor, named in this chapter. The mother of the Lord could not afford a lamb. She was carrying him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of livestock from the herd or from the flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exodus ended with the glory filling the tabernacle so completely that Moses was not able to enter (Ex. 40:35). Leviticus opens with the next problem: God has moved in, and nobody can go near him. The LORD called Moses and spoke to him from the tent of meeting.

That is what this book is for. It is not a legal appendix; it is the answer to the question Exodus left hanging — how do sinful people live next door to a holy God without being destroyed? Every sacrifice, every washing, every distinction between clean and unclean is an attempt on that question.

And the first word about the offerings is a permission, not a demand: When any one of you brings an offering to the LORD. The Hebrew is adam, the word for a human being. Not when a priest brings, not when an Israelite brings — when a person brings. The door is opened as wide as the language allows before a single regulation follows.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that he may be accepted before the LORD. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall bring the blood and throw the blood against the sides of the altar that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Then he shall flay the burnt offering and cut it into pieces, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and arrange wood on the fire. And Aaron's sons the priests shall arrange the pieces, the head, and the fat, on the wood that is on the fire on the altar; but its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, as a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The burnt offering is the first described and the most complete. The Hebrew is olah, from the verb to go up — the ascending offering, because all of it goes up in smoke. Nothing is eaten by the priest, nothing is returned to the worshipper. It is the only sacrifice entirely consumed.

Then verse 4, which contains the whole logic of the system in one sentence: He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.

The gesture is not affection and not ownership. A man puts his hand on a living animal, presses down, and identifies himself with it — and then the animal is killed and he is not. The verse says plainly what the transaction achieves: accepted for him, atonement for him. The acceptance is transferred.

And then he kills it himself. Then he shall kill the bull before the LORD. Not the priest — the worshipper. Whoever brought the animal cut its throat and watched it die, and the priests handled the blood afterwards. Nobody in Israel was permitted to be sentimental about what sin costs, because everyone who dealt with it did the killing personally.

The last phrase of verse 9 is the one the New Testament picks up: a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. Paul writes: Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Eph. 5:2). He is calling the cross a burnt offering — the whole of it given, nothing held back, entirely consumed, and the smell of it acceptable to God.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his gift for a burnt offering is from the flock, from the sheep or goats, he shall bring a male without blemish, and he shall kill it on the north side of the altar before the LORD, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. And he shall cut it into pieces, with its head and its fat, and the priest shall arrange them on the wood that is on the fire on the altar, but the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water. And the priest shall offer all of it and burn it on the altar; it is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same procedure is repeated for a sheep or a goat, and the repetition is the point of the chapter's structure. A worshipper who could not afford a bull brought a sheep, and the ritual is described in identical terms, with the identical result — a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

Nothing in the outcome is scaled down. The poorer man's offering is not a lesser atonement or a partial acceptance. It is the same phrase, word for word.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or pigeons. And the priest shall bring it to the altar and wring off its head and burn it on the altar. Its blood shall be drained out on the side of the altar. He shall remove its crop with its contents and cast it beside the altar on the east side, in the place for ashes. He shall tear it open by its wings, but shall not sever it completely. And the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then the third tier: If his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds. Two turtledoves or two young pigeons, which anyone could catch.

Notice what changes with the bird. The priest wrings its neck himself rather than the worshipper killing it, and the crop and its contents are thrown away beside the altar — a detail that is almost tender. A man too poor to bring a lamb is not asked to do the slaughtering, and the small indignities of a small offering are handled discreetly. And the chapter ends on the identical sentence: a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.

Three times, at three prices, and the same acceptance every time. God builds the poor into the system on the first page, and refuses to describe their offering in weaker terms than anyone else's.

Follow that provision to where it ends up. When Mary and Joseph came to the temple to present their firstborn, they brought a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24) — the offering of the poor, named in this chapter. The mother of the Lord could not afford a lamb. She was carrying him.

1.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. The laid-on hand and the slain victim teach that sin is dealt with not by human effort but by a divinely provided substitute. This is the spine of biblical religion and the heart of the cross.

Total consecration. The wholly consumed offering models the surrender Christ rendered to the Father and which the Spirit now works in us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1).

The pleasing aroma. What the burnt offering symbolized, Christ accomplished — he is "a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Eph 5:2), and in him our worship rises acceptably.
1.examples:
Then: An Israelite, conscious of sin, brought a bull from his own herd, pressed his hand upon its head, and watched it die and ascend in flame — a vivid, costly, bloody lesson that approaching God requires a substitute.

Now: We come to God through the once-for-all offering of Christ. The burnt offering calls us to a worship that holds nothing back — to lay our whole selves on the altar, knowing we are already accepted in the Beloved.

2.title: The Grain Offering: The Labor of Our Hands
2.text: <sup>1</sup>"When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it<sup>2</sup>and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>3</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>4</sup>"When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil.<sup>5</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil.<sup>6</sup>You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>7</sup>And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.<sup>8</sup>And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar.<sup>9</sup>And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>10</sup>But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.<sup>11</sup>"No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma.<sup>13</sup>You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.<sup>14</sup>"If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain.<sup>15</sup>And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
2.overview:
After the bloody burnt offering comes the bloodless grain offering, the minchah — a gift, a tribute. Where the burnt offering speaks of atonement, the grain offering speaks of consecrated labor. Grain does not grow wild and ready; it is the product of plowing, sowing, reaping, threshing, grinding. To bring fine flour is to bring the fruit of one's toil, the offering of one's working life laid upon the altar of God.

Wenham notes that the grain offering often accompanied the burnt offering, so that the dedication of the self (the burnt offering) was joined to the dedication of the self's labor (the grain offering). The God who redeems us claims not only our souls but our Mondays — our work, our wages, our ordinary industry.

Three details preach. No leaven, for leaven, the fermenting agent of corruption, is throughout Scripture a symbol of sin (1 Cor 5:8). No honey, for the sweetness of the world's natural fermentation has no place on God's altar. But salt — "the salt of the covenant" — must season every offering, for salt preserves, salt does not corrupt, salt seals a covenant as an enduring bond.

And here is Christ, the true bread offered to the Father. He is the grain of wheat that fell into the ground and died (John 12:24); he is the bread of life (John 6:35); his was the only human life ever lived wholly without the leaven of sin, seasoned through and through with the salt of unbreakable covenant faithfulness. The grain offering, ground fine and passed through fire, whispers of the One whose perfect life of labor and obedience was offered up, a pleasing aroma, for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-3: The grain offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense; a memorial portion burned and the rest given to the priests.

Verses 4-10: Three ways of preparing it — oven, griddle or pan — each with the same result.

Verses 11-13: No leaven and no honey; but you shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing.

Verses 14-16: The offering of firstfruits, roasted and crushed.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Offering With No Blood in It

Minchah is a word used elsewhere for a gift brought to a superior, and what is brought is not an animal but the product of work — grain sown, watched, harvested, threshed and ground by somebody's hands. And since the remainder feeds the priests, Israel's worship and Israel's ministers are funded by the same act.

Leaven and Honey, Salt and Covenant

Both banned substances share one property: they ferment. Leaven works through dough by corruption and honey ferments as it warms, so nothing that spreads by souring goes on the altar — the sense the New Testament gives it exactly (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

Salt does the opposite. It preserves, and in the ancient Near East a covenant sealed with a shared meal of salt was a bond that did not spoil. Every offering in Israel carried a pinch of the thing that stops decay. Jesus handed the image to his disciples — You are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13), Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another (Mark 9:50) — and Paul told the Colossians to let their speech be seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6). What was sprinkled on every sacrifice is now said of the people bringing them.

Firstfruits

To give away the first of the crop is to act on the belief that the rest is coming, and coming from God — the offering of a man not yet certain of his year. Paul uses the word for the resurrection: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). One sheaf brought in early is the guarantee of a whole field behind it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Oven, griddle or pan — the offering fits the household. A woman with an oven brings loaves, a family with only a griddle brings wafers.

Now: God specifies the flour and the oil and leaves the kitchen arrangements to whoever is doing the cooking. Not everything in worship is regulated, and the parts that are not are not thereby unimportant.

verseByVerse.quote: "When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it and bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. And he shall take from it a handful of the fine flour and oil, with all of its frankincense, and the priest shall burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second offering has no blood in it at all. When anyone brings a grain offering as an offering to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it.

The Hebrew is minchah, a word used elsewhere for a gift brought to a superior. And what is brought is not a living animal but the product of work — grain that was sown, watched, harvested, threshed and ground into fine flour by somebody's hands. A man who brought this was handing over a portion of his own labour.

The priest burns a memorial portion and the rest belongs to Aaron and his sons. So the grain offering is also how the priesthood eats. Israel's worship and Israel's ministers are funded by the same act.

verseByVerse.quote: "When you bring a grain offering baked in the oven as an offering, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil or unleavened wafers smeared with oil. And if your offering is a grain offering baked on a griddle, it shall be of fine flour unleavened, mixed with oil. You shall break it in pieces and pour oil on it; it is a grain offering. And if your offering is a grain offering cooked in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil. And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of these things to the LORD, and when it is presented to the priest, he shall bring it to the altar. And the priest shall take from the grain offering its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD. But the rest of the grain offering shall be for Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three ways of preparing it are given — baked in an oven, cooked on a griddle, or made in a pan — and the point of listing them is that the offering fits the household. A woman with an oven brings loaves; a family with only a griddle brings wafers. God specifies the flour and the oil and leaves the kitchen arrangements to whoever is cooking.

In every case a memorial portion goes up in smoke and the remainder is a most holy part of the LORD's food offerings for the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: "No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD. As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not be offered on the altar for a pleasing aroma. You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then two prohibitions and one requirement, and they are the heart of the chapter.

No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall burn no leaven nor any honey as a food offering to the LORD.

Both banned substances have the same property: they ferment. Leaven works through dough by corruption, and honey ferments as it warms. Nothing that spreads by souring may go on the altar — which is exactly the sense the New Testament gives it: a little leaven leavens the whole lump, so cleanse out the old leaven and keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

And then the requirement: You shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing from your grain offering; with all your offerings you shall offer salt.

Salt does the opposite of leaven. It preserves rather than corrupts, and in the ancient Near East a covenant sealed with a shared meal of salt was a bond that did not spoil. So every offering in Israel carried a pinch of the thing that stops decay, and God calls it the salt of the covenant.

Jesus took the same image and handed it to his disciples: You are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13), and Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another (Mark 9:50). Paul told the Colossians to let their speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col. 4:6). What was sprinkled on every sacrifice is now said of the people who bring them.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you offer a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall offer for the grain offering of your firstfruits fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain. And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it; it is a grain offering. And the priest shall burn as its memorial portion some of the crushed grain and some of the oil with all of its frankincense; it is a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with the offering of firstfruits — fresh ears, roasted with fire, crushed new grain — with oil and frankincense, and the same memorial portion burned.

Firstfruits are the first of the crop to ripen, brought before the rest of the harvest is in. To give them away is to act on the belief that the remainder is coming, and that it is coming from God. It is the offering of a man who is not yet certain of his year and gives anyway.

Paul uses the word for the resurrection: Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor. 15:20). One sheaf brought in early is the guarantee of a whole field standing behind it.

2.theology:
Consecrated work. The fruit of human labor, offered to God, becomes worship. There is no merely secular work for the believer; all is dedicated to the Lord.

The exclusion of corruption. No leaven, no honey — holiness admits no fermenting agent of sin. Christ alone was utterly unleavened, the sinless bread offered to God.

The covenant of salt. The enduring, incorruptible faithfulness of God's covenant, kept perfectly by Christ and reflected in a people called to be salt.
2.examples:
Then: The Israelite farmer brought the ground fruit of his fields, seasoned with salt, free of leaven — dedicating the produce of his labor to the God who gave the increase.

Now: We offer our work, our wages, our ordinary toil to God as worship. And we look to Christ, the true bread, the grain of wheat that died to bring forth much fruit.

3.title: The Peace Offering: Communion Restored
3.text: <sup>1</sup>"If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails,<sup>4</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>"If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish.<sup>7</sup>If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD,<sup>8</sup>lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>9</sup>Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>10</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>11</sup>And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD<sup>13</sup>and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>14</sup>Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>15</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>16</sup>And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's.<sup>17</sup>It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
3.overview:
The peace offering, the shelamim — from the great word shalom — is the offering of fellowship, of communion, of restored relationship. It is unique among the sacrifices in that the worshipper eats it. After God receives the fat and the priests their portion, the offerer and his household sit down to a sacred meal in the presence of God. This is the only sacrifice that ends in a feast.

Wenham points out that the peace offering celebrates the reconciliation that the other offerings make possible. The burnt offering atones; the peace offering rejoices. Here is the goal of all sacrifice: not merely the removal of guilt but the restoration of communion, table-fellowship with the living God. Sin had banished man from God's presence; the peace offering brings him back to the table.

The fat and the blood belong to God alone — the fat as the richest portion, the choicest part reserved for him, and the blood because it is the life, sacred and not to be consumed. The worshipper learns that even in joyful fellowship, God is God; the best is his.

And Christ is our peace (Eph 2:14). "Since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom 5:1). The peace offering anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled people of God sit down to eat in his presence, sharing in the body and blood of the one whose sacrifice made peace "by the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). Every Communion is a peace-offering feast — the celebration meal of those brought home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The peace offering from the herd, shared three ways — part to God on the altar, part to the priests, part eaten by the worshipper.

Verses 6-11: The same from the flock, with the fat and the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone specified for God.

Verses 12-17: A goat may be brought; and two permanent statutes — all fat is the LORD's, and you eat neither fat nor blood.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Only Sacrifice the Worshipper Eats

Shelamim is built on the root shalom. The burnt offering was entirely consumed and the grain offering fed the priests; this one is shared, and the family sits down to its portion in the sanctuary, in God's presence, eating what was offered. Nothing about it is solemn in the way a sin offering is solemn. It is dinner — and it is not brought to fix anything. No guilt is named and no wrong is being put right. The peace offering is what you bring when things are well.

Peace Is Something to Be Eaten

A shared meal in God's presence with no guilt on the table is what Israel had a category for and rarely enough confidence to enjoy. Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1); for he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14). And the last picture Scripture gives of it is not an altar but a supper table, with a door being knocked on: if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev. 3:20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a fat-tailed desert sheep the tail is the choicest part — the store of energy, the piece anyone would want. It is specified for God by name.

Now: The rule about fat guards against a very natural drift: a man carving up his own peace offering, deciding the best portion is wasted in smoke, and keeping it. When worship starts being managed rather than offered, the first thing to go is the best part.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offering, if he offers an animal from the herd, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the LORD. And he shall lay his hand on the head of his offering and kill it at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and Aaron's sons the priests shall throw the blood against the sides of the altar. And from the sacrifice of the peace offering, as a food offering to the LORD, he shall offer the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. Then Aaron's sons shall burn it on the altar on top of the burnt offering, which is on the wood on the fire; it is a food offering with a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third offering is the shelamim, built on the root shalom — the peace offering, and it is unlike the two before it in one decisive respect.

The burnt offering was entirely consumed. The grain offering fed the priests. This one is shared three ways: part goes up to God on the altar, part belongs to the priests, and part is eaten by the worshipper and his family. It is the only sacrifice in Leviticus that the person who brought it gets to eat.

So this is a meal with God. A man brings an animal, God receives his portion in smoke, the priest takes his, and the family sits down to the rest — in the sanctuary, in God's presence, eating what was offered. Nothing about it is solemn in the way the sin offering is solemn. It is dinner.

And it is not brought to fix anything. There is no guilt named here and no wrong being put right. The peace offering is what you bring when things are well.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering for a sacrifice of peace offering to the LORD is an animal from the flock, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish. If he offers a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the LORD, lay his hand on the head of his offering, and kill it in front of the tent of meeting; and Aaron's sons shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then from the sacrifice of the peace offering he shall offer as a food offering to the LORD its fat; he shall remove the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn it on the altar as a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same procedure follows for a lamb, and the description of what goes to God is oddly precise: the fat covering the entrails, the two kidneys, the long lobe of the liver, and in the case of a lamb the whole fat tail, cut off close to the backbone.

In a fat-tailed desert sheep that tail is the choicest part of the animal — the store of energy, the piece anyone would want. It is specified for God by name.

The phrase that closes the paragraph makes the point: food offering to the LORD. Scripture elsewhere is emphatic that God does not eat — if I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine (Ps. 50:12). The language is deliberately domestic, describing a shared table rather than a transaction, and the best cut is put in front of the host.

verseByVerse.quote: "If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the LORD and lay his hand on its head and kill it in front of the tent of meeting, and the sons of Aaron shall throw its blood against the sides of the altar. Then he shall offer from it, as his offering for a food offering to the LORD, the fat covering the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. And the priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering with a pleasing aroma. All fat is the LORD's. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with two permanent restrictions, and both will matter enormously later.

All fat is the LORD's. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood.

The fat is God's because it is the best, and the rule guards against a very natural drift — a man carving up his own peace offering, deciding the choice portion is wasted in smoke, and keeping it. The first thing to go, when worship starts to be managed rather than offered, is the best part.

The blood is God's for a different reason, and Leviticus will give it in full at 17:11: the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood that makes atonement by the life. Blood is not food because blood is life, and life belongs to the one who gave it.

Hold the two halves of this offering together, because the New Testament does. A shared meal in God's presence, eaten in peace, with no guilt on the table — that is what Israel had a category for and almost never enough confidence to enjoy. Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. 5:1). For he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).

Peace with God was always a thing to be sat down to and eaten, not merely believed. And the last picture Scripture gives of it is not an altar but a supper table, with a door being knocked on and a voice saying if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me (Rev. 3:20).

3.theology:
Peace with God. The reconciliation accomplished by atonement issues in restored fellowship — the very heart of shalom, fulfilled in Christ "who is our peace" (Eph 2:14).

The fellowship meal. The shared meal anticipates the Lord's Table, where the reconciled feast in God's presence on the body and blood of Christ.

God's claim on the best. The fat belongs to the LORD — God receives the choicest portion, not the leftovers.
3.examples:
Then: An Israelite family, reconciled to God, sat down to a joyful sacred meal in his courts, the fat ascending to God, the meat shared in fellowship and thanksgiving.

Now: At the Lord's Table we celebrate the peace Christ made by his blood. The peace offering teaches us that the gospel's goal is not mere pardon but feasting fellowship with our God.

4.title: The Sin Offering: Even Unintended Sin
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them,<sup>3</sup>if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering.<sup>4</sup>He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting,<sup>6</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>8</sup>And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails<sup>9</sup>and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys<sup>10</sup>(just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering.<sup>11</sup>But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung—<sup>12</sup>all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.<sup>13</sup>"If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt,<sup>14</sup>when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting.<sup>15</sup>And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting,<sup>17</sup>and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil.<sup>18</sup>And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>19</sup>And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar.<sup>20</sup>Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.<sup>21</sup>And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.<sup>22</sup>"When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>23</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish,<sup>24</sup>and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering.<sup>25</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering.<sup>26</sup>And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>27</sup>"If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt,<sup>28</sup>or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed.<sup>29</sup>And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering.<sup>30</sup>And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>31</sup>And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>32</sup>"If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish<sup>33</sup>and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.<sup>34</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar.<sup>35</sup>And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
4.overview:
Now the tone deepens. The burnt, grain, and peace offerings were largely voluntary expressions of devotion. The sin offering, the chatta't, is mandatory — it deals with the dreadful fact of guilt. And its first and most arresting lesson is this: it is provided for sins committed unintentionally. Sins we never noticed, never meant, never even knew we were committing — these too defile, these too require blood.

Sproul drove this home with terrifying clarity: we so easily measure sin by our intentions, but God measures it by his holiness. The sin offering teaches that guilt is not chiefly a matter of malice but of contamination. Even the sin we stumble into unawares pollutes the sanctuary and bars us from God. If unintentional sin is this serious, what shall we say of the high-handed, deliberate rebellions of our hearts?

The chapter is structured by a striking gradation of rank. The anointed priest, the whole congregation, the leader, the common person — each requires an offering, and the higher the office, the costlier the sacrifice. The priest and the congregation require a bull; the leader a male goat; the common person a female goat or lamb. Leadership carries greater accountability before God.

And here Christ bears the sins of the whole people. He is the sin offering — "For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Cor 5:21). The blood of the sin offering was taken into the Holy Place; Christ entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, bearing not the unintentional sins of one man but the mountainous, deliberate sins of a countless multitude. "They shall be forgiven" — the most beautiful refrain in the chapter — is purchased for us at infinite cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The Sin Offering: When the Anointed Priest Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: The sin offering for unintentional sin, beginning with the anointed priest — a bull, blood sprinkled seven times before the veil and put on the horns of the incense altar, the carcass burned outside the camp.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why Unintentional Sin Needs Atoning

Shegagah is sin committed in error, by straying, without meaning to — and it raises the obvious question. Guilt in Scripture is not measured by the offender's awareness of it: a man who unknowingly breaks a law has still broken it, and the damage is done whether or not he intended it. Leviticus assumes what every honest person eventually discovers, that we are not reliable judges of our own record and that I did not realise is an explanation rather than an acquittal. David prayed from the same conviction — Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12).

Outside the Camp

Hebrews reaches for verse 12: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The priest's offering is a bull, the most expensive animal in the list, with the most elaborate blood ritual in the chapter.

Now: The same bull is required for the sin of the entire congregation. A priest's private failure is costed at exactly the same rate as a national one — thus bringing guilt on the people. Leadership is weighted, and Scripture prices it accordingly.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done, and does any one of them, if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people, then he shall offer for the sin that he has committed a bull from the herd without blemish to the LORD for a sin offering. He shall bring the bull to the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD and lay his hand on the head of the bull and kill the bull before the LORD. And the anointed priest shall take some of the blood of the bull and bring it into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle part of the blood seven times before the LORD in front of the veil of the sanctuary. And the priest shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before the LORD that is in the tent of meeting, and all the rest of the blood of the bull he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all the fat of the bull of the sin offering he shall remove from it, the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is on the entrails and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys (just as these are taken from the ox of the sacrifice of the peace offerings); and the priest shall burn them on the altar of burnt offering. But the skin of the bull and all its flesh, with its head, its legs, its entrails, and its dung— all the rest of the bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, to the ash heap, and shall burn it up on a fire of wood. On the ash heap it shall be burned up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth offering deals with something the first three did not: guilt that needs removing rather than devotion that needs expressing. And the opening words define its scope carefully — If anyone sins unintentionally in any of the LORD's commandments about things not to be done.

The Hebrew is shegagah: sin committed in error, by straying, without meaning to. That is the entire subject of this chapter, and it raises the question a modern reader asks immediately. Why would you need atonement for something you did not know you were doing?

Because guilt in Scripture is not measured by the offender's awareness of it. A man who unknowingly breaks a law has still broken it, and the damage is done whether or not he intended it. Leviticus assumes what every honest person eventually discovers: that we are not reliable judges of our own record, and that I did not realise is an explanation rather than an acquittal. David prayed out of the same conviction — Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults (Ps. 19:12).

The first case is the priest, and the offering required is a bull — the most expensive animal in the list. His blood ritual is also the most elaborate: sprinkled seven times before the veil, put on the horns of the altar of incense inside the tent, and poured out at the base of the bronze altar.

The reason is given in the text: if it is the anointed priest who sins, thus bringing guilt on the people. His sin does not stay with him. And the same bull is required in the next paragraph for the sin of the entire congregation — so a priest's private failure is costed at exactly the same rate as a national one. Leadership is weighted, and Scripture prices it accordingly.

Then verse 12: the rest of the bull — hide, flesh, head, entrails, dung — is carried outside the camp to a clean place and burned. It is the detail Hebrews reaches for: the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:11-12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — When the Whole Congregation Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: When the whole congregation sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, the elders lay hands on a bull on the people's behalf.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guilt Nobody Has Noticed

A nation can be guilty of something none of its members has individually observed. That is the assumption here, and it is not comfortable — corporate sin, hidden from the assembly, real enough to require the most expensive sacrifice in the system.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The elders lay their hands on the bull on behalf of everybody. One animal, a few hands, a whole people covered.

Now: The mechanism depends on discovery — when the sin which they have committed becomes known. Until it is recognised there is no offering, so the whole arrangement depends on a community willing to have its blind spots pointed out.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly, and they do any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and they realize their guilt, when the sin which they have committed becomes known, the assembly shall offer a bull from the herd for a sin offering and bring it in front of the tent of meeting. And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands on the head of the bull before the LORD, and the bull shall be killed before the LORD. Then the anointed priest shall bring some of the blood of the bull into the tent of meeting, and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle it seven times before the LORD in front of the veil. And he shall put some of the blood on the horns of the altar that is in the tent of meeting before the LORD, and the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of burnt offering that is at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And all its fat he shall take from it and burn on the altar. Thus shall he do with the bull. As he did with the bull of the sin offering, so shall he do with this. And the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven. And he shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it up as he burned the first bull; it is the sin offering for the assembly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the whole congregation of Israel sins unintentionally and the thing is hidden from the eyes of the assembly.

A nation can be guilty of something none of its members has individually noticed. That is the assumption behind this paragraph, and it is not a comfortable one — corporate sin, hidden from the assembly, real enough to require the most expensive sacrifice in the system.

And the mechanism for dealing with it depends on discovery: when the sin which they have committed becomes known. Until it is recognised there is no offering, which means the health of the whole arrangement depends on a community willing to have its blind spots pointed out.

The elders lay their hands on the bull's head on behalf of everybody. Representation runs right through this book. One animal, a few hands, a whole people covered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — When a Leader or a Common Person Sins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-35: A leader brings a male goat, a common person a female goat or a lamb — each paragraph closing and the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness Stated as Fact

Not he may hope to be forgiven and not he shall feel forgiven. It is announced as accomplished, to a man who did not know he had done anything wrong until somebody told him. And then Hebrews looks at this chapter and observes that the mechanism had to keep running, year after year, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb. 10:4). The forgiveness announced here was real, and it was underwritten by a payment not yet made.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The offering shrinks with the rank of the offender — the reverse of how most societies price wrongdoing, where the powerful make things go away more cheaply than the poor.

Now: One small change of wording is worth catching. For the priest and the congregation the text says if he sins. For the leader it says when. Scripture does not entertain the possibility that a man in authority will get through his term without needing this.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a leader sins, doing unintentionally any one of all the things that by the commandments of the LORD his God ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring as his offering a goat, a male without blemish, and shall lay his hand on the head of the goat and kill it in the place where they kill the burnt offering before the LORD; it is a sin offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out the rest of its blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering. And all its fat he shall burn on the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of peace offerings. So the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone of the common people sins unintentionally in doing any one of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, and realizes his guilt, or the sin which he has committed is made known to him, he shall bring for his offering a goat, a female without blemish, for his sin which he has committed. And he shall lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill the sin offering in the place of burnt offering. And the priest shall take some of its blood with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove, as the fat is removed from the peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven. "If he brings a lamb as his offering for a sin offering, he shall bring a female without blemish and lay his hand on the head of the sin offering and kill it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and put it on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour out all the rest of its blood at the base of the altar. And all its fat he shall remove as the fat of the lamb is removed from the sacrifice of peace offerings, and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on top of the LORD's food offerings. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last two cases scale downward. A leader brings a male goat; a common person brings a female goat or a lamb. The offering shrinks with the rank of the offender — which is the reverse of how most societies price wrongdoing, where the powerful are able to make things go away more cheaply than the poor.

There is one small difference in wording worth catching. For the priest and the congregation the text says if he sins. For the leader it says when a leader sins. Scripture does not entertain the possibility that a man in authority will get through his term without needing this.

And each paragraph ends with the same formula, four times in the chapter: and the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be forgiven.

Not he may hope to be forgiven, and not he shall feel forgiven. It is stated as an accomplished fact, and it is stated to a man who did not know he had done anything wrong until somebody told him. Israel is given a mechanism by which discovered guilt can be dealt with completely — and then Hebrews looks at the same chapter and observes that the mechanism had to keep running, year after year, because it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins (Heb. 10:4). The forgiveness announced here was real, and it was underwritten by a payment that had not yet been made.

4.theology:
The gravity of unintentional sin. Sin defiles whether or not we intend it; guilt is measured by God's holiness, not our awareness. This shatters self-righteousness.

Graded accountability. The higher the office, the costlier the offering — leadership carries greater responsibility before God (cf. James 3:1).

'They shall be forgiven.' The refrain of grace. Christ the sin offering secures the forgiveness the bulls and goats could only foreshadow (2 Cor 5:21; Heb 10:4).
4.examples:
Then: An Israelite, suddenly conscious of a sin he had committed unawares, brought a goat, laid his hand on its head, and heard the priest pronounce him forgiven.

Now: We are guiltier than we know — but in Christ, more loved than we dared hope. The sin offering drives us to the cross, where the deepest, most hidden guilt is fully and finally covered.

5.title: The Guilt Offering: Forgiveness and Restoration
5.text: <sup>1</sup>"If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity;<sup>2</sup>or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt;<sup>3</sup>or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt;<sup>4</sup>or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these;<sup>5</sup>when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed,<sup>6</sup>he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.<sup>7</sup>"But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering.<sup>8</sup>He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely,<sup>9</sup>and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering.<sup>10</sup>Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>11</sup>"But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering.<sup>12</sup>And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering.<sup>13</sup>Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."<sup>14</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>15</sup>"If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering.<sup>16</sup>He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>17</sup>"If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity.<sup>18</sup>He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven.<sup>19</sup>It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
5.overview:
The guilt offering, the 'asham (also called the reparation offering), overlaps with the sin offering but adds a vital dimension: restitution. Where a sin has caused measurable loss — a debt to God's holy things or a fraud against a neighbor — the guilty party must not only bring a sacrifice but make full restitution, adding a fifth. Forgiveness does not float free of repair. Grace does not excuse us from making things right; it empowers us to.

This is the offering that demands confession (5:5) — the open naming of sin before God. And it is the offering that joins atonement to amendment, the altar to the ledger. The reconciled sinner returns the stolen, repays the defrauded, and adds twenty percent on top. Zacchaeus, climbing down from his tree to give back fourfold (Luke 19:8), is a son of the guilt offering, transformed by grace into a maker of restitution.

Wenham observes the moral seriousness here: God cares not only that we feel forgiven but that the web of relationships torn by our sin be rewoven. The guilt offering refuses cheap grace.

And Christ is the One who not only forgives but restores. Isaiah 53:10 says, "when his soul makes an offering for guilt" — the suffering Servant is himself the 'asham. He pays not only the principal of our debt but the added fifth and infinitely more, restoring to God a glory greater than Adam lost, and restoring to us a sonship richer than Eden. He gives back what he never took away (Ps 69:4). The guilt offering points to a Savior who does not merely cancel our debt but rebuilds what sin demolished.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Sin Offering Scaled to the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-6: Three cases — a witness who stays silent under public adjuration, unnoticed contact with uncleanness, and a rash oath — each resolved when he realizes his guilt.

Verses 7-13: The offering scaled to poverty: a lamb, or two birds, or a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering, and he shall be forgiven.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Sin Offering of Flour

In a book that will shortly say without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, there is a provision for the destitute to be forgiven by bringing a bag of flour — and the text insists on calling it a sin offering and closes with the same formula as every other case.

Two details keep it honest. The flour comes without oil or frankincense, unlike the grain offering of chapter 2 — nothing celebratory, because this is a substitute rather than a gift. And the priest burns it on the LORD's food offerings, on top of the blood sacrifices already burning. The poor man's flour goes into a fire that blood has already lit. His forgiveness is not bloodless; it is borrowed.

Which is the position of everyone who has ever been forgiven. Nobody's atonement is self-funded, and the destitute Israelite carrying flour to the altar is the plainest picture in Leviticus of being saved by a payment somebody else made.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The first case is not an action. A man knows something, is publicly asked, and says nothing — no lie told, simply silence while an injustice proceeds. Leviticus files that under sin requiring blood, and the guilt is the witness's own.

Now: All three cases end in the same place: when he realizes his guilt. The trigger is recognition. Israel's remedy begins the moment a man admits he has a problem, and not before.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity; or if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether a carcass of an unclean wild animal or a carcass of unclean livestock or a carcass of unclean swarming things, and it is hidden from him and he has become unclean, and he realizes his guilt; or if he touches human uncleanness, of whatever sort the uncleanness may be with which one becomes unclean, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and realizes his guilt; or if anyone utters with his lips a rash oath to do evil or to do good, any sort of rash oath that people swear, and it is hidden from him, when he comes to know it, and he realizes his guilt in any of these; when he realizes his guilt in any of these and confesses the sin he has committed, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed, a female from the flock, a lamb or a goat, for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter opens with three specific cases, and the first is not an action at all.

If anyone sins in that he hears a public adjuration to testify, and though he is a witness, whether he has seen or come to know the matter, yet does not speak, he shall bear his iniquity.

A man who knows something, is publicly asked, and says nothing. No lie is told; he simply keeps quiet while an injustice proceeds. Leviticus files that under sin requiring blood. Silence in a courtroom is treated as an act, and the guilt is the witness's own — he shall bear his iniquity.

The second case is touching something unclean without noticing. The third is a rash oath — swearing to do something whatever it is that people rashly swear, and forgetting it. Words spoken carelessly are still words spoken.

All three end in the same place: when he realizes his guilt, he confesses and brings his offering. The trigger is recognition. Israel's remedy for sin begins the moment a man admits he has a problem, and not before.

verseByVerse.quote: "But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer first the one for the sin offering. He shall wring its head from its neck but shall not sever it completely, and he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar, while the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar; it is a sin offering. Then he shall offer the second for a burnt offering according to the rule. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin that he has committed, and he shall be forgiven. "But if he cannot afford two turtledoves or two pigeons, then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil on it and shall put no frankincense on it, for it is a sin offering. And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take a handful of it as its memorial portion and burn this on the altar, on the LORD's food offerings; it is a sin offering. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin which he has committed in any one of these things, and he shall be forgiven. And the remainder shall be for the priest, as in the grain offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the provision that makes this chapter remarkable. But if he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation for the sin that he has committed two turtledoves or two pigeons.

And if he cannot manage even birds: then he shall bring as his offering for the sin that he has committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering.

Read that again. A sin offering of flour. In a book that will shortly state that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, there is a provision for the destitute to be forgiven by bringing a bag of flour, and the text insists on calling it what it is — it is a sin offering — and closes with the same formula as every other case: and he shall be forgiven.

Two details keep it honest. The flour is brought without oil or frankincense, unlike the grain offering of chapter 2 — nothing celebratory about it, because this is not a gift but a substitute. And the priest burns it on the LORD's food offerings, on top of the blood sacrifices already burning there. The poor man's flour goes into a fire that blood has already lit. His forgiveness is not bloodless; it is borrowed.

Which is exactly the position of everyone who has ever been forgiven. Nobody's atonement is self-funded. The destitute Israelite carrying a bag of flour to the altar is the plainest picture in Leviticus of what it is to be saved by a payment somebody else made.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-19: The guilt offering for a breach of faith, requiring restitution and shall add a fifth to it — including for a man who acted though he did not know it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Repentance With an Arithmetic

The wrong is repaid in full, plus twenty per cent, and only then is the sacrifice offered. Israel could not use worship as a substitute for putting something right.

He Did Not Know, and He Is Guilty

Both are stated in the same breath and neither cancels the other. That is why the sacrificial system exists — not to make people feel proportionate to their offence, but to deal with what is actually true about them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asham covers not merely sin but damage — something owed as well as something confessed.

Now: The restitution comes first and the sacrifice second. That order is not incidental.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone commits a breach of faith and sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the LORD, he shall bring to the LORD as his compensation, a ram without blemish out of the flock, valued in silver shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, for a guilt offering. He shall also make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering, and he shall be forgiven. "If anyone sins, doing any of the things that by the LORD's commandments ought not to be done, though he did not know it, then realizes his guilt, he shall bear his iniquity. He shall bring to the priest a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him for the mistake that he made unintentionally, and he shall be forgiven. It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guilt offering — asham — deals with a different category: not merely sin but damage. It is required for a breach of faith in the holy things, and it carries a distinctive feature. Alongside the ram, the offender must make restitution for what he has done amiss in the holy thing and shall add a fifth to it.

Repentance here has an arithmetic. The wrong is repaid in full, plus twenty per cent, and only then is the sacrifice offered. Israel could not use worship as a substitute for putting something right.
