The chapter closes with a case that stretches the principle to its limit: an offering required for a man who has done something forbidden though he did not know it, and he shall bear his iniquity. It is a guilt offering; he has indeed incurred guilt before the LORD.

He did not know. He is guilty. Both are stated in the same breath and neither cancels the other, which is why the sacrificial system exists — not to make people feel proportionate to their offence, but to deal with what is actually true about them.

5.theology:
Confession. Sin must be named openly before God. The guilt offering enshrines confession as the gateway to forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

Restitution. Grace does not bypass repair; it empowers it. The forgiven make things right, even adding a fifth — repentance overpays.

Christ our restorer. The suffering Servant is himself the guilt offering (Isa 53:10), who does not merely forgive but restores, giving back what he never took away (Ps 69:4).
5.examples:
Then: An Israelite who had defrauded another or robbed God's holy things confessed, repaid the loss with a fifth added, and brought a ram — his repentance bearing fruit in restored relationships.

Now: Real repentance still makes restitution. And we rest in Christ, the guilt offering who not only cancels our debt but rebuilds everything sin destroyed.

6.title: Laws for the Priests: The Fire That Never Goes Out
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor<sup>3</sup>or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby—<sup>4</sup>if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found<sup>5</sup>or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt.<sup>6</sup>And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering.<sup>7</sup>And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."<sup>8</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it.<sup>10</sup>And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar.<sup>11</sup>Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.<sup>12</sup>The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings.<sup>13</sup>Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.<sup>14</sup>"And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar.<sup>15</sup>And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it.<sup>17</sup>It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering.<sup>18</sup>Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy."<sup>19</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>20</sup>"This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening.<sup>21</sup>It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.<sup>22</sup>The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned.<sup>23</sup>Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."<sup>24</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>25</sup>"Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy.<sup>26</sup>The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting.<sup>27</sup>Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place.<sup>28</sup>And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water.<sup>29</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy.<sup>30</sup>But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
6.overview:
Chapters 6 and 7 turn from the worshipper's instructions to the priests' instructions — the administrative regulations for handling each offering. This may seem the dustiest corner of Leviticus, yet it glows with quiet glory. The God who is a consuming fire orders his worship down to the disposal of ashes, because nothing about approaching him is trivial.

The towering image of chapter 6 is the perpetual fire: "Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out" (6:13). Twice the command is repeated. The flame that first fell from God himself (9:24) was never to be allowed to die. The priests fed it every morning. It burned through the night. It was the visible sign that atonement was always available, that the door to God never closed, that the fire of his presence and the fire of sacrifice burned on, unceasing.

Begg loves to draw the line to the believer's heart: there is a fire that must never go out, a devotion fed morning by morning, a flame of love for God tended daily lest it gutter into cold ash. "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thess 5:19). The Reformers spoke of the daily mortification of sin and the daily stoking of grace — the morning wood laid on the altar of the heart.

Above all, the perpetual fire foreshadows the perpetual efficacy of Christ's sacrifice. The altar fire never went out because Israel sinned without ceasing and needed atonement without ceasing. But Christ "offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins" (Heb 10:12). The one offering that need never be repeated has made the endless fire unnecessary — yet the devotion it symbolized burns brighter than ever in hearts set aflame by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Restitution for Sins Against a Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: Deceiving, robbing, oppressing a neighbour or lying about something found is a breach of faith against the LORD — remedied by full restitution plus a fifth, on the day he realizes his guilt, and then the guilt offering.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wrongs Against People Are Breaches of Faith Against God

Every offence listed is committed against a person, and the verse calls all of them a breach of faith against the LORD. Cheating a neighbour over a deposit is not a civil matter with a religious dimension; it is an act against God, done to a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order is fixed — the neighbour is paid first, and only then is God approached.

Now: There is no arrangement in Israel by which a person makes peace with heaven while the man he defrauded is still out of pocket. Which is why Zacchaeus started calculating the moment grace reached him (Luke 19:8), and why Jesus told people to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled to a brother first (Matt. 5:23-24).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor or has found something lost and lied about it, swearing falsely—in any of all the things that people do and sin thereby— if he has sinned and has realized his guilt and will restore what he took by robbery or what he got by oppression or the deposit that was committed to him or the lost thing that he found or anything about which he has sworn falsely, he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt. And he shall bring to the priest as his compensation to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flock, or its equivalent, for a guilt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD, and he shall be forgiven for any of the things that one may do and thereby become guilty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone sins and commits a breach of faith against the LORD by deceiving his neighbor in a matter of deposit or security, or through robbery, or if he has oppressed his neighbor or has found something lost and lied about it.

Every offence in that list is committed against a person, and the verse calls all of them a breach of faith against the LORD. Cheating a neighbour over a deposit is not merely a civil matter with a religious dimension; Leviticus treats it as an act against God, done to a man.

The remedy has two halves and the order is fixed. First: he shall restore it in full and shall add a fifth to it, and give it to him to whom it belongs on the day he realizes his guilt. On the day. Not when convenient. And then, second, he brings his guilt offering to the priest.

The man is paid before God is approached. There is no arrangement in Israel by which a person could make peace with heaven while the person he defrauded was still out of pocket — which is why Zacchaeus, the moment grace reached him, started calculating (Luke 19:8), and why Jesus told people to leave the gift at the altar and go and be reconciled to a brother first (Matt. 5:23-24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Fire That Never Goes Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-13: The law of the burnt offering, with one instruction three times over — fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out — and the priest changing his garments to carry the ashes outside the camp.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Fire Nobody Was Allowed to Let Die

It began as fire from God himself, falling from his presence in chapter 9, and Israel's task from then on was to keep it alight. Every night somebody fed it — through every siege, every festival, and every ordinary Tuesday for centuries.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He changes clothes to take out the ashes. The holy garments are for the altar; the ash run is done in working clothes.

Now: Somebody had to shovel out yesterday's fire before today's offering could be made, every morning, in a country that never saw him do it. Most of what keeps worship going has always looked like that.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Command Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the burnt offering. The burnt offering shall be on the hearth on the altar all night until the morning, and the fire of the altar shall be kept burning on it. And the priest shall put on his linen garment and put his linen undergarment on his body, and he shall take up the ashes to which the fire has reduced the burnt offering on the altar and put them beside the altar. Then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it; it shall not go out. The priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and he shall arrange the burnt offering on it and shall burn on it the fat of the peace offerings. Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law of the burnt offering, and one instruction is repeated three times in six verses.

The fire on the altar shall be kept burning on it... Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.

It began as fire from God himself — it will fall from his presence in chapter 9 — and Israel's job from then on is to keep it alight. Every night somebody fed it. Through every siege, every festival, every ordinary Tuesday for centuries, the altar was never allowed to go cold.

And the mechanics of that duty are given with an odd amount of care. The priest puts on linen garments and carries the ashes to the side of the altar; then he shall take off his garments and put on other garments and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. He changes clothes to take out the ashes. The holy garments are for the altar; the ash run is done in working clothes.

Somebody had to shovel out yesterday's fire before today's offering could be made, every morning, in a country that never saw him do it. Most of what keeps worship going has always looked like that.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-23 — The Priests and the Grain Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-23: The priests' portion of the grain offering, eaten unleavened in a holy place; and the high priest's own daily offering, half in the morning and half in the evening, which shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Is Also a Worshipper

The men who live off the offerings of others must bring one that feeds nobody, twice a day, every day of their lives. Nothing about the office exempts a priest from needing what the office provides, and his own sacrifice is the one he gets no dinner out of.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The priests' portion is most holy — so much so that whatever touches them shall become holy.

Now: It is eaten in the court of the tent of meeting, not carried home. Even the priests' meals happened where God was.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the grain offering. The sons of Aaron shall offer it before the LORD in front of the altar. And one shall take from it a handful of the fine flour of the grain offering and its oil and all the frankincense that is on the grain offering and burn this as its memorial portion on the altar, a pleasing aroma to the LORD. And the rest of it Aaron and his sons shall eat. It shall be eaten unleavened in a holy place. In the court of the tent of meeting they shall eat it. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion of my food offerings. It is a thing most holy, like the sin offering and the guilt offering. Every male among the children of Aaron may eat of it, as decreed forever throughout your generations, from the LORD's food offerings. Whatever touches them shall become holy." The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This is the offering that Aaron and his sons shall offer to the LORD on the day when he is anointed: a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a regular grain offering, half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be made with oil on a griddle. You shall bring it well mixed, in baked pieces like a grain offering, and offer it for a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The priest from among Aaron's sons, who is anointed to succeed him, shall offer it to the LORD as decreed forever. The whole of it shall be burned. Every grain offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grain offering is restated from the priests' side. They eat it unleavened in a holy place, in the court of the tent of meeting, and the portion is called most holy — so holy that whatever touches them shall become holy.

Then a striking provision: the priests have their own offering to bring. On the day Aaron is anointed, and every day thereafter, the high priest offers a tenth of an ephah of flour half of it in the morning and half in the evening — and unlike the people's grain offering, it shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten.

The men who live off the offerings of others must bring one that feeds nobody, twice a day, every day of their lives. Nothing about the priesthood exempts a priest from being a worshipper, and his own sacrifice is the one he gets no dinner out of.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 24-30: The law of the sin offering — whoever touches its flesh shall be holy, splashed garments washed, an earthenware vessel broken and a bronze one scoured — and any offering whose blood enters the tent shall not be eaten; it shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Holiness Running the Other Way

Through most of Leviticus contact spreads uncleanness: touch a corpse and you are unclean. Here it reverses — what touches the sin offering is made holy, and the vessel it was cooked in cannot simply be reused, because something has happened to it that will not scrub off.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An earthenware pot is broken; a bronze one is scoured and rinsed.

Now: The offerings that go furthest in are the ones nobody gets to share. Chapter 16 will show why.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying, This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is killed shall the sin offering be killed before the LORD; it is most holy. The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. In a holy place it shall be eaten, in the court of the tent of meeting. Whatever touches its flesh shall be holy, and when any of its blood is splashed on a garment, you shall wash that on which it was splashed in a holy place. And the earthenware vessel in which it is boiled shall be broken. But if it is boiled in a bronze vessel, that shall be scoured and rinsed in water. Every male among the priests may eat of it; it is most holy. But no sin offering shall be eaten from which any blood is brought into the tent of meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place; it shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law of the sin offering, and the emphasis falls on contagion. It is killed in the same place as the burnt offering; the priest eats it in a holy place; anything its blood splashes must be washed; an earthenware vessel it was boiled in must be broken, and a bronze one scoured and rinsed.

Note the direction the holiness travels. Whoever touches its flesh shall be holy. In most of Leviticus contact spreads uncleanness — a person who touches a corpse becomes unclean. Here the sin offering runs the other way: what touches it is made holy, and the vessel it was cooked in cannot simply be reused because something has happened to it that cannot be scrubbed off.

And the chapter ends with the one exception: any sin offering whose blood is brought into the tent shall not be eaten; it shall be burned up with fire. The offerings that go furthest in are the ones nobody gets to share. Chapter 16 will show why.

6.theology:
The perpetual fire. The unceasing altar flame signified the constant availability of atonement and the constant need of a sinful people — a need answered once for all in Christ (Heb 10:12).

Daily devotion. The morning wood on the altar pictures the discipline of tending the heart's fire lest it grow cold. 'Do not quench the Spirit' (1 Thess 5:19).

Provision for ministers. Those who serve at the altar share in the altar; God provides for his servants through the offerings of his people.
6.examples:
Then: Before dawn the priest stirred the embers, laid on fresh wood, and removed the night's ashes — guarding the flame God himself had kindled so that it never died.

Now: We tend the fire of devotion daily by the Word, prayer, and the Spirit. And we rest in the finished sacrifice that ended the need for endless offerings, even as our hearts burn within us (Luke 24:32).

7.title: The Portion of the Priests: Order in Holy Things
7.text: <sup>1</sup>"This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy.<sup>2</sup>In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar.<sup>3</sup>And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails,<sup>4</sup>the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys.<sup>5</sup>The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering.<sup>6</sup>Every male among the priests may eat of it. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations."<sup>37</sup>This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering,<sup>38</sup>which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 completes the priestly handbook, covering the guilt offering, the peace offering, and the assignment of the priests' portions. To modern ears these are dry logistics; to the eye of faith they reveal the beauty of God's ordered worship. "God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Cor 14:33). The meticulous care given to who eats what, when, and how, teaches that the worship of a holy God is never careless or improvised.

The peace offering is here divided into thanksgiving, vow, and freewill varieties (7:12–16), with the thanksgiving offering to be eaten the same day — joy is not to be hoarded but shared while it is fresh. The breast and the right thigh are assigned to the priests as their "wave offering" and "contribution" (7:30–34), God's gracious provision for those who serve.

Twice more the prohibition of blood and fat is pressed (7:22–27). The blood belongs to God because the life is in it; to eat blood is to seize what is sacred to the Lord alone. This single principle — that blood is life and life is God's — will become the explicit theology of chapter 17 and the foundation of all that Hebrews says about the blood of Christ.

The whole chapter exalts the orderliness of grace. Carson reminds us that the God who saves is the God who orders; redemption is not chaos but the careful, costly, beautiful arrangement of holy things. And every portion reserved, every drop of blood withheld, every wave of the priest's hands points to the day when the perfect Priest would offer the perfect sacrifice and assign to his people the choicest portion of all — himself, the bread and the cup of the new covenant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Guilt Offering and the Priests' Portions
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-10: The guilt offering, and the priests' portions — the hide of the burnt offering to the priest who handles it, each cooked grain offering to the one who presents it, the dry ones shared equally.
verseByVerse.theology:
Income Specified in Law

The men who served at the altar had no farmland — Levi received no territory — so their entire living was set out in legislation rather than left to whoever happened to turn up. Paul quotes the arrangement directly: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple?... In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13-14).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: It reads like accountancy.

Now: Which is the point. Provision for those who serve is put beyond negotiation and beyond embarrassment by being written down.

verseByVerse.quote: "This is the law of the guilt offering. It is most holy. In the place where they kill the burnt offering they shall kill the guilt offering, and its blood shall be thrown against the sides of the altar. And all its fat shall be offered, the fat tail, the fat that covers the entrails, the two kidneys with the fat that is on them at the loins, and the long lobe of the liver that he shall remove with the kidneys. The priest shall burn them on the altar as a food offering to the LORD; it is a guilt offering. Every male among the priests may eat of it. It shall be eaten in a holy place. It is most holy. The guilt offering is just like the sin offering; there is one law for them. The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it. And the priest who offers any man's burnt offering shall have for himself the skin of the burnt offering that he has offered. And every grain offering baked in the oven and all that is prepared on a pan or a griddle shall belong to the priest who offers it. And every grain offering, mixed with oil or dry, shall be shared equally among all the sons of Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The guilt offering's blood is thrown against the altar and its fat burned, and the priest who offers it eats it. Then a short paragraph settles who gets what: the priest who makes atonement keeps the hide of the burnt offering he handles, and each baked or fried grain offering belongs to the priest who presents it, while the dry ones are shared equally among Aaron's sons.

It reads like accountancy and it is doing something important. The men who served at the altar had no farmland — Levi received no territory — and their entire income was specified in law rather than left to the generosity of whoever turned up. Paul quotes this arrangement directly when arguing that gospel workers should be supported: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple?... In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Cor. 9:13-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-21 — The Peace Offering: Thanksgiving and Vows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11-21: The peace offering subdivided into thanksgiving, vow and freewill — the thanksgiving offering eaten on the day of his offering, the others allowed a second day — with anyone unclean who eats it cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Gratitude That Cannot Be Stored

A whole animal has to be eaten before nightfall, which is far more meat than one household can manage. So the thanksgiving offering forces a party: neighbours are called in and the reason for the celebration announced, because otherwise the food spoils. Gratitude in Israel could not be conducted privately and could not be kept. It had to be spent at once, in company, on people.

A Closed Table

The meal of fellowship is shut to those not fit for fellowship — the same concern Paul brings to a very different table: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 11:27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Meat left to the third day is burned, and the whole sacrifice is invalidated — it shall not be credited to him.

Now: A freewill offering is brought for no stated reason at all. Israel had a category for worship that is not prompted by anything.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that one may offer to the LORD. If he offers it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the thanksgiving sacrifice unleavened loaves mixed with oil, unleavened wafers smeared with oil, and loaves of fine flour well mixed with oil. With the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving he shall bring his offering with loaves of leavened bread. And from it he shall offer one loaf from each offering, as a gift to the LORD. It shall belong to the priest who throws the blood of the peace offerings. And the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning. But if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow offering or a freewill offering, it shall be eaten on the day that he offers his sacrifice, and on the next day what remains of it shall be eaten. But what remains of the flesh of the sacrifice on the third day shall be burned up with fire. If any of the flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offering is eaten on the third day, he who offers it shall not be accepted, neither shall it be credited to him. It is tainted, and he who eats of it shall bear his iniquity. "Flesh that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten. It shall be burned up with fire. All who are clean may eat flesh, but the person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings while an uncleanness is on him, that person shall be cut off from his people. And if anyone touches an unclean thing, whether human uncleanness or an unclean beast or any unclean detestable creature, and then eats some flesh from the sacrifice of the LORD's peace offerings, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the peace offering is subdivided, and the distinctions are worth having. A thanksgiving offering is brought for something God has done. A vow offering discharges a promise. A freewill offering is brought for no stated reason at all.

And the rule about eating them differs. The thanksgiving offering shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning. A vow or freewill offering may be eaten on the second day as well, but anything left to the third day is burned and the whole sacrifice is invalidated — it shall not be credited to him.

Consider what the one-day rule does to a family. A whole animal has to be eaten before nightfall, which is far more meat than any household can manage. So the thanksgiving offering forces a party: neighbours are called in, and the reason for the celebration is announced, because otherwise the food spoils. Gratitude in Israel could not be conducted privately and could not be stored. It had to be spent immediately, in company, on people.

Then the warnings. Anyone unclean who eats the peace offering shall be cut off from his people — the meal of fellowship is closed to those not fit for fellowship, which is the same concern Paul brings to a very different table: whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord (1 Cor. 11:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-27: No fat and no blood, as permanent statutes — if anyone eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Heaviest Penalty in the Dietary Law

The reason is held back until 17:11, but the severity is already plain. And when the first Christian council decided what to ask of Gentile converts, having released them from circumcision and the food laws, this was one of the four things kept: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood (Acts 15:29).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Both rules are repeated from chapter 3 and restated here as permanent.

Now: Repetition in Leviticus is usually a measure of how easily a thing is let slide.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, You shall eat no fat, of ox or sheep or goat. The fat of an animal that dies of itself and the fat of one that is torn by beasts may be put to any other use, but on no account shall you eat it. For every person who eats of the fat of an animal of which a food offering may be made to the LORD shall be cut off from his people. Moreover, you shall eat no blood whatever, whether of fowl or of animal, in any of your dwelling places. Whoever eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two absolute prohibitions, repeated from chapter 3 and given here as permanent statutes: no fat, and no blood. If anyone eats any blood, that person shall be cut off from his people.

The reason is held back until 17:11, but the severity is already clear. Of all the dietary rules in this book, blood is the one carrying the heaviest penalty — and when the first Christian council had to decide what to ask of Gentile converts, having released them from circumcision and the food laws, this is one of the four things they kept: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood (Acts 15:29).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-38: The wave offering brought with the worshipper's own hands, the breast to the priests and the right thigh to the officiant — and the closing summary of the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Remarkable Provision, and a Provisional One

Israel now has a way to approach God for devotion, for gratitude, for guilt known and unknown, for damage needing repayment, and for ordinary fellowship — scaled from a bull to a bag of flour so nobody is priced out. It is a generous system and it ran for fifteen centuries.

The New Testament's verdict is not that it was primitive but that it was temporary: Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Heb. 10:11-12). The detail carrying the argument is the sitting. There were no chairs in the tabernacle, because the work was never finished.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The worshipper carries the fat and the breast forward himself rather than handing the animal over at the gate.

Now: Seven chapters, five offerings, one system — and the summary names them all, so that nobody could claim a category had been forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, Whoever offers the sacrifice of his peace offerings to the LORD shall bring his offering to the LORD from the sacrifice of his peace offerings. His own hands shall bring the LORD's food offerings. He shall bring the fat with the breast, that the breast may be waved as a wave offering before the LORD. The priest shall burn the fat on the altar, but the breast shall be for Aaron and his sons. And the right thigh you shall give to the priest as a contribution from the sacrifice of your peace offerings. Whoever among the sons of Aaron offers the blood of the peace offerings and the fat shall have the right thigh for a portion. For the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed I have taken from the people of Israel, out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons, as a perpetual due from the people of Israel. This is the portion of Aaron and of his sons from the LORD's food offerings, from the day they were presented to serve as priests of the LORD. The LORD commanded this to be given them by the people of Israel, from the day that he anointed them. It is a perpetual due throughout their generations." This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering, which the LORD commanded Moses on Mount Sinai, on the day that he commanded the people of Israel to bring their offerings to the LORD, in the wilderness of Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with the wave offering: the worshipper brings the fat and the breast with his own hands, the breast is waved before the LORD and given to the priests, and the right thigh goes to the priest who officiated.

Then the summary that closes the whole section on offerings — This is the law of the burnt offering, of the grain offering, of the sin offering, of the guilt offering, of the ordination offering, and of the peace offering. Seven chapters, five offerings, one system.

Stand back from it for a moment before the narrative resumes. Israel now has a way to approach God for devotion, for gratitude, for guilt they knew about and guilt they did not, for damage that needed repaying, and for ordinary fellowship — scaled from a bull to a bag of flour so that nobody was priced out. It is a remarkable provision, and it ran for fifteen centuries.

And the New Testament's verdict on it is not that it was primitive but that it was provisional. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God (Heb. 10:11-12). The detail that carries the argument is the sitting. There were no chairs in the tabernacle, because the work was never finished. He sat down.

7.theology:
The order of worship. God's meticulous regulation of holy things reflects that he is 'not a God of confusion but of peace' (1 Cor 14:33). Redemption is ordered, not chaotic.

The sanctity of blood. The life is in the blood, and the blood belongs to God — the foundation of atonement theology fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ.

The sacrifice of thanksgiving. The todah offering becomes, in Christ, the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15).
7.examples:
Then: The reconciled Israelite shared a thanksgiving feast the same day, the priests received the breast and thigh, and not a drop of blood was consumed — every detail ordered by God.

Now: We offer the sacrifice of praise through Christ, support those who serve God's people, and marvel that the blood once forbidden is now, in Christ, the cup of salvation.

8.title: The Ordination of Aaron: Consecrated by Blood and Oil
8.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread.<sup>3</sup>And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting."<sup>4</sup>And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>5</sup>And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."<sup>6</sup>And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water.<sup>7</sup>And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band.<sup>8</sup>And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim.<sup>9</sup>And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>10</sup>Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them.<sup>11</sup>And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them.<sup>12</sup>And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him.<sup>13</sup>And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>14</sup>Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering.<sup>15</sup>And he killed it, and Moses took the blood, and with his finger put it on the horns of the altar around it and purified the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it.<sup>16</sup>And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar.<sup>17</sup>But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>18</sup>Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>19</sup>And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>20</sup>He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat.<sup>21</sup>He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>22</sup>Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram.<sup>23</sup>And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>24</sup>Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.<sup>25</sup>Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh,<sup>26</sup>and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh.<sup>27</sup>And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>29</sup>And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>30</sup>Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.<sup>31</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.'<sup>32</sup>And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire.<sup>33</sup>And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you.<sup>34</sup>As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you.<sup>35</sup>At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded."<sup>36</sup>And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
8.overview:
From the laws of sacrifice we turn to the consecration of those who will administer them. Chapters 8–10 form the great narrative center of the offering section: the ordination of Aaron and his sons, their first ministry, and the catastrophe that follows. Chapter 8 is the seven-day investiture of the priesthood, carried out by Moses, who here acts as the presiding priest, mediating the very mediators.

The ritual is rich with gospel symbol. Aaron is washed with water (8:6) — the cleansing every minister of God needs. He is clothed in the glorious garments (8:7–9), arrayed not in his own righteousness but in robes provided. He is anointed with oil (8:12), set apart by the Spirit's symbol. And he is marked with blood on the ear, the thumb, and the toe (8:23) — the whole man, hearing, working, walking, consecrated to God by sacrifice.

Wenham notes the sevenfold sprinkling and the seven days of waiting (8:33–35): the number of completeness, the patient setting-apart of those who would draw near to God. Aaron could not appoint himself; he was called, washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. "No one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was" (Heb 5:4).

And all of it anticipates Christ's consecration. At his baptism the sinless Son went down into the water, and the Spirit descended like a dove and the Father spoke — the true Aaron washed and anointed for his priestly work (Matt 3:16–17; Acts 10:38). Yet how the contrast dazzles: Aaron needed blood applied to himself for his own sin; Christ needed no cleansing, but became himself the blood of consecration. He is at once the Priest who is anointed and the sacrifice whose blood consecrates. The ear that perfectly heard the Father, the hands that only did good, the feet that never strayed — wholly consecrated, he ordains us "a kingdom, priests to his God" (Rev 1:6).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: Assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting — the ordination is public.

Verses 6-9: Aaron and his sons are washed, then clothed: coat, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and the Thummim, and the turban with the golden plate, the holy crown.

Verses 10-13: The anointing oil goes on the tabernacle and its furniture first, the altar seven times, and then on Aaron's head.
verseByVerse.theology:
Anointed

The verb is the root behind mashiach, messiah — the anointed one. Priests were anointed, and kings, and prophets, and every one of those anointings was a small advance payment on a title that would finally belong to one man holding all three offices at once.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Exodus tells us what was engraved on the golden plate: Holy to the LORD (Ex. 28:36). Aaron wore those words on his forehead, where everyone could read them and he could not.

Now: A man declared holy by an inscription he was never able to see for himself. And the whole nation is summoned to watch, because a priesthood that installs itself is answerable to nobody — no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was (Heb. 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Take Aaron and his sons with him, and the garments and the anointing oil and the bull of the sin offering and the two rams and the basket of unleavened bread. And assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting." And Moses did as the LORD commanded him, and the congregation was assembled at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And Moses said to the congregation, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded to be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven chapters of instruction end and the narrative starts again. God had given the design for the priesthood back in Exodus 29; now it is carried out, and the first thing the text insists on is the audience: assemble all the congregation at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

The whole nation is called to watch men become priests. Nothing here is done privately. Israel needs to see with its own eyes who has been appointed, by whose authority, and at what cost — because a priesthood that installs itself is answerable to nobody.

The New Testament makes the same point about the same office: no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was (Heb. 5:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water. And he put the coat on him and tied the sash around his waist and clothed him with the robe and put the ephod on him and tied the skillfully woven band of the ephod around him, binding it to him with the band. And he placed the breastpiece on him, and in the breastpiece he put the Urim and the Thummim. And he set the turban on his head, and on the turban, in front, he set the golden plate, the holy crown, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sequence is washing, then clothing. Moses brought Aaron and his sons and washed them with water before a single garment went on. Whatever else ordination is, it begins with a man being cleaned by somebody else.

Then the vestments, layer by layer: the coat, the sash, the robe, the ephod, the breastpiece — and into the breastpiece, the Urim and the Thummim. On his head the turban, and on the front of the turban the golden plate, the holy crown.

Exodus tells us what was engraved on it: Holy to the LORD (Ex. 28:36). Aaron walked around with those words on his forehead, where everyone could read them and he could not. A man was declared holy by an inscription he was never able to see for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses took the anointing oil and anointed the tabernacle and all that was in it, and consecrated them. And he sprinkled some of it on the altar seven times, and anointed the altar and all its utensils and the basin and its stand, to consecrate them. And he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him to consecrate him. And Moses brought Aaron's sons and clothed them with coats and tied sashes around their waists and bound caps on them, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The anointing oil is used before it touches any person. Moses anoints the tabernacle and everything in it, the altar seven times, the basin and its stand — objects first, and only then he poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron's head and anointed him, to consecrate him.

The word for anointed is the root behind mashiach, messiah — the anointed one. Priests were anointed, and kings, and prophets, and every one of those anointings was a small advance payment on a title that would eventually belong to one man who held all three offices at once.

Then Aaron's sons are brought forward and clothed. The office is not his alone and it does not end with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-21 — The Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-21: Before the new priests serve anyone, two animals die for them — the bull of the sin offering, with Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull, and the ram of the burnt offering, wholly consumed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest Needed What He Was Appointed to Administer

Nothing about ordination made Aaron less of a sinner. The men about to be installed as the nation's mediators first stand in the position of any guilty Israelite, hands pressed down on an animal dying in their place. That he needed it first is exactly what Hebrews seizes on: He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself (Heb. 7:27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order is fixed — sin offering, then burnt offering. Guilt dealt with before devotion expressed.

Now: No one in Israel administered a remedy he had not first needed himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought the bull of the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull of the sin offering. And he killed it, and Moses took the blood, and with his finger put it on the horns of the altar around it and purified the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar and consecrated it to make atonement for it. And he took all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat, and Moses burned them on the altar. But the bull and its skin and its flesh and its dung he burned up with fire outside the camp, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then he presented the ram of the burnt offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar. He cut the ram into pieces, and Moses burned the head and the pieces and the fat. He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and Moses burned the whole ram on the altar. It was a burnt offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering for the LORD, as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the new priests can do anything for anyone else, two animals die for them.

First the bull of the sin offering — and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the bull. The men about to be installed as the nation's mediators must first stand in the position of any guilty Israelite, hands pressed down on an animal that is dying in their place. Then the ram of the burnt offering, wholly consumed, a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.

Nothing about ordination made Aaron less of a sinner. He needed the same remedy he was being appointed to administer, and the fact that he needed it first is exactly what Hebrews seizes on when it describes a better priest: He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself (Heb. 7:27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 22-24: The ram of ordination, with its blood placed on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, and the same for each of his sons.

Verses 25-30: The fat, the right thigh and the bread are placed in the hands of Aaron and waved; then oil and blood are sprinkled on the men and on their garments.
verseByVerse.theology:
Ear, Thumb, Toe

The three points are not chosen at random. The ear is what he hears God's word with; the thumb is what he does his work with, since no hand grips anything without it; the big toe is what he stands and walks on. Hearing, working, going — the blood is applied to the faculties a priest will actually use. Consecration is not an inward mood but a claim on the parts of a person that do things, which is what Paul asks for in present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12:1).

Filling of the Hands

The Hebrew for ordination is literally that. A man was made a priest by having his hands filled with something he immediately gave away.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those vestments were made by craftsmen to a specification — gold thread, blue and scarlet, the finest work in Israel.

Now: And on the day they were first worn they were splashed with sacrificial blood. Nobody in the tabernacle wore clean clothes. The garments that made a priest look holy were permanently marked with the evidence of what holiness had cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on the head of the ram. And he killed it, and Moses took some of its blood and put it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then he presented Aaron's sons, and Moses put some of the blood on the lobes of their right ears and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the big toes of their right feet. And Moses threw the blood against the sides of the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the second ram, and the strangest gesture in the ceremony. Moses takes its blood and puts it on the lobe of Aaron's right ear and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot — and then does the same for each of his sons.

Three points on a man's body, and they are not chosen at random. The ear is what he hears God's word with. The thumb is what he does his work with — no hand grips anything without it. The big toe is what he stands and walks on. Hearing, working, going: the blood is applied to the faculties a priest will actually use.

It is a vivid way of saying that consecration is not an inward mood but a claim on the parts of a person that do things. Paul is asking for the same when he says present your bodies as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12:1) — not your sentiments, your body, the thing that turns up places and handles things.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he took the fat and the fat tail and all the fat that was on the entrails and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with their fat and the right thigh, and out of the basket of unleavened bread that was before the LORD he took one unleavened loaf and one loaf of bread with oil and one wafer and placed them on the pieces of fat and on the right thigh. And he put all these in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons and waved them as a wave offering before the LORD. Then Moses took them from their hands and burned them on the altar with the burnt offering. This was an ordination offering with a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. And Moses took the breast and waved it for a wave offering before the LORD. It was Moses' portion of the ram of ordination, as the LORD commanded Moses. Then Moses took some of the anointing oil and of the blood that was on the altar and sprinkled it on Aaron and his garments, and also on his sons and his sons' garments. So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fat, the right thigh and one of each kind of bread are placed in the hands of Aaron and in the hands of his sons, and waved before the LORD. The Hebrew for ordination here is literally filling of the hands. A man was made a priest by having his hands filled with something he then gave away.

Then the final act: Moses takes anointing oil and blood from the altar and sprinkles both on Aaron, on his garments, on his sons and on their garments. Oil and blood together, on the men and on the clothes.

Those vestments had been made by craftsmen to a specification, gold thread and blue and scarlet, the finest work in Israel. And on the day they were first worn they were splashed with sacrificial blood. Nobody in the tabernacle wore clean clothes. The garments that made a priest look holy were permanently marked with the evidence of what holiness had cost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-36 — Seven Days at the Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 31-36: Seven days at the door — you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days — closing with Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence Laid Down Before It Detonates

Chapters 8 and 9 turn on that final clause: they did all that the LORD commanded. Chapter 10 opens with two men doing something the LORD had not commanded. The narrator sets the contrast deliberately, and he sets it one verse before it goes off.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ceremony was not a morning's event but a week of it.

Now: For seven days Aaron and his sons live at the threshold, going nowhere, repeating the same offerings daily before they are trusted with anyone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Aaron and his sons, "Boil the flesh at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and there eat it and the bread that is in the basket of ordination offerings, as I commanded, saying, 'Aaron and his sons shall eat it.' And what remains of the flesh and the bread you shall burn up with fire. And you shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you. As has been done today, the LORD has commanded to be done to make atonement for you. At the entrance of the tent of meeting you shall remain day and night for seven days, performing what the LORD has charged, so that you do not die, for so I have been commanded." And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last instruction is about staying put. You shall not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are completed, for it will take seven days to ordain you.

Seven days at the door. The ceremony was not a morning's event but a week of it, and for that week Aaron and his sons live at the threshold of the tent, going nowhere, doing the same offerings over again each day.

The chapter ends with a sentence Leviticus uses like a refrain: And Aaron and his sons did all the things that the LORD commanded by Moses. Everything in chapters 8 to 9 turns on that clause, and chapter 10 opens with two men who did something the LORD had not commanded. The narrator is laying the contrast deliberately, and he lays it one verse before it detonates.

8.theology:
Priesthood conferred from outside. Aaron is washed, robed, anointed, and atoned for by another. No one takes this honor for himself (Heb 5:4); so we are made priests by grace.

Whole-life consecration. Blood on ear, hand, and foot claims the entire person for God — fulfilled as Christ consecrates every faculty of those he saves.

The anointing of the Spirit. The oil poured on Aaron foreshadows the Spirit who anointed Christ at his baptism and now anoints his people (1 John 2:20; Acts 10:38).
8.examples:
Then: For seven days Moses washed, robed, anointed, and blooded Aaron and his sons, setting apart Israel's priesthood with patient, fearful reverence.

Now: Christ, washed and anointed at his baptism, is our consecrated High Priest, and by his blood and Spirit he makes us 'a royal priesthood' (1 Pet 2:9), our whole lives set apart for God.

9.title: The Glory Appears: Fire from Heaven
9.text: <sup>1</sup>On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel,<sup>2</sup>and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering,<sup>4</sup>and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'"<sup>5</sup>And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you."<sup>7</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>8</sup>So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself.<sup>9</sup>And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar.<sup>10</sup>But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>11</sup>The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>13</sup>And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar.<sup>14</sup>And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.<sup>15</sup>Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one.<sup>16</sup>And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning.<sup>18</sup>Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar.<sup>19</sup>But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver—<sup>20</sup>they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar,<sup>21</sup>but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.<sup>22</sup>Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings.<sup>23</sup>And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people.<sup>24</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
9.overview:
The seven days of preparation are over; the eighth day dawns. Aaron, newly consecrated, offers his first sacrifices — first for himself, then for the people. The whole drama drives toward a single promised climax: "that the glory of the LORD may appear to you" (9:6). All the offerings, all the blood, all the careful ritual aim at this — that sinners might behold the glory of God and live.

And the glory comes. When Aaron and Moses bless the people, "the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people" (9:23). Then fire — the holy fire of God's own presence — flashes out and consumes the offering on the altar. This is heaven's amen, God's visible acceptance of the sacrifice, the divine seal upon the whole sacrificial system. The God who is a consuming fire consumes the substitute and spares the people.

The response is the only fitting one: "when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces" (9:24). Joy and awe, ecstasy and prostration, together. This is worship in the presence of glory — not the casual familiarity of a trifling age but the trembling, exultant adoration of those who have seen the fire fall and lived. Sproul often said that the proper response to the holiness of God is to fall on our faces; here Israel does exactly that, even as they shout for joy.

The fire that fell on the altar fell, at the last, on Christ. At Calvary the consuming fire of God's holiness fell upon the true sacrifice, and he was wholly consumed in our place. And because the fire fell on him, it need never fall on us. The glory that Israel glimpsed for a moment now shines "in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6), and we who behold it are summoned to the same response: shouting joy and prostrate awe before the God who accepts us in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: On the eighth day the priesthood begins work. Moses tells them why — today the LORD will appear to you — and gives the order: make atonement for yourself and for the people.
verseByVerse.theology:
For Yourself First

Aaron cannot carry anyone else's guilt until his own has been dealt with, and the sequence is stated so plainly that it becomes the hinge of the argument in Hebrews for why we needed a different priest — one holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, with no sins of his own to clear out of the way first (Heb. 7:26-27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything since Exodus 25 — materials, design, craftsmen, tent, seven days of ordination — has been arranged so that a nation of former slaves can survive the presence of God in their camp.

Now: Today he arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel, and he said to Aaron, "Take for yourself a bull calf for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the LORD. And say to the people of Israel, 'Take a male goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a lamb, both a year old without blemish, for a burnt offering, and an ox and a ram for peace offerings, to sacrifice before the LORD, and a grain offering mixed with oil, for today the LORD will appear to you.'" And they brought what Moses commanded in front of the tent of meeting, and all the congregation drew near and stood before the LORD. And Moses said, "This is the thing that the LORD commanded you to do, that the glory of the LORD may appear to you." Then Moses said to Aaron, "Draw near to the altar and offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people, and bring the offering of the people and make atonement for them, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel. The week at the door is over. This is the first day the priesthood actually works.

And Moses tells them why they are doing it: for today the LORD will appear to you. Everything since Exodus 25 — the materials, the design, the craftsmen, the tent, the seven days of ordination — has been arranged so that a nation of former slaves can survive the presence of God in their camp. Today he arrives.

But before that, an order which the New Testament will never stop pointing at: Offer your sin offering and your burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people. For yourself first. Aaron cannot carry anyone else's guilt until his own has been dealt with, and the sequence is stated so plainly that it becomes the hinge of the argument in Hebrews for why we needed a different priest — one holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, who had no sins of his own to clear out of the way first (Heb. 7:26-27).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-14: Aaron makes his own sin offering and burnt offering, step by step — blood on the horns of the altar, the fat burned, the flesh and skin taken outside the camp, the burnt offering handed to him piece by piece by his sons.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unhurried Prose on a Momentous Day

Nothing dramatic has happened yet. A man in new clothes is carefully doing what he was told, in order, while a nation watches — and the whole weight of the day rests on his getting it right.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: His sons hand him the pieces.

Now: The narrator records every step rather than summarising. In Leviticus, the procedure is the story.

verseByVerse.quote: So Aaron drew near to the altar and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself. And the sons of Aaron presented the blood to him, and he dipped his finger in the blood and put it on the horns of the altar and poured out the blood at the base of the altar. But the fat and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as the LORD commanded Moses. The flesh and the skin he burned up with fire outside the camp. Then he killed the burnt offering, and Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. And they handed the burnt offering to him, piece by piece, and the head, and he burned them on the altar. And he washed the entrails and the legs and burned them with the burnt offering on the altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron does his own offerings, and the narrator slows down to record each step: the blood put on the horns of the altar, the fat and the kidneys burned, the flesh and the skin taken outside the camp. Then the burnt offering, handed to him piece by piece by his sons, and washed, and burned.

It is deliberately unhurried prose. Nothing dramatic has happened yet. A man in new clothes is carefully doing what he was told, in order, while a nation watches — and the whole weight of the day rests on his getting it right.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The People's Offerings, and the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 15-21: The people's offerings in order — sin, burnt, grain, then peace — with the breasts and right thigh waved as Moses commanded.

Verses 22-24: Aaron blesses the people; the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering, and the people shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fire as Answer

Not fire as spectacle but fire as reply. God specified an offering; the offering was made exactly as specified; God came out and took it. The shout and the faces in the dust are the response of people who have just watched heaven accept something on their behalf.

The Same Fire, Three Times

In the very next chapter the same fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes two men — identical words, opposite outcome, and the difference is not the intensity of the fire but whether what it fell on had been authorised.

Centuries later, in an upstairs room, divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them (Acts 2:3). Fire came down and settled on people, and they were not consumed; they stood up and began to speak. The difference is not that God had become less holy. It is that by then the offering had been made, once, outside a city wall, and accepted — so when the fire came at last to rest on human beings there was nothing left in them for it to burn.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The order runs sin, consecration, ordinary produce, shared meal — from guilt removed to a family sitting down to dinner in God's presence. The shape of the whole book compressed into one morning.

Now: Even on the greatest day of his life, the measure of Aaron's action is not his instinct but his instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he presented the people's offering and took the goat of the sin offering that was for the people and killed it and offered it as a sin offering, like the first one. And he presented the burnt offering and offered it according to the rule. And he presented the grain offering, took a handful of it, and burned it on the altar, besides the burnt offering of the morning. Then he killed the ox and the ram, the sacrifice of peace offerings for the people. And Aaron's sons handed him the blood, and he threw it against the sides of the altar. But the fat pieces of the ox and of the ram, the fat tail and that which covers the entrails and the kidneys and the long lobe of the liver— they put the fat pieces on the breasts, and he burned the fat pieces on the altar, but the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the people's offerings: a goat for their sin, a calf and a lamb for the burnt offering, a grain offering, and an ox and a ram for the peace offering.

The sequence matters as much as the animals. Sin dealt with, then total consecration, then the gift of ordinary produce, and last of all the shared meal — because the peace offering is the one Israel eats. The order runs from guilt removed to a family sitting down to dinner in God's presence, and that is the shape of the whole book compressed into one morning.

One detail is easy to miss: the breasts and the right thigh Aaron waved for a wave offering before the LORD, as Moses commanded. Even in the middle of the greatest day of his life, the measure of Aaron's action is not his instinct but his instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them, and he came down from offering the sin offering and the burnt offering and the peace offerings. And Moses and Aaron went into the tent of meeting, and when they came out they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Aaron lifts his hands toward the people and blesses them, and comes down. He and Moses go into the tent, and come out, and bless the people again.

And the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the pieces of fat on the altar, and when all the people saw it, they shouted and fell on their faces.

This is what the whole book has been building toward. Not the fire as spectacle, but the fire as answer. God had specified an offering; the offering was made exactly as specified; and God came out and took it. The shout and the faces in the dust are the response of people who have just watched heaven accept something on their behalf.

Hold the picture, because Scripture returns to it twice more and the second time it inverts.

In the very next chapter the same fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes two men. Identical words, opposite outcome — and the difference is not the intensity of the fire but whether what it fell on had been authorised.

And then, centuries later, in an upstairs room in Jerusalem, divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them (Acts 2:3). Fire came down and settled on people — and they were not consumed. They stood up and started speaking. The difference between Leviticus 9 and Acts 2 is not that God had become less holy. It is that by then the offering had already been made, once, outside a city wall, and accepted; so when the fire finally came to rest on human beings there was nothing left in them for it to burn.

9.theology:
The goal of worship: glory. All the offerings aim at the appearing of God's glory (9:6, 23), now seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ' (2 Cor 4:6).

Divine acceptance. The fire from heaven seals God's acceptance of the sacrifice; the fire that fell on the altar fell ultimately on Christ, so it need never fall on us.

Worship in the presence of glory. Shouting joy and prostrate awe together — the fitting response of redeemed sinners who behold God's glory and live.
9.examples:
Then: Israel watched fire flash from God's presence to consume the offering, and the whole nation shouted and fell prostrate — joy and trembling fused in the sight of glory.

Now: Because the fire of judgment fell on Christ, we behold God's glory not in terror but in worship. The right response to grace is still to shout for joy and fall on our faces.

10.title: Nadab and Abihu: Unauthorized Fire
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them.<sup>2</sup>And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace.<sup>4</sup>And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp."<sup>5</sup>So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said.<sup>6</sup>And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled.<sup>7</sup>And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you."
