And they did according to the word of Moses.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying,<sup>9</sup>"Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations.<sup>10</sup>You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean,<sup>11</sup>and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."<sup>12</sup>Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy.<sup>13</sup>You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded.<sup>14</sup>But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel.<sup>15</sup>The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."<sup>16</sup>Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying,<sup>17</sup>"Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD?<sup>18</sup>Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded."<sup>19</sup>And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?"<sup>20</sup>And when Moses heard that, he approved.
10.overview:
The same fire that fell in blessing now falls in judgment. Before the smoke of acceptance has cleared, the joy of chapter 9 is shattered. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's own sons, just consecrated to the priesthood, take their censers and offer "unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them" (10:1). And the holy fire that consumed the sacrifice now consumes the priests. They die before the LORD.

This is the most sobering passage in Leviticus, and Sproul's The Holiness of God circles back to it again and again. We instinctively recoil — was the punishment not severe? But Sproul presses us: our shock reveals how little we grasp the holiness of God and how much we presume upon his grace. The wonder is not that Nadab and Abihu died, but that we live. The fire of judgment is the default reality for sinful creatures who approach a holy God on their own terms.

The exact nature of their sin is debated — strange fire not taken from the altar, presumption, perhaps drunkenness (note the prohibition that follows in v. 9). But the heart of it is clear: they approached God in a way "he had not commanded." They presumed to worship on their own terms. And God's verdict is unbending: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified" (10:3). The closer one draws to God, the more his holiness must be honored. Privilege heightens accountability.

How desperately this drives us to Christ. We too have offered unauthorized fire — worship of our own devising, approach on our own terms, presumption upon grace. We have all deserved the fire. But Christ stepped into the place of judgment; the consuming fire fell on him at Calvary. He is the only authorized way to the Father (John 14:6), the new and living way opened through his flesh (Heb 10:20). Nadab and Abihu teach us, with terrible clarity, that there is no casual coming to God — and that the way which is open is open only because Another bore the fire we earned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire... which he had not commanded them, and fire from the LORD consumes them. Aaron held his peace — and is then forbidden the customary signs of mourning.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Same Fire, One Chapter Apart

In 9:24 fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the offering, and the people shouted. Here the identical phrase consumes two priests. The difference is not the intensity of the fire but whether what it fell on had been authorised. Among those who are near me I will be sanctified — and nobody stood nearer than these two.

A Priest Who Was Not Permitted to Weep

The loosened hair and the torn garment were Israel's two customary signs of grief, and both are forbidden to Aaron while the nation is expressly permitted them. Israel had a high priest who could not mourn at his own sons' deaths. We have a High Priest who wept at a tomb, knowing he would empty it within the hour (John 11:35).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The happiest day in the history of the priesthood becomes its most terrible, within hours.

Now: This is the sober counterweight to all the grace of Leviticus. God has flung open a way to himself — and he is still a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29), approached with reverence and awe rather than casual familiarity.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace. And Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel the uncle of Aaron, and said to them, "Come near; carry your brothers away from the front of the sanctuary and out of the camp." So they came near and carried them in their coats out of the camp, as Moses had said. And Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, and do not tear your clothes, lest you die, and wrath come upon all the congregation; but let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled. And do not go outside the entrance of the tent of meeting, lest you die, for the anointing oil of the LORD is upon you." And they did according to the word of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The happiest day becomes the most terrible. Only moments after fire fell from God to consume the sacrifice in acceptance, Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's own sons, offer "unauthorized fire... which he had not commanded them" — worship of their own devising, on their own terms, perhaps in careless presumption. And the same fire that had blessed now kills: it comes out from the LORD and consumes them where they stand. It is a passage that stops us cold, and it is meant to. Moses explains it in words that tremble: "Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified." The nearer a person stands to God — and no one stood nearer than these priests — the more seriously God's holiness must be honored. God will not be approached carelessly, treated as common, worshiped however we please.

This is the sober counterweight to all the grace of Leviticus. Yes, God has flung open a way to himself; but he is still the God who is "a consuming fire" (Heb 12:29), and we come with reverence and awe, not casual familiarity. And then, most movingly of all: "Aaron held his peace." No protest, no bitter word. In the crushing loss of his two sons, in the very hour of his triumph, Aaron is silent — faith bowing before the righteous holiness of God, saying with his silence what Job said with his words: "the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD" (Job 1:21).

And then comes the hardest thing in the chapter, and it is almost never preached. The bodies must be carried out — not by Aaron, not by his surviving sons, but by cousins, Mishael and Elzaphan, who lift them by their coats and carry them beyond the camp. And to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, Moses says: do not let the hair of your heads hang loose, do not tear your clothes, do not step outside the entrance — lest you die. The loosened hair and the torn garment were Israel's two customary signs of grief. Both are forbidden. Aaron may not mourn his own sons.

Why? Not because the grief was wrong. Notice that Israel is expressly given what Aaron is denied: "let your brothers, the whole house of Israel, bewail the burning that the LORD has kindled." The nation may weep. The father may not. Two reasons stand together. "The anointing oil of the LORD is upon you" — they are in the middle of their ordination, seven days set apart at the tent (chs 8-9); to walk out now would be to desert the post God had just given them. And deeper: for the priests to take up the public signs of mourning would be a public protest, a way of saying before all Israel that God's verdict on the strange fire was wrong. They must stand in the hour of their own bereavement and let God be right.

So read verse 3 again. "Aaron held his peace" is not the composure of a man who felt little. It is the silence of a man forbidden to make a sound — a father with two dead sons and a command not to weep. And his grief does surface, quietly, at the end of the chapter: "such things as these have happened to me" (v. 19). It was there all along. Israel had a high priest who was not permitted to weep at a tomb. We have a High Priest who wept at one — standing at the grave of his friend, knowing he would raise him within the hour, Jesus wept (John 11:35). The priest who could not mourn points us to the Priest who could, and who would himself become the burning that the LORD kindled, so that the fire which fell on Nadab and Abihu need never fall on us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-11 — Distinguish the Holy from the Common
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-11: No wine or strong drink before entering the tent — so that the priests may distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean, and teach the people of Israel all the statutes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priest's Essential Work

To know the difference between the holy and the common, and to help God's people see it — which is the pulse of the entire book. Strong drink blurs exactly the lines God calls his servants to keep razor-sharp, and when these distinctions are lost, holiness itself is lost (Ezek. 22:26).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The command comes immediately after the deaths, which may suggest what lay behind them.

Now: What the priest discerns, he must teach. Learning to see as God sees is still the work of his word in his people, training them to distinguish good from evil (Heb. 5:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Aaron, saying, "Drink no wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you go into the tent of meeting, lest you die. It shall be a statute forever throughout your generations. You are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean, and you are to teach the people of Israel all the statutes that the LORD has spoken to them by Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary: Immediately after the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, God speaks to Aaron with a pointed command: no wine or strong drink before entering the tent. The timing suggests the warning may be connected to what had just happened — careless, perhaps intoxicated, worship. But the reason God gives opens up the whole calling of the priest: they must be clear-headed "to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean," and "to teach the people" all of God's statutes. Here is the priest's essential work, and indeed the pulse of the entire book of Leviticus: to know the difference between the holy and the common, and to help God's people see it. A drunken priest cannot tell holy from profane; strong drink blurs exactly the lines God calls his servants to keep razor-sharp. And what the priest discerns, he must teach. When these distinctions are lost, holiness itself is lost (Ezek 22:26). The recovery of them — learning to see as God sees, to call holy what he calls holy — is still the work of God's word in his people, training us "to distinguish good from evil" (Heb 5:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-20 — Grief and Grace at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 12-15: With the bodies just carried out, Moses tells the surviving priests to eat their portion — you and your sons and your daughters with you.

Verses 16-20: The goat of the sin offering has been burned rather than eaten and Moses is angry; Aaron answers — such things as these have happened to me! — and when Moses heard that, he approved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law Was Never a Machine

The same chapter in which fire killed two men for doing what was not commanded ends with a man not doing what was commanded, giving his reason, and being told he was right. Aaron's argument is not a technicality: the sin offering was eaten as an act of confident mediation, and he could not perform confident mediation on the day God had killed his sons for presumption. To go through the motions would have been the very sin the day had just punished.

He is a consuming fire, and he makes room for a father who cannot eat. Both stand in the same twenty verses and neither cancels the other — the God who knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14) does not break a bruised reed (Isa. 42:3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Such things as these have happened to me is the grief finally surfacing. In verse 3 he held his peace; seventeen verses later, a father forbidden to tear his clothes says the one sentence he is allowed.

Now: And there is mercy in the detail your sons and your daughters with you. The family that has just lost two of its men is named, together, as the people who will eat this. Grief does not put a household outside the provision of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: "Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy. You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due, from the LORD's food offerings, for so I am commanded. But the breast that is waved and the thigh that is contributed you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you, for they are given as your due and your sons' due from the sacrifices of the peace offerings of the people of Israel. The thigh that is contributed and the breast that is waved they shall bring with the food offerings of the fat pieces to wave for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a due forever, as the LORD has commanded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With two bodies just carried out of the camp, Moses turns to the surviving priests and tells them to eat their dinner.

Take the grain offering that is left of the LORD's food offerings, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy. And the wave breast and the contributed thigh may be eaten in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you.

It sounds almost brutal until you see what it is doing. The offerings are still holy; the priests are still priests; the arrangement God made has not been suspended because a disaster has happened inside it. Aaron is being told that his sons' sin has not disqualified the office or contaminated the food. Life at the altar goes on, and he is to sit down and eat as the law provides.

There is a particular mercy in the detail your sons and your daughters with you. The family that has just lost two of its men is named, together, as the people who will eat this. Grief does not put a household outside the provision of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burned up! And he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying, "Why have you not eaten the sin offering in the place of the sanctuary, since it is a thing most holy and has been given to you that you may bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD? Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You certainly ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as I commanded." And Aaron said to Moses, "Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?" And when Moses heard that, he approved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Moses discovers that the goat of the sin offering has been burned up instead of eaten, and he is angry with Eleazar and Ithamar. The rule was clear: the priests eat the sin offering to bear the iniquity of the congregation. It had not been kept.

And Aaron answers his brother. It is the only thing he says in the whole chapter.

Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and yet such things as these have happened to me! If I had eaten the sin offering today, would the LORD have approved?

Notice the phrase in the middle — such things as these have happened to me. That is the grief finally surfacing. In verse 3 he held his peace; here, seventeen verses later, a father who was forbidden to tear his clothes or let his hair down says the one sentence he is allowed. It is restrained almost past bearing, and it is unmistakably the speech of a man who has been holding something in all day.

His argument is not a technicality. The sin offering was to be eaten as an act of confident mediation, and Aaron is saying that he could not perform confident mediation on the day God had killed his sons for presumption. To go through the motions would have been the very sin the day had just punished.

And when Moses heard that, he approved.

Four words, and they say something about the God whose law this is that the rest of the chapter might have obscured. This is the same chapter in which fire came out and killed two men for doing what was not commanded — and it ends with a man not doing what was commanded, giving his reason, and being told he was right. The law was never a machine. It was always administered by a God who knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14), and who does not break a bruised reed (Isa. 42:3).

Both things stand in the same twenty verses and neither cancels the other. He is a consuming fire, and he makes room for a father who cannot eat.

10.theology:
The holiness of God. Sproul's great theme: God must be approached on his terms, not ours. The fire that consumed Nadab and Abihu reveals the deadly seriousness of presumptuous worship.

Privilege heightens accountability. 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified' (10:3) — the closer one is brought to God, the more his holiness must be honored.

The only authorized way. There is one acceptable approach to the Father, and it is Christ (John 14:6); the fire we deserved fell on him.
10.examples:
Then: Aaron's sons offered worship of their own devising and were consumed by holy fire; their father stood in silent, submissive grief before the holiness of God.

Now: We are warned against casual, self-styled worship and driven to Christ, the only authorized way to God, who bore in his own body the fire of judgment we deserved.

11.title: Clean and Unclean: A People Set Apart
11.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth.<sup>3</sup>Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>5</sup>And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>6</sup>And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you.<sup>7</sup>And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you.<sup>8</sup>You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you.<sup>9</sup>"These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat.<sup>10</sup>But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you.<sup>11</sup>You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses.<sup>12</sup>Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you.<sup>13</sup>"And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,<sup>14</sup>the kite, the falcon of any kind,<sup>15</sup>every raven of any kind,<sup>16</sup>the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind,<sup>17</sup>the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl,<sup>18</sup>the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture,<sup>19</sup>the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.<sup>20</sup>"All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you.<sup>21</sup>Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground.<sup>22</sup>Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind.<sup>23</sup>But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.<sup>24</sup>"And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>25</sup>and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>26</sup>Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean.<sup>27</sup>And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>28</sup>and he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening; they are unclean to you.<sup>29</sup>"And these are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole rat, the mouse, the great lizard of any kind,<sup>30</sup>the gecko, the monitor lizard, the lizard, the sand lizard, and the chameleon.<sup>31</sup>These are unclean to you among all that swarm. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>32</sup>And anything on which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it is an article of wood or a garment or a skin or a sack, any article that is used for any purpose. It must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean.<sup>33</sup>And if any of them falls into any earthenware vessel, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it.<sup>34</sup>Any food in it that could be eaten, on which water comes, shall be unclean. And all drink that could be drunk from every such vessel shall be unclean.<sup>35</sup>And everything on which any part of their carcass falls shall be unclean. Whether oven or stove, it shall be broken in pieces. They are unclean and shall remain unclean for you.<sup>36</sup>Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern holding water shall be clean, but whoever touches a carcass in them shall be unclean.<sup>37</sup>And if any part of their carcass falls upon any seed grain that is to be sown, it is clean,<sup>38</sup>but if water is put on the seed and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean to you.<sup>39</sup>"And if any animal which you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>40</sup>and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries the carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.<sup>41</sup>"Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten.<sup>42</sup>Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on all fours, or whatever has many feet, any swarming thing that swarms on the ground, you shall not eat, for they are detestable.<sup>43</sup>You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and you shall not defile yourselves with them, and become unclean through them.<sup>44</sup>For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground.<sup>45</sup>For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy."<sup>46</sup>This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground,<sup>47</sup>to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.
11.overview:
Now begins the section on clean and unclean (chs 11–15), opening with the dietary laws. Which animals may Israel eat, and which not? On the surface these seem arbitrary; in reality they are a daily, table-level catechism in the great theme of separation. Three times a day, at every meal, Israel was reminded that they were a people set apart, that distinctions matter, that the holy and the common are not the same.

Wenham's classic study shows that the categories are not finally about hygiene but about symbolism: the animals that conform to the created order of their domain are clean; the anomalous, the boundary-crossing, the predatory and death-associated are unclean. The clean animal is a living parable of the people who keep within God's appointed bounds. Every meal preached: be distinct, be whole, be set apart unto God.

And the climax of the chapter is the towering refrain that will dominate the rest of Leviticus: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (11:44–45). The dietary laws are not ends in themselves; they serve this. God grounds the call in redemption — "I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (11:45). Holiness is the grateful response of a redeemed people to their redeeming God.

In Christ, the dietary distinctions are fulfilled and lifted. Jesus "declared all foods clean" (Mark 7:19), and Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10) abolishes the wall between clean and unclean nations: "What God has made clean, do not call common." The deeper purpose endures — God still calls his people to be holy and distinct — but the boundary now runs not between Jew and Gentile, kosher and non-kosher, but between those who are in Christ and those who are not. Peter himself quotes Leviticus to the church: "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet 1:16). The table-level lesson becomes a life-level call.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-23: The tests are simple and doubled — land animals must both part the hoof and chew the cud, water creatures must have both fins and scales. Birds of prey and scavengers are listed by name; winged insects are excluded but for the locust family.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Criterion Is the Point

Explanations have been offered for centuries — hygiene, avoiding the animals of Canaanite worship, creatures that move improperly in their element. Some have something in them; none is what the text says. What the text says, over and over, is the test itself: does it have both marks? The laws train a whole nation, at every meal, in one skill — telling one thing from another. And that skill has just been named as the priest's essential work: you are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean (10:10). Israel practised discrimination three times a day with a fork in its hand.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The camel, the rock badger, the hare and the pig are each named as failing on one count while passing on the other. One criterion was never enough.

Now: A rule you can apply at a glance, several times a day, without a priest present.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying to them, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, These are the living things that you may eat among all the animals that are on the earth. Whatever parts the hoof and is cloven-footed and chews the cud, among the animals, you may eat. Nevertheless, among those that chew the cud or part the hoof, you shall not eat these: The camel, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the rock badger, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the hare, because it chews the cud but does not part the hoof, is unclean to you. And the pig, because it parts the hoof and is cloven-footed but does not chew the cud, is unclean to you. You shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses; they are unclean to you. "These you may eat, of all that are in the waters. Everything in the waters that has fins and scales, whether in the seas or in the rivers, you may eat. But anything in the seas or the rivers that does not have fins and scales, of the swarming creatures in the waters and of the living creatures that are in the waters, is detestable to you. You shall regard them as detestable; you shall not eat any of their flesh, and you shall detest their carcasses. Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales is detestable to you. "And these you shall detest among the birds; they shall not be eaten; they are detestable: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture, the kite, the falcon of any kind, every raven of any kind, the ostrich, the nighthawk, the sea gull, the hawk of any kind, the little owl, the cormorant, the short-eared owl, the barn owl, the tawny owl, the carrion vulture, the stork, the heron of any kind, the hoopoe, and the bat. "All winged insects that go on all fours are detestable to you. Yet among the winged insects that go on all fours you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet, with which to hop on the ground. Of them you may eat: the locust of any kind, the bald locust of any kind, the cricket of any kind, and the grasshopper of any kind. But all other winged insects that have four feet are detestable to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dietary laws arrive without a word of explanation for the individual rules, and the tests are simple enough to apply at a glance. Land animals must both part the hoof and chew the cud — one criterion is not enough, which is why the camel, the rock badger, the hare and the pig are each named as failing on one count while passing on the other. Water creatures must have both fins and scales. Birds of prey and scavengers are listed by name. Winged insects are out except for the locust family.

Readers have offered explanations for centuries — hygiene, avoiding the animals of Canaanite worship, a preference for creatures that move in the way proper to their element. Some of these have something in them. None of them is what the text says.

What the text says is the criterion itself. Over and over: does it have both marks? The laws are training an entire nation, at every meal, in a single skill — telling one thing from another. And that skill has just been named as the priest's essential work: you are to distinguish between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean (10:10). Israel practised discrimination three times a day with a fork in its hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24-47 — Uncleanness, Death, and 'Be Holy, for I Am Holy'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 24-43: From eating to touching — carcasses defile, and a dead creature falling into an oven, a pot, a spring or a seed store brings the law into the kitchen.

Verses 44-47: The reason for the chapter: Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy.
verseByVerse.theology:
Behind Almost Every Uncleanness Law Stands Death

A corpse defiles; a skin eaten away defiles; blood lost defiles. God is the living God, and what has been touched by death is disqualified from approaching him — not because it is wicked, but because it carries the mark of the thing he intends to abolish.

What Was Set Aside, and What Was Not

Jesus set the food rules aside: arguing that defilement comes out of a person rather than into him, he said whatever enters the stomach is expelled — and Mark adds the comment that lands like a thunderclap, Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Peter was then shown a sheet of unclean animals and told What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15) — and while he was still puzzling over it, Gentiles knocked at the door. The abolition of this chapter is the doorway the mission to the nations walked through.

But the verse the chapter ends on was not set aside. The same Peter quotes it directly: as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet. 1:15-16). The menu changed; the reason for the menu did not.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The food laws were never about food. They were about a people recognisably different in the most ordinary and unavoidable area of life, because the God who brought them out of Egypt was different.

Now: What was once practised over a cooking pot is now required in all your conduct — which is a great deal harder than checking a hoof.

verseByVerse.quote: "And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever carries any part of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. Every animal that parts the hoof but is not cloven-footed or does not chew the cud is unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean. And all that walk on their paws, among the animals that go on all fours, are unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening; they are unclean to you. "And these are unclean to you among the swarming things that swarm on the ground: the mole rat, the mouse, the great lizard of any kind, the gecko, the monitor lizard, the lizard, the sand lizard, and the chameleon. These are unclean to you among all that swarm. Whoever touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening. And anything on which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it is an article of wood or a garment or a skin or a sack, any article that is used for any purpose. It must be put into water, and it shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean. And if any of them falls into any earthenware vessel, all that is in it shall be unclean, and you shall break it. Any food in it that could be eaten, on which water comes, shall be unclean. And all drink that could be drunk from every such vessel shall be unclean. And everything on which any part of their carcass falls shall be unclean. Whether oven or stove, it shall be broken in pieces. They are unclean and shall remain unclean for you. Nevertheless, a spring or a cistern holding water shall be clean, but whoever touches a carcass in them shall be unclean. And if any part of their carcass falls upon any seed grain that is to be sown, it is clean, but if water is put on the seed and any part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean to you. "And if any animal which you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever eats of its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries the carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. "Every swarming thing that swarms on the ground is detestable; it shall not be eaten. Whatever goes on its belly, and whatever goes on all fours, or whatever has many feet, any swarming thing that swarms on the ground, you shall not eat, for they are detestable. You shall not make yourselves detestable with any swarming thing that swarms, and you shall not defile yourselves with them, and become unclean through them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second half moves from what may be eaten to what may be touched, and a pattern emerges that runs through the rest of the book: uncleanness is contracted from carcasses. An animal that dies is a source of defilement — touch it, carry it, or let it fall into your oven, and something has to be washed or broken.

This is the thread worth following. Behind almost every uncleanness law in Leviticus stands death or the leaking away of life. A corpse defiles. A skin eaten away defiles. Blood lost defiles. God is the living God, and what has been touched by death is disqualified from approaching him — not because it is wicked, but because it now carries the mark of the thing he is going to abolish.

Note also that these rules are relentlessly domestic. A dead lizard falling into a pot, a spring, a seed store, a cooking vessel. The holiness of God is not confined to the tabernacle; it reaches into the kitchen.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy. You shall not defile yourselves with any swarming thing that crawls on the ground. For I am the LORD who brought you up out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy." This is the law about beast and bird and every living creature that moves through the waters and every creature that swarms on the ground, to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean and between the living creature that may be eaten and the living creature that may not be eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And here, at the end, the reason for the whole chapter: For I am the LORD your God. Consecrate yourselves therefore, and be holy, for I am holy.

The food laws were never about the food. They were about a people who were to be recognisably different, in the most ordinary and unavoidable area of life, because the God who had taken them out of Egypt was different. You cannot eat a meal without remembering whose you are.

Two things happened to this chapter in the New Testament, and both matter.

The first is that Jesus set the food rules aside. Arguing that defilement comes out of a person rather than into him, he said that whatever enters the stomach is expelled — and Mark adds the editorial comment that lands like a thunderclap: Thus he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Then Peter, on a rooftop in Joppa, was shown a sheet of unclean animals three times and told to eat, and the voice said What God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15) — and while he was still puzzling over it, Gentiles knocked at the door. The abolition of Leviticus 11 is the doorway through which the mission to the nations walked.

The second is that the verse the chapter ends on was not set aside at all. Peter — the same man from the rooftop — quotes it directly: as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy" (1 Pet. 1:15-16). The menu changed. The reason for the menu did not. What was once practised over a cooking pot is now required in all your conduct, which is a great deal harder than checking a hoof.

11.theology:
Separation unto God. The dietary laws trained Israel, at every meal, in the distinction between holy and common — a people visibly set apart.

'Be holy, for I am holy.' The defining refrain (11:44-45), grounded in God's character and his redemptive act, quoted by Peter for the church (1 Pet 1:16).

Fulfilled in Christ. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and abolished the Jew-Gentile wall (Acts 10); the call to holiness endures, now defined by union with Christ.
11.examples:
Then: An Israelite, choosing what to eat, was reminded three times a day that he belonged to a holy God and a set-apart people, distinct from the nations around him.

Now: We are no longer bound by kosher laws, but the call to be holy and distinct is heightened in Christ. 'As he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct' (1 Pet 1:15).

12.title: Purification After Childbirth: The Offering of the Poor
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days. As at the time of her menstruation, she shall be unclean.<sup>3</sup>And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.<sup>4</sup>Then she shall continue for thirty-three days in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are completed.<sup>5</sup>But if she bears a female child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her menstruation. And she shall continue in the blood of her purifying for sixty-six days.<sup>6</sup>"And when the days of her purifying are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering,<sup>7</sup>and he shall offer it before the LORD and make atonement for her. Then she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a child, either male or female.<sup>8</sup>And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."
12.overview:
This brief chapter addresses purification after childbirth. To modern sensibilities it can seem strange, even offensive — why should the joyful, God-ordained act of bringing forth life render a woman ceremonially unclean? But we must read it within Leviticus's symbolic world. The issue is not that childbirth is sinful, but that it involves the flow of blood, and blood is life, and the loss of life-fluid touches the deep biblical association between fallenness, mortality, and the need for cleansing. Every birth, since Eden, comes trailing the shadow of the curse — "in pain you shall bring forth children" (Gen 3:16) — and every new life born is a life born into a world of sin and death, needing redemption.

Wenham notes that the purification ritual does not stigmatize motherhood; it dignifies it by drawing it into the sphere of God's holiness. The mother brings a burnt offering and a sin offering, and is pronounced clean. The wonder of birth is honored, and the reality of a fallen world is acknowledged, both at once.

But the chapter's deepest glory shines in the New Testament. For Luke records that Mary and Joseph fulfilled exactly this law for the infant Jesus: "And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses... they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord... and to offer a sacrifice... 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons'" (Luke 2:22–24). Two birds — the offering specifically appointed in 12:8 for those who could not afford a lamb. The offering of the poor.

Stop and feel the weight of it. The Lamb of God himself was brought to the temple, and for him was offered the poor woman's two birds — because the Holy Family could not afford a lamb. They did not need to buy a lamb; they were carrying him. The Maker of heaven and earth entered our world in such poverty that his mother brought the cheapest legal offering. "Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9). Leviticus 12, fulfilled in a Bethlehem-born baby, becomes one of the tenderest gospel windows in all the Old Testament.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-5: The purification period after childbirth — forty days for a son, eighty for a daughter.

Verses 6-8: A lamb and a bird are brought; and if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons... and she shall be clean.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unclean Does Not Mean Sinful

It is a ritual status, not a moral verdict, and here it attaches to something God commanded in the first chapter of Genesis. What the mother had done was lose a great deal of blood — and blood, in this book, is life. Where life visibly drains away, a person is temporarily disqualified from approaching the living God. The rule is a statement about mortality, not morality.

On the doubling for a daughter, honesty requires admitting the text gives no reason. Explanations have been proposed and none is stated. What can be said is what the chapter does not say: nothing about a daughter being worth less or more defiling. The offering is identical for both. Whatever the doubling means, it does not touch the price of restoration.

The Family That Qualified for the Reduced Rate

Luke records exactly what Mary and Joseph offered: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24). They brought the poor woman's offering. The concession clause of verse 8, written for a household that could not manage a lamb, is the line the mother of the Lord was living under.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A family brings a sin offering on behalf of a household that included the sinless Son of God, submitting to a purification law with nothing in him to purify.

Now: Born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4-5). He kept it from the inside, at forty days old, before he could hold his head up. And the lamb the family could not afford was lying in the arms of the woman who came to buy the birds.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel, saying, If a woman conceives and bears a male child, then she shall be unclean seven days. As at the time of her menstruation, she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised. Then she shall continue for thirty-three days in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy, nor come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are completed. But if she bears a female child, then she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her menstruation. And she shall continue in the blood of her purifying for sixty-six days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A short chapter that needs two misunderstandings cleared away before it can be read at all.

The first: unclean in Leviticus does not mean sinful. It is a ritual status, not a moral verdict, and it attaches here to something God commanded in the first chapter of Genesis. Nobody thought childbirth was wrong. A woman was not being blamed for having a baby.

What she had done was lose a great deal of blood — and blood, in this book, is life. Every law about discharge, disease and death works on the same principle: where life visibly drains away, a person is temporarily disqualified from approaching the living God. The rule is a statement about mortality, not morality.

The second difficulty is the doubling — forty days for a son, eighty for a daughter — and honesty requires saying that the text gives no reason for it. Explanations have been proposed and none is stated here. What can be said is what the chapter does not say: nothing about the daughter being worth less, and nothing about her being more defiling. The offering at the end is identical for both. Whatever the doubling means, it does not affect the price of restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the days of her purifying are completed, whether for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, and he shall offer it before the LORD and make atonement for her. Then she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a child, either male or female. And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days are complete she brings a lamb a year old for a burnt offering, and a pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering.

And then verse 8, which is the reason this chapter matters more than its length suggests: And if she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean.

Now turn to Luke. Mary and Joseph bring the child to the temple, and Luke records precisely what they offered: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24).

They brought the poor woman's offering. The concession clause in Leviticus 12:8, written for a household that could not manage a lamb, is the line the mother of the Lord was living under. He was born into a family that qualified for the reduced rate.

And there is more in it than poverty. The whole scene is a family bringing a sin offering on behalf of a household that included the sinless Son of God, submitting to a purification law that had nothing in him to purify — born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4-5). He kept it from the inside, from forty days old, before he could hold his head up.

The lamb the family could not afford was lying in the arms of the woman who came to buy the birds.

12.theology:
Born into a fallen world. Even the joy of birth, marked by blood, points to the universal need for cleansing — every life enters the shadow of sin and death.

Atonement scaled to poverty. The provision of two birds for the poor (12:8) shows that no one is shut out from God by want.

The poverty of Christ. Mary's offering of two birds (Luke 2:24) reveals that the Lamb of God entered the world in real poverty — 'for your sake he became poor' (2 Cor 8:9).
12.examples:
Then: A new mother in Israel, after the appointed days, brought her offering — a lamb if she could, two birds if she could not — and was pronounced clean before the LORD.

Now: We marvel that Mary brought the offering of the poor for the Son of God. The King of glory met us in poverty; let no one think themselves too lowly for his grace.

13.title: Skin Disease: The Priest Who Examines
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests,<sup>3</sup>and the priest shall examine the diseased area on the skin of his body. And if the hair in the diseased area has turned white and the disease appears to be deeper than the skin of his body, it is a case of leprous disease. When the priest has examined him, he shall pronounce him unclean.<sup>4</sup>But if the spot is white in the skin of his body and appears no deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall shut up the diseased person for seven days.<sup>5</sup>And the priest shall examine him on the seventh day, and if in his eyes the disease is checked and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall shut him up for another seven days.<sup>6</sup>And the priest shall examine him again on the seventh day, and if the diseased area has faded and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is only an eruption. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.<sup>7</sup>But if the eruption spreads in the skin, after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall appear again before the priest.<sup>8</sup>And the priest shall look, and if the eruption has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a leprous disease.<sup>9</sup>"When a man is afflicted with a leprous disease, he shall be brought to the priest,<sup>10</sup>and the priest shall look. And if there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,<sup>11</sup>it is a chronic leprous disease in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not shut him up, for he is unclean.<sup>12</sup>And if the leprous disease breaks out in the skin, so that the leprous disease covers all the skin of the diseased person from head to foot, so far as the priest can see,<sup>13</sup>then the priest shall look, and if the leprous disease has covered all his body, he shall pronounce him clean of the disease; it has all turned white, and he is clean.<sup>14</sup>But when raw flesh appears on him, he shall be unclean.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall examine the raw flesh and pronounce him unclean. Raw flesh is unclean, for it is a leprous disease.<sup>16</sup>But if the raw flesh recovers and turns white again, then he shall come to the priest,<sup>17</sup>and the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce the diseased person clean; he is clean.<sup>18</sup>"If there is in the skin of one's body a boil and it heals,<sup>19</sup>and in the place of the boil there comes a white swelling or a reddish-white spot, then it shall be shown to the priest.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall look, and if it appears deeper than the skin and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is a case of leprous disease that has broken out in the boil.<sup>21</sup>But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it and it is not deeper than the skin, but has faded, then the priest shall shut him up seven days.<sup>22</sup>And if it spreads in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a disease.<sup>23</sup>But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.<sup>24</sup>"Or, when the body has a burn on its skin and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a spot, reddish-white or white,<sup>25</sup>the priest shall examine it, and if the hair in the spot has turned white and it appears deeper than the skin, then it is a leprous disease. It has broken out in the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease.<sup>26</sup>But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot and it is no deeper than the skin, but has faded, the priest shall shut him up seven days,<sup>27</sup>and the priest shall examine him the seventh day. If it is spreading in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease.<sup>28</sup>But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread in the skin, but has faded, it is a swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is the scar of the burn.<sup>29</sup>"When a man or woman has a disease on the head or the beard,<sup>30</sup>the priest shall examine the disease. And if it appears deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is an itch, a leprous disease of the head or the beard.<sup>31</sup>And if the priest examines the itching disease and it appears no deeper than the skin and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for seven days,<sup>32</sup>and on the seventh day the priest shall examine the disease. If the itch has not spread, and there is in it no yellow hair, and the itch appears to be no deeper than the skin,<sup>33</sup>then he shall shave himself, but the itch he shall not shave; and the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for another seven days.<sup>34</sup>And on the seventh day the priest shall examine the itch, and if the itch has not spread in the skin and it appears to be no deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean.<sup>35</sup>But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing,<sup>36</sup>then the priest shall examine him, and if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest need not seek for the yellow hair; he is unclean.<sup>37</sup>But if in his eyes the itch is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, the itch is healed and he is clean, and the priest shall pronounce him clean.<sup>38</sup>"When a man or a woman has spots on the skin of the body, white spots,<sup>39</sup>the priest shall look, and if the spots on the skin of the body are of a dull white, it is leukoderma that has broken out in the skin; he is clean.<sup>40</sup>"If a man's hair falls out from his head, he is bald; he is clean.<sup>41</sup>And if a man's hair falls out from his forehead, he has baldness of the forehead; he is clean.<sup>42</sup>But if there is on the bald head or the bald forehead a reddish-white diseased area, it is a leprous disease breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead.<sup>43</sup>Then the priest shall examine him, and if the diseased swelling is reddish-white on his bald head or on his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprous disease in the skin of the body,<sup>44</sup>he is a leprous man, he is unclean. The priest must pronounce him unclean; his disease is on his head.<sup>45</sup>"The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.'<sup>46</sup>He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.<sup>47</sup>"When there is a case of leprous disease in a garment, whether a woolen or a linen garment,<sup>48</sup>in warp or woof of linen or wool, or in a skin or in anything made of skin,<sup>49</sup>if the disease is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin or in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, it is a case of leprous disease, and it shall be shown to the priest.<sup>50</sup>And the priest shall examine the disease and shut up that which has the disease for seven days.<sup>51</sup>Then he shall examine the disease on the seventh day. If the disease has spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in the skin, whatever be the use of the skin, the disease is a persistent leprous disease; it is unclean.<sup>52</sup>And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the woof, the wool or the linen, or any article made of skin that is diseased, for it is a persistent leprous disease. It shall be burned in the fire.<sup>53</sup>"And if the priest examines, and if the disease has not spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin,<sup>54</sup>then the priest shall command that they wash the thing in which is the disease, and he shall shut it up for another seven days.<sup>55</sup>And the priest shall examine the diseased thing after it has been washed. And if the appearance of the diseased area has not changed, though the disease has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire, whether the rot is on the back or on the front.<sup>56</sup>"But if the priest examines, and if the diseased area has faded after it has been washed, he shall tear it out of the garment or the skin or the warp or the woof.<sup>57</sup>Then if it appears again in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn with fire whatever has the disease.<sup>58</sup>But the garment, or the warp or the woof, or any article made of skin from which the disease departs when you have washed it, shall then be washed a second time, and be clean."<sup>59</sup>This is the law for a case of leprous disease in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, to determine whether it is clean or unclean.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the long, painstaking law of tsara'at — usually translated "leprosy," though it covers a range of skin conditions and even mold in fabrics. The priest is appointed as the examiner, the one who looks closely, declares clean or unclean, and pronounces the verdict. The detail is exhausting precisely because the stakes are so high: a wrong diagnosis means either a clean person banished or an unclean person spreading defilement through the camp.

The disease becomes, in Scripture's symbolic vocabulary, the great picture of sin: it spreads, it disfigures, it works beneath the surface and erupts visibly, it isolates, and it makes one unfit for the presence of God. The verdict "unclean" carries a terrible weight — the leper must tear his clothes, cover his lip, cry "Unclean, unclean," and live alone outside the camp (13:45–46). Cut off from worship, from family, from community — a living picture of the alienation that sin works.

Sproul and Ferguson both draw the line: this is what sin does to the soul. It defiles, it spreads, it cuts off from God and others, and no amount of self-cleansing can reverse it. The leper could not heal himself; he could only be examined and declared. The priest's verdict was final and the sentence was exile.

And here the heart aches for the Great Priest who is coming. For the law could only diagnose; it could not cure. The priest could declare a leper unclean but could not make him clean. Then came One who, when a leper fell before him crying "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean," stretched out his hand and touched him — the unthinkable, defiling touch — and said, "I will; be clean" (Matt 8:2–3). He did not become unclean by the touch; the leper became clean. The Great High Priest both examines and heals, both pronounces the verdict and bears it away. Where Aaron could only send the leper outside the camp, Jesus "suffered outside the gate" (Heb 13:12) to bring the outcast home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Leprous Disease and the Priest's Examination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-28: Tsara'at is brought not to a doctor but to Aaron the priest, who prescribes no treatment and only examines — shutting the doubtful case up for seven days, and seven more, before any verdict.

Verses 29-44: The examination extends to head, beard, bald patches, and the difference between a scaly itch and ordinary skin.

Verses 45-46: The verdict, and its cost: torn clothes, loosened hair, the cry Unclean, unclean, and He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Is Actually Being Described

Tsara'at is not modern leprosy — Hansen's disease — and the traditional English rendering has caused much confusion. It covers a range of surface conditions affecting skin, hair, cloth and even walls, some of which clearly clear up on their own. And no treatment is prescribed anywhere: the priest is not there to cure but to look, and to say which of two words applies.

The Touch That Ran Backwards

Under this chapter, contact with the unclean makes the clean man unclean. And a leper came to him... "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:40-41). He did not have to — he healed a centurion's servant from another town without moving. He touched this man because nobody had touched him since the priest said the word. And it ran backwards because the one doing the touching would in due course go out to the place this chapter assigns: so Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The torn clothes and loosened hair are the signs of mourning — the same signs Aaron was forbidden three chapters ago. A man with this condition dresses for a funeral, and the funeral is his own.

Now: Notice how unhurried the procedure is, and how often the priest is instructed to pronounce a man clean — a rash that has faded, hair that has not turned white, a burn that is healing. The chapter is at least as concerned with not condemning the healthy as with identifying the sick. A wrong verdict either way does damage: a diseased man left in the camp, or a healthy man put out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "When a person has on the skin of his body a swelling or an eruption or a spot, and it turns into a case of leprous disease on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons the priests, and the priest shall examine the diseased area on the skin of his body. And if the hair in the diseased area has turned white and the disease appears to be deeper than the skin of his body, it is a case of leprous disease. When the priest has examined him, he shall pronounce him unclean. But if the spot is white in the skin of his body and appears no deeper than the skin, and the hair in it has not turned white, the priest shall shut up the diseased person for seven days. And the priest shall examine him on the seventh day, and if in his eyes the disease is checked and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall shut him up for another seven days. And the priest shall examine him again on the seventh day, and if the diseased area has faded and the disease has not spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean; it is only an eruption. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean. But if the eruption spreads in the skin, after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall appear again before the priest. And the priest shall look, and if the eruption has spread in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a leprous disease. "When a man is afflicted with a leprous disease, he shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall look. And if there is a white swelling in the skin that has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling, it is a chronic leprous disease in the skin of his body, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean. He shall not shut him up, for he is unclean. And if the leprous disease breaks out in the skin, so that the leprous disease covers all the skin of the diseased person from head to foot, so far as the priest can see, then the priest shall look, and if the leprous disease has covered all his body, he shall pronounce him clean of the disease; it has all turned white, and he is clean. But when raw flesh appears on him, he shall be unclean. And the priest shall examine the raw flesh and pronounce him unclean. Raw flesh is unclean, for it is a leprous disease. But if the raw flesh recovers and turns white again, then he shall come to the priest, and the priest shall examine him, and if the disease has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce the diseased person clean; he is clean. "If there is in the skin of one's body a boil and it heals, and in the place of the boil there comes a white swelling or a reddish-white spot, then it shall be shown to the priest. And the priest shall look, and if it appears deeper than the skin and its hair has turned white, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is a case of leprous disease that has broken out in the boil. But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in it and it is not deeper than the skin, but has faded, then the priest shall shut him up seven days. And if it spreads in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a disease. But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall pronounce him clean. "Or, when the body has a burn on its skin and the raw flesh of the burn becomes a spot, reddish-white or white, the priest shall examine it, and if the hair in the spot has turned white and it appears deeper than the skin, then it is a leprous disease. It has broken out in the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease. But if the priest examines it and there is no white hair in the spot and it is no deeper than the skin, but has faded, the priest shall shut him up seven days, and the priest shall examine him the seventh day. If it is spreading in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean; it is a case of leprous disease. But if the spot remains in one place and does not spread in the skin, but has faded, it is a swelling from the burn, and the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is the scar of the burn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fifty-nine verses on skin conditions, and the first thing to get right is what is being described. The Hebrew is tsara'at. It is not modern leprosy — Hansen's disease — and the traditional English rendering has caused a good deal of confusion. It covers a range of surface conditions affecting skin, hair, cloth and even walls, some of which clearly clear up on their own.

The second thing to notice is who handles it. Not a doctor: he shall be brought to Aaron the priest. No treatment is prescribed anywhere in the chapter. The priest is not there to cure anything; he is there to look, and to say which of two words applies.

And the procedure is strikingly unhurried. If the case is doubtful the man is shut up for seven days. The priest looks again. If it is still doubtful — seven days more. Only then is a verdict given. Two weeks of careful observation before anyone is declared unclean, and the text repeatedly instructs the priest to pronounce men clean: a rash that has faded, hair that has not turned white, a burn that is healing. The chapter is at least as concerned with not condemning the healthy as with identifying the sick.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man or woman has a disease on the head or the beard, the priest shall examine the disease. And if it appears deeper than the skin, and the hair in it is yellow and thin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean. It is an itch, a leprous disease of the head or the beard. And if the priest examines the itching disease and it appears no deeper than the skin and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for seven days, and on the seventh day the priest shall examine the disease. If the itch has not spread, and there is in it no yellow hair, and the itch appears to be no deeper than the skin, then he shall shave himself, but the itch he shall not shave; and the priest shall shut up the person with the itching disease for another seven days. And on the seventh day the priest shall examine the itch, and if the itch has not spread in the skin and it appears to be no deeper than the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him clean. And he shall wash his clothes and be clean. But if the itch spreads in the skin after his cleansing, then the priest shall examine him, and if the itch has spread in the skin, the priest need not seek for the yellow hair; he is unclean. But if in his eyes the itch is unchanged and black hair has grown in it, the itch is healed and he is clean, and the priest shall pronounce him clean. "When a man or a woman has spots on the skin of the body, white spots, the priest shall look, and if the spots on the skin of the body are of a dull white, it is leukoderma that has broken out in the skin; he is clean. "If a man's hair falls out from his head, he is bald; he is clean. And if a man's hair falls out from his forehead, he has baldness of the forehead; he is clean. But if there is on the bald head or the bald forehead a reddish-white diseased area, it is a leprous disease breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead. Then the priest shall examine him, and if the diseased swelling is reddish-white on his bald head or on his bald forehead, like the appearance of leprous disease in the skin of the body, he is a leprous man, he is unclean. The priest must pronounce him unclean; his disease is on his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The examination extends to the head and the beard, to bald patches, to the difference between a scaly itch and ordinary skin, and to spots that are dull white rather than bright. The distinctions are fine and the priest is expected to know them.

Underneath the detail is the same principle that governed the food laws: someone must be trained to tell one thing from another, and the whole community depends on his getting it right. A wrong verdict either way does damage — a diseased man left in the camp, or a healthy man put out of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, 'Unclean, unclean.' He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then two verses that carry the human weight of the whole chapter.

The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, "Unclean, unclean." He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease. He is unclean. He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp.

Consider what is being described. The torn clothes and loosened hair are the signs of mourning — the same signs Aaron was forbidden three chapters ago. A man with this condition dresses for a funeral, and the funeral is his own. He must announce his own defilement aloud so that nobody comes close by accident. And the sentence that ends it is the flattest in Leviticus: He shall live alone.

He is not merely ill. He is cut off from the camp, which means cut off from the tabernacle, which means cut off from the worship of God and from every human touch, for as long as it lasts. In a book about drawing near, here is a man who may not.

Which is why the Gospels keep bringing lepers to Jesus, and why what he does with them is never merely a healing. And a leper came to him, imploring him, and kneeling said to him, "If you will, you can make me clean." Moved with pity, he stretched out his hand and touched him (Mark 1:40-41). He did not have to touch him. He healed a centurion's servant from another town without moving. He touched this man because this man had not been touched by anyone since the priest said the word.

And the direction of that touch is the gospel in one gesture. Under Leviticus, contact with the unclean makes the clean man unclean. Here it ran backwards, and the leper walked away whole. It ran backwards because the one doing the touching would in due course go out to the place this chapter assigns — so Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:12) — and take the sentence himself. He was made what we were so that we could be made what he is. The man who cried Unclean, unclean has a Saviour who was numbered with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 47-59: The same procedure applied to fabric — wool, linen and leather — with the same seven-day quarantine, the same re-examination, and the possibility of washing and re-inspection before a garment is finally burned.
verseByVerse.theology:
Corruption Was Not Treated as Purely Personal

It could get into the things people owned and the cloth they wore, and it had to be looked for there too. The next chapter takes it one step further and finds it in the walls of a house.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A garment is washed and re-inspected before anyone gives up on it.

Now: Even here the procedure resists a quick verdict. Burning the cloth is the last resort, not the first.

verseByVerse.quote: "When there is a case of leprous disease in a garment, whether a woolen or a linen garment, in warp or woof of linen or wool, or in a skin or in anything made of skin, if the disease is greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin or in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, it is a case of leprous disease, and it shall be shown to the priest. And the priest shall examine the disease and shut up that which has the disease for seven days. Then he shall examine the disease on the seventh day. If the disease has spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in the skin, whatever be the use of the skin, the disease is a persistent leprous disease; it is unclean. And he shall burn the garment, or the warp or the woof, the wool or the linen, or any article made of skin that is diseased, for it is a persistent leprous disease. It shall be burned in the fire. "And if the priest examines, and if the disease has not spread in the garment, in the warp or the woof or in any article made of skin, then the priest shall command that they wash the thing in which is the disease, and he shall shut it up for another seven days. And the priest shall examine the diseased thing after it has been washed. And if the appearance of the diseased area has not changed, though the disease has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire, whether the rot is on the back or on the front. "But if the priest examines, and if the diseased area has faded after it has been washed, he shall tear it out of the garment or the skin or the warp or the woof. Then if it appears again in the garment, in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, it is spreading. You shall burn with fire whatever has the disease. But the garment, or the warp or the woof, or any article made of skin from which the disease departs when you have washed it, shall then be washed a second time, and be clean." This is the law for a case of leprous disease in a garment of wool or linen, either in the warp or the woof, or in any article made of skin, to determine whether it is clean or unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends by applying the same procedure to fabric — wool, linen, leather — with the same seven-day quarantine, the same re-examination, the same possibility of washing and re-inspection before a garment is finally burned.

It is a strange coda, and it makes a point the human cases do not. Corruption in Israel was not treated as a purely personal matter. It could get into the things people owned and the cloth they wore, and it had to be looked for there too. Chapter 14 will take it a step further and find it in the walls of a house.

13.theology:
Sin's nature pictured. Skin disease, working beneath the surface and erupting visibly, images sin: it defiles, spreads, disfigures, and cuts off from God.

The priest's verdict. The priest could diagnose and declare but not cure; only the Great High Priest both pronounces and heals.

Outside the camp. The exile of the leper is reversed by Christ, who 'suffered outside the gate' (Heb 13:12) to bring the outcast home.
13.examples:
Then: A suspected leper was brought to the priest, examined, and, if diseased, sent out of the camp to live alone, crying 'Unclean' — cut off from worship and community.
