Now: We bring our defilement honestly to the Great Priest, who does not banish us but touches us and makes us clean, having taken our place outside the camp.

14.title: The Cleansing of the Leper: Two Birds and Living Water
14.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"This shall be the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,<sup>3</sup>and the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look. Then, if the case of leprous disease is healed in the leprous person,<sup>4</sup>the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds and cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop.<sup>5</sup>And the priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water.<sup>6</sup>He shall take the live bird with the cedarwood and the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water.<sup>7</sup>And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed of the leprous disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and shall let the living bird go into the open field.<sup>8</sup>And he who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes and shave off all his hair and bathe himself in water, and he shall be clean. And after that he may come into the camp, but live outside his tent seven days.<sup>9</sup>And on the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair from his head, his beard, and his eyebrows. He shall shave off all his hair, and then he shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean.<sup>10</sup>"And on the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish, and a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, and one log of oil.<sup>11</sup>And the priest who cleanses him shall set the man who is to be cleansed and these things before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>12</sup>And the priest shall take one of the male lambs and offer it for a guilt offering, along with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And he shall kill the lamb in the place where they kill the sin offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary. For the guilt offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest; it is most holy.<sup>14</sup>The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>15</sup>Then the priest shall take some of the log of oil and pour it into the palm of his own left hand<sup>16</sup>and dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand and sprinkle some oil with his finger seven times before the LORD.<sup>17</sup>And some of the oil that remains in his hand the priest shall put on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering.<sup>18</sup>And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed. Then the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD.<sup>19</sup>The priest shall offer the sin offering, to make atonement for him who is to be cleansed from his uncleanness. And afterward he shall kill the burnt offering.<sup>20</sup>And the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean.<sup>21</sup>"But if he is poor and cannot afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil;<sup>22</sup>also two turtledoves or two pigeons, whichever he can afford. The one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.<sup>23</sup>And on the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And the priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>25</sup>And he shall kill the lamb of the guilt offering. And the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot.<sup>26</sup>And the priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand,<sup>27</sup>and shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, in the place where the blood of the guilt offering was put.<sup>29</sup>And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And he shall offer, of the turtledoves or pigeons, whichever he can afford,<sup>31</sup>one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, along with a grain offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for him who is being cleansed.<sup>32</sup>This is the law for him in whom is a case of leprous disease, who cannot afford the offerings for his cleansing."<sup>33</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>34</sup>"When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house in the land of your possession,<sup>35</sup>then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, 'There seems to me to be some case of disease in my house.'<sup>36</sup>Then the priest shall command that they empty the house before the priest goes to examine the disease, lest all that is in the house be declared unclean. And afterward the priest shall go in to see the house.<sup>37</sup>And he shall examine the disease. And if the disease is in the walls of the house with greenish or reddish spots, and if it appears to be deeper than the surface,<sup>38</sup>then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house and shut up the house seven days.<sup>39</sup>And the priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the disease has spread in the walls of the house,<sup>40</sup>then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the disease and throw them into an unclean place outside the city.<sup>41</sup>And he shall have the inside of the house scraped all around, and the plaster that they scrape off they shall pour out in an unclean place outside the city.<sup>42</sup>Then they shall take other stones and put them in the place of those stones, and he shall take other plaster and plaster the house.<sup>43</sup>"If the disease breaks out again in the house, after he has taken out the stones and scraped the house and plastered it,<sup>44</sup>then the priest shall go and look. And if the disease has spread in the house, it is a persistent leprous disease in the house; it is unclean.<sup>45</sup>And he shall break down the house, its stones and timber and all the plaster of the house, and he shall carry them out of the city to an unclean place.<sup>46</sup>Moreover, whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening,<sup>47</sup>and whoever sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes, and whoever eats in the house shall wash his clothes.<sup>48</sup>"But if the priest comes and looks, and if the disease has not spread in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, for the disease is healed.<sup>49</sup>And for the cleansing of the house he shall take two small birds, with cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop,<sup>50</sup>and shall kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water<sup>51</sup>and shall take the cedarwood and the hyssop and the scarlet yarn, along with the live bird, and dip them in the blood of the bird that was killed and in the fresh water and sprinkle the house seven times.<sup>52</sup>Thus he shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh water and with the live bird and with the cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn.<sup>53</sup>And he shall let the live bird go out of the city into the open country. So he shall make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean."<sup>54</sup>This is the law for any case of leprous disease: for an itch,<sup>55</sup>for leprous disease in a garment or in a house,<sup>56</sup>and for a swelling or an eruption or a spot,<sup>57</sup>to show when it is unclean and when it is clean. This is the law for leprous disease.
14.overview:
If chapter 13 is the law of diagnosis, chapter 14 is the liturgy of restoration — and it is breathtaking. For here, against all expectation, the law makes provision for what it could not produce: the cleansing of a healed leper, his joyful return to the camp and the worship of God. The ritual is among the most vividly gospel-shaped in all of Leviticus.

The centerpiece is the rite of the two birds (14:4–7). Two clean birds are taken. One is killed over fresh (literally "living") water in an earthen vessel, its blood mingling with the running water. The living bird, together with cedarwood, scarlet yarn, and hyssop, is dipped in the blood of the slain bird. Then the priest sprinkles the cleansed leper seven times — and releases the living bird into the open field, to fly away free.

Wenham and many after him have seen the unmistakable shape of the gospel here. One bird dies; the other, dipped in the blood of the first, is set free to soar into the open sky. Is this not death and resurrection? The slain bird is Christ crucified, his blood mingled with living water (recall the blood and water from his side, John 19:34); the released bird is Christ risen, ascending free into the heavens, and with him the cleansed sinner soars into liberty. The hyssop recalls the Passover and reappears at the cross (John 19:29); the scarlet, the blood; the cedar, the enduring tree.

The leper, once exiled and crying "Unclean," is now sprinkled, washed, shaved, and brought back — back to the camp, back to his family, back to the worship of God. This is the homecoming of the outcast, the resurrection of the living dead. And every cleansed leper is a portrait of every sinner saved by grace: brought from the place of death, washed in blood, sealed by the Spirit, and welcomed home — while the living bird, dipped in saving blood, flies free into the open field of the new creation. "If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed" (John 8:36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-32 — The Cleansing of the Leper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-9: The priest shall go out of the camp to the healed man. Two birds: one killed over fresh water, the other dipped in its blood with cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop, and let go into the open field. Then washing, shaving, seven days, and it all again.

Verses 10-32: On the eighth day, blood and then oil are placed on the man's right ear, thumb and big toe — and the whole ceremony is scaled for a man who is poor and cannot afford so much.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Birds, One Death

The second bird is dipped in the blood of the first and released alive over open country. Everyone standing there watched a bird go up into the sky wearing the blood of its substitute. Leviticus does this again with two goats in chapter 16 — one killed, one sent away — and the picture is identical: a death happens, and something walks free, marked by that death, carrying it out of sight.

Hyssop and scarlet are worth holding. Hyssop was the brush Israel used to paint blood on the doorposts at Passover (Ex. 12:22), and hyssop was lifted to the mouth of Christ on the cross (John 19:29). The plant that applied the blood of the first exodus was in someone's hand at the last.

The Outcast Treated Like a Priest

Blood and then oil on the right ear, thumb and big toe are the ordination rites — precisely what was done to Aaron and his sons in chapter 8 — now performed on a man who last week was living alone outside the camp crying Unclean. He is not merely readmitted; he is brought back by the ceremony that installed the high priest. Scripture never explains the parallel because it does not need to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The man cannot come in until he is pronounced clean, so the priest walks out to where he is.

Now: And the cheapest version of the ceremony still ends with blood and oil on the man's ear, thumb and toe. God will not have a poor man half-restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "This shall be the law of the leprous person for the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall look. Then, if the case of leprous disease is healed in the leprous person, the priest shall command them to take for him who is to be cleansed two live clean birds and cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop. And the priest shall command them to kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water. He shall take the live bird with the cedarwood and the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them and the live bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water. And he shall sprinkle it seven times on him who is to be cleansed of the leprous disease. Then he shall pronounce him clean and shall let the living bird go into the open field. And he who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes and shave off all his hair and bathe himself in water, and he shall be clean. And after that he may come into the camp, but live outside his tent seven days. And on the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair from his head, his beard, and his eyebrows. He shall shave off all his hair, and then he shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chapter 13 had no cure in it. Chapter 14 opens with a ceremony for a man who has one — and the first thing the text does is send the priest out to him: he shall be brought to the priest, and the priest shall go out of the camp. The man cannot come in until he is pronounced clean, so the priest walks out to where he is.

Then a ritual unlike anything else in Leviticus. Two live birds are taken. One is killed in an earthenware vessel over fresh water — literally living water, running water, not drawn from a cistern. Cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop are bound together with the second bird, and the whole bundle is dipped in the blood of the first. The man is sprinkled seven times. And then: He shall let the living bird go into the open field.

Two birds, and only one dies. The other is dipped in the blood of the one that did, and released alive over open country. Everyone standing there watched a bird go up into the sky wearing the blood of its substitute.

Leviticus will do this again with two goats in chapter 16 — one killed, one sent away — and the picture is the same both times. A death happens; and something walks free, marked by that death, carrying it out of sight.

Note the hyssop and the scarlet, because they turn up together at the end. Hyssop was the brush Israel used to paint blood on the doorposts at Passover (Ex. 12:22), and hyssop is what was lifted to the mouth of Christ on the cross (John 19:29). The plant that applied the blood of the first exodus was in someone's hand at the last.

Then the man washes, shaves off all his hair, bathes, waits seven days, and does it all again. Only then may he come into the camp — and even then he lives outside his tent for a week. Restoration in Israel was thorough and it was slow.

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without blemish, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish, and a grain offering of three tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil, and one log of oil. And the priest who cleanses him shall set the man who is to be cleansed and these things before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the priest shall take one of the male lambs and offer it for a guilt offering, along with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. And he shall kill the lamb in the place where they kill the sin offering and the burnt offering, in the place of the sanctuary. For the guilt offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest; it is most holy. The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then the priest shall take some of the log of oil and pour it into the palm of his own left hand and dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand and sprinkle some oil with his finger seven times before the LORD. And some of the oil that remains in his hand the priest shall put on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering. And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed. Then the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD. The priest shall offer the sin offering, to make atonement for him who is to be cleansed from his uncleanness. And afterward he shall kill the burnt offering. And the priest shall offer the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean. "But if he is poor and cannot afford so much, then he shall take one male lamb for a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil; also two turtledoves or two pigeons, whichever he can afford. The one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering. And on the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD. And the priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. And he shall kill the lamb of the guilt offering. And the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. And the priest shall pour some of the oil into the palm of his own left hand, and shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the LORD. And the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot, in the place where the blood of the guilt offering was put. And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put on the head of him who is to be cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD. And he shall offer, of the turtledoves or pigeons, whichever he can afford, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, along with a grain offering. And the priest shall make atonement before the LORD for him who is being cleansed. This is the law for him in whom is a case of leprous disease, who cannot afford the offerings for his cleansing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day the offerings are made, and the ceremony reaches something extraordinary.

The priest takes blood from the guilt offering and puts it on the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed and on the thumb of his right hand and on the big toe of his right foot. Then he takes oil and puts it on the same three places, on top of the blood.

Those are the ordination rites. That is precisely what was done to Aaron and his sons in chapter 8 — blood, then oil, on ear and thumb and toe — and it is now being done to a man who last week was living alone outside the camp crying Unclean.

He is not merely readmitted. He is treated like a priest. The outcast is brought back by the same ceremony that installed the high priest, and Scripture never explains the parallel because it does not need to. A man goes from the far edge of the community to the rite reserved for those who stand nearest to God, in eight days.

And the chapter then scales the whole thing for poverty. But if he is poor and cannot afford so much — one lamb instead of two, and two birds instead of the rest. The cheapest version of this ceremony still ends with blood and oil on the man's ear, thumb and toe. God will not have a poor man half-restored.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 33-57: Disease in a house — inspection, seven days, stones replaced, the building scraped and replastered, and if it returns, pulled down and carried outside the city. A house that can be cleansed is cleansed with the two birds, as the man was.
verseByVerse.theology:
Provided For Before They Arrive

The law concerns a land Israel has not yet entered, given as a gift, in houses they did not build. God tells them in advance that corruption will be found there too, and makes provision for it before they get there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The priest orders the house emptied before he goes in to look, so that everything in it does not become unclean along with the walls.

Now: The law protects the family's possessions while it examines their home. And even a building gets a substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house in the land of your possession, then he who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, 'There seems to me to be some case of disease in my house.' Then the priest shall command that they empty the house before the priest goes to examine the disease, lest all that is in the house be declared unclean. And afterward the priest shall go in to see the house. And he shall examine the disease. And if the disease is in the walls of the house with greenish or reddish spots, and if it appears to be deeper than the surface, then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house and shut up the house seven days. And the priest shall come again on the seventh day, and look. If the disease has spread in the walls of the house, then the priest shall command that they take out the stones in which is the disease and throw them into an unclean place outside the city. And he shall have the inside of the house scraped all around, and the plaster that they scrape off they shall pour out in an unclean place outside the city. Then they shall take other stones and put them in the place of those stones, and he shall take other plaster and plaster the house. "If the disease breaks out again in the house, after he has taken out the stones and scraped the house and plastered it, then the priest shall go and look. And if the disease has spread in the house, it is a persistent leprous disease in the house; it is unclean. And he shall break down the house, its stones and timber and all the plaster of the house, and he shall carry them out of the city to an unclean place. Moreover, whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening, and whoever sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes, and whoever eats in the house shall wash his clothes. "But if the priest comes and looks, and if the disease has not spread in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall pronounce the house clean, for the disease is healed. And for the cleansing of the house he shall take two small birds, with cedarwood and scarlet yarn and hyssop, and shall kill one of the birds in an earthenware vessel over fresh water and shall take the cedarwood and the hyssop and the scarlet yarn, along with the live bird, and dip them in the blood of the bird that was killed and in the fresh water and sprinkle the house seven times. Thus he shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh water and with the live bird and with the cedarwood and hyssop and scarlet yarn. And he shall let the live bird go out of the city into the open country. So he shall make atonement for the house, and it shall be clean." This is the law for any case of leprous disease: for an itch, for leprous disease in a garment or in a house, and for a swelling or an eruption or a spot, to show when it is unclean and when it is clean. This is the law for leprous disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last section deals with a house — when you come into the land of Canaan, which I give you for a possession, and I put a case of leprous disease in a house. The same procedure follows: inspection, seven days shut up, stones removed and replaced, the house scraped and replastered, and re-examined. If it returns, the house is pulled down and carried outside the city.

Two details deserve notice. The first is the mercy of verse 36: the priest orders the house emptied before he goes in to look, so that everything in it does not become unclean along with the walls. The law protects the family's possessions while it examines their home.

The second is that a house with the disease in it can be cleansed — and the ritual used is the two birds again, one killed and one released over open country, exactly as for the man. Even a building gets a substitute.

And the placement of this law is deliberate. It concerns a land Israel has not yet entered, given to them as a gift, in houses they did not build. God tells them in advance that corruption will be found there too, and provides for it before they arrive.

14.theology:
Death and resurrection. The two birds — one slain, one freed in its blood — portray the gospel: Christ crucified and risen, and the sinner set free to soar.

Blood and water. The slain bird over living water anticipates the blood and water from Christ's pierced side (John 19:34) — atonement and cleansing together.

From outcast to priest. The cleansed leper is consecrated like a priest; grace does not merely readmit but elevates the forgiven to holy service.
14.examples:
Then: A healed leper watched one bird die and another fly free in its blood, was sprinkled seven times, washed, and brought home — restored to family, community, and worship.

Now: Every sinner cleansed by Christ is the leper brought home: washed in blood, raised to new life, set free to soar, and consecrated as a priest to God.

15.title: Bodily Discharges: The Pervasiveness of Defilement
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean.<sup>3</sup>And this is the law of his uncleanness for a discharge: whether his body runs with his discharge, or his body is blocked up by his discharge, it is his uncleanness.<sup>4</sup>Every bed on which the one with the discharge lies shall be unclean, and everything on which he sits shall be unclean.<sup>5</sup>And anyone who touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>6</sup>And whoever sits on anything on which the one with the discharge has sat shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>7</sup>And whoever touches the body of the one with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>8</sup>And if the one with the discharge spits on someone who is clean, then he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>9</sup>And any saddle on which the one with the discharge rides shall be unclean.<sup>10</sup>And whoever touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries such things shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>11</sup>Anyone whom the one with the discharge touches without having rinsed his hands in water shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>12</sup>And an earthenware vessel that the one with the discharge touches shall be broken, and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water.<sup>13</sup>"And when the one with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes. And he shall bathe his body in fresh water and shall be clean.<sup>14</sup>And on the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and come before the LORD to the entrance of the tent of meeting and give them to the priest.<sup>15</sup>And the priest shall use them, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD for his discharge.<sup>16</sup>"If a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>17</sup>And every garment and every skin on which the semen comes shall be washed with water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>18</sup>If a man lies with a woman and has an emission of semen, both of them shall bathe themselves in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>19</sup>"When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>20</sup>And everything on which she lies during her menstrual impurity shall be unclean. Everything also on which she sits shall be unclean.<sup>21</sup>And whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>22</sup>And whoever touches anything on which she sits shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>23</sup>Whether it is the bed or anything on which she sits, when he touches it he shall be unclean until the evening.<sup>24</sup>And if any man lies with her and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he shall be unclean seven days, and every bed on which he lies shall be unclean.<sup>25</sup>"If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstrual impurity, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her impurity, all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness. As in the days of her impurity, she shall be unclean.<sup>26</sup>Every bed on which she lies, all the days of her discharge, shall be to her as the bed of her impurity. And everything on which she sits shall be unclean, as in the uncleanness of her menstrual impurity.<sup>27</sup>And whoever touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening.<sup>28</sup>But if she is cleansed of her discharge, she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be clean.<sup>29</sup>And on the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and bring them to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>30</sup>And the priest shall use one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.<sup>31</sup>"Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst."<sup>32</sup>This is the law for him who has a discharge and for him who has an emission of semen, becoming unclean thereby;<sup>33</sup>also for her who is unwell with her menstrual impurity, that is, for anyone, male or female, who has a discharge, and for the man who lies with a woman who is unclean.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 completes the section on clean and unclean by addressing bodily discharges — the most intimate and unavoidable realities of human physical life. Normal and abnormal flows alike render one ceremonially unclean. The effect of the chapter, when read whole, is to teach the sheer pervasiveness of ritual uncleanness. It touches everyone, repeatedly, in the ordinary course of bodily existence. No one can escape it; everyone needs cleansing again and again.

This is precisely the point. Wenham argues that the very inescapability of uncleanness is the lesson: it teaches the inescapability of sin's contamination. Just as no Israelite could pass through life without becoming ceremonially unclean, so no human being can pass through life without becoming morally defiled. The contamination is woven into our very nature; it touches everything we are and do. The chapter is a sustained sermon on total depravity — not that we are as bad as we could be, but that no part of us is untouched by the fall.

And the climax (15:31) reveals the deadly seriousness: this is all about being able to dwell near "my tabernacle that is in their midst." Uncleanness defiles the sanctuary; it threatens the very thing Israel most needs — the presence of God among them. The whole elaborate system exists to guard that presence.

Then comes the gospel reversal that takes the breath away. In Mark 5, a woman with a flow of blood for twelve years — a woman who, by this very chapter, was perpetually unclean, perpetually contagious, cut off from worship and ordinary human touch for over a decade — pushes through the crowd to touch the hem of Jesus' garment. By every rule of Leviticus 15, her touch should have made him unclean. Instead, "immediately the flow of blood dried up" (Mark 5:29), and Jesus, far from recoiling, says, "Daughter... your faith has made you well; go in peace" (Mark 5:34). The current of contamination is reversed. Where uncleanness once flowed from the defiled to the holy, now cleansing flows from the Holy One to the defiled. Jesus does not catch our uncleanness; he heals it. The pervasive defilement of Leviticus 15 meets its match in the more pervasive grace of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 1-18: Genital discharges in men, chronic and ordinary, each transmitting uncleanness to beds, chairs, saddles, pots and people.

Verses 19-30: The same for women, including the chronic case — all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness.

Verses 31-33: The reason for it all: lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Sins

Most of what is described here is either an illness nobody chose or a normal function of a working body — and each puts a person temporarily outside the sphere of worship. Lived out, the law is a constant low-level reminder that being a body in a fallen world means being touched by corruption without doing anything wrong. Uncleanness is not what happens when you misbehave; it is the condition you live in.

The Woman Who Had Twelve Years of This Chapter

There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years... and was no better but rather grew worse (Mark 5:25-26). Twelve years in which nobody could touch her without consequence, twelve years shut out of worship. She comes up behind Jesus in a crowd she is defiling with every step, touches his cloak, and hopes nobody notices. By this chapter her uncleanness should pass to him. Instead immediately the flow of blood dried up.

Then he does the thing she dreaded — stops the crowd, asks who touched him, and lets her tell the whole truth in public. He could have let her slip away healed; he would not let her leave as a woman who had stolen something. He made her testify so everyone present would know she was clean, and then called her Daughter, which is the only time in the Gospels he calls anyone that.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God has taken the extraordinary risk of pitching his tent in the middle of a camp full of mortal, leaking, dying people, and the arrangement requires care from both sides.

Now: Take the whole block together — food, childbirth, disease, discharge — and the message is cumulative: no area of ordinary human life is untouched by corruption, and none of it can be argued away as somebody's fault. Which is exactly the problem the next chapter exists to solve. Leviticus has spent five chapters proving the tent cannot stay clean. It is about to show what God does about that.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying, "Speak to the people of Israel and say to them, When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean. And this is the law of his uncleanness for a discharge: whether his body runs with his discharge, or his body is blocked up by his discharge, it is his uncleanness. Every bed on which the one with the discharge lies shall be unclean, and everything on which he sits shall be unclean. And anyone who touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever sits on anything on which the one with the discharge has sat shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever touches the body of the one with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And if the one with the discharge spits on someone who is clean, then he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And any saddle on which the one with the discharge rides shall be unclean. And whoever touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until the evening. And whoever carries such things shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. Anyone whom the one with the discharge touches without having rinsed his hands in water shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And an earthenware vessel that the one with the discharge touches shall be broken, and every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water. "And when the one with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, then he shall count for himself seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes. And he shall bathe his body in fresh water and shall be clean. And on the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and come before the LORD to the entrance of the tent of meeting and give them to the priest. And the priest shall use them, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD for his discharge. "If a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water and be unclean until the evening. And every garment and every skin on which the semen comes shall be washed with water and be unclean until the evening. If a man lies with a woman and has an emission of semen, both of them shall bathe themselves in water and be unclean until the evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter deals with genital discharges, male and female, chronic and ordinary, and it is fair to ask at the outset why Scripture spends thirty-three verses on it.

These are not sins. Most of what is described here is either an illness nobody chose or a normal function of a working body. Yet each of them puts a person temporarily outside the sphere of worship, and transmits that status to beds, chairs, saddles, pots and people.

The effect of the law, lived out, is a constant low-level reminder that being a body in a fallen world means being touched by corruption without doing anything wrong. Israel could not go a month without the point being made in the most private area of life. Uncleanness is not something that happens when you misbehave. It is the condition you live in.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her menstrual impurity for seven days, and whoever touches her shall be unclean until the evening. And everything on which she lies during her menstrual impurity shall be unclean. Everything also on which she sits shall be unclean. And whoever touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. And whoever touches anything on which she sits shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. Whether it is the bed or anything on which she sits, when he touches it he shall be unclean until the evening. And if any man lies with her and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he shall be unclean seven days, and every bed on which he lies shall be unclean. "If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstrual impurity, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her impurity, all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness. As in the days of her impurity, she shall be unclean. Every bed on which she lies, all the days of her discharge, shall be to her as the bed of her impurity. And everything on which she sits shall be unclean, as in the uncleanness of her menstrual impurity. And whoever touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water and be unclean until the evening. But if she is cleansed of her discharge, she shall count for herself seven days, and after that she shall be clean. And on the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons and bring them to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting. And the priest shall use one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. And the priest shall make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean discharge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same rules are given for women, and the second case is the one the Gospels pick up: If a woman has a discharge of blood for many days, not at the time of her menstrual impurity, or if she has a discharge beyond the time of her impurity, all the days of the discharge she shall continue in uncleanness.

Read what that meant in practice. Every bed she lay on and everything she sat on was unclean. Anyone who touched those things had to wash and remain unclean until evening. A woman in this condition could not be embraced by her husband or her children without passing her status on. She was excluded from the tabernacle for as long as it lasted. If it did not stop, it did not stop.

Now Mark: There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse (Mark 5:25-26).

Twelve years under Leviticus 15. Twelve years in which nobody could touch her without consequence, twelve years shut out of worship, and every physician's bill making it worse. And she comes up behind Jesus in a crowd — a crowd she was defiling with every step — and touches his cloak, and hopes nobody notices.

By this chapter, what should have happened is obvious: her uncleanness passes to him. Instead immediately the flow of blood dried up. It went the other way, exactly as it went with the leper, exactly as it goes every time holiness meets defilement in the Gospels.

And then he does the thing she was dreading. He stops the crowd and asks who touched him, and she comes in fear and trembling and tells him the whole truth in public — twelve years of it. He could have let her slip away healed. He would not let her leave as a woman who had stolen something. He made her testify so that everyone present would know she was clean, and then he called her Daughter, which is the only time in the Gospels he calls anyone that.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst." This is the law for him who has a discharge and for him who has an emission of semen, becoming unclean thereby; also for her who is unwell with her menstrual impurity, that is, for anyone, male or female, who has a discharge, and for the man who lies with a woman who is unclean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with its reason, and it is the reason for the whole run of purity laws: Thus you shall keep the people of Israel separate from their uncleanness, lest they die in their uncleanness by defiling my tabernacle that is in their midst.

The danger is not the uncleanness itself. It is uncleanness brought into the presence of God — because God has taken the extraordinary risk of pitching his tent in the middle of a camp full of mortal, leaking, dying people, and the arrangement requires care from both sides.

Take the whole block of chapters together — food, childbirth, disease, discharge — and the cumulative message is unmistakable. There is no area of ordinary human life that is not touched by corruption, and none of it can be argued away as somebody's fault. Which is precisely the problem chapter 16 exists to solve. After five chapters demonstrating that the defilement is total and continuous, the next chapter provides one day in the year when all of it, known and unknown, is dealt with at once.

Leviticus has spent five chapters proving that the tent cannot stay clean. It is about to show what God does about that.

15.theology:
The pervasiveness of defilement. The inescapability of ritual uncleanness teaches the inescapability of sin's contamination — no part of us is untouched by the fall.

Guarding God's presence. The purity laws exist to protect the dwelling of God among his people (15:31), the very thing Israel could not live without.

The reversal in Christ. The woman of Mark 5, perpetually unclean, touches Jesus and is healed — in Christ, holiness is the stronger contagion, and cleansing flows from him to us.
15.examples:
Then: Every Israelite, through ordinary bodily life, repeatedly became unclean and needed cleansing — a daily lesson in the all-pervading reach of defilement.

Now: Like the bleeding woman, we come unclean to Jesus, and his touch does not defile him but heals us. The flow of grace reverses the flow of contamination.

16.title: The Day of Atonement: The Heart of the Gospel
16.text: <sup>2</sup>..."Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat... so that he may not die." <sup>15</sup>Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering... and bring its blood inside the veil... and sprinkle it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. <sup>21</sup>And Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel... <sup>22</sup>The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area...
16.overview:
We come now to the summit. If Leviticus is a mountain range, chapter 16 is its Everest; if the whole Old Testament sacrificial system is a great cathedral, the Day of Atonement is its high altar. Here, once a year, on the tenth day of the seventh month, the high priest did what was done on no other day: he passed through the veil into the Most Holy Place, into the immediate presence of God, bearing blood. Everything in the book has been building to this. Carson rightly calls Hebrews 9–10 the inspired commentary on this chapter, and we will not be able to read it without weeping.

First, the awful approach. Aaron may not come "at any time" into the Holy Place "so that he may not die" (16:2). Only on this one day, and only by blood. He sets aside his glorious garments and dresses in simple linen — the high priest humbled, stripped of splendor, to enter as a servant. He offers a bull for his own sin first, for even the high priest is a sinner. Then he takes the blood and the incense, and passes alone through the veil, into the blinding presence of the Holy One, where the cloud of glory dwells above the mercy seat.

Then, the two goats — the theological heart of the chapter and perhaps of the entire Bible. Lots are cast. One goat is for the LORD; it is slaughtered, and its blood is carried within the veil and sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, the atonement cover over the ark. This is propitiation — the turning away of wrath, the satisfaction of justice, the blood presented before the throne of God himself. The second goat is for Azazel; over its head Aaron lays both hands and confesses all the sins of Israel, transferring them to the animal, which is then led away into the wilderness, never to return. This is expiation — the bearing away of sin, its removal "as far as the east is from the west" (Ps 103:12). Two goats, one truth: sin must be both paid for (the blood on the mercy seat) and carried away (the scapegoat into the wilderness). Keller loved to say that on the cross both happened at once — Jesus is both the goat slain and the goat sent away, both our propitiation and our expiation.

And oh, the glory of the fulfillment. The mercy seat — the hilasterion, the place of atonement — is the very word Paul uses of Christ: "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25). Christ is the mercy seat, the place where blood meets the broken law and wrath is satisfied. He entered "once for all into the holy places... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). Aaron entered yearly, with another's blood, trembling lest he die; Christ entered once, with his own blood, and sat down. And when he died, "the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom" (Matt 27:51) — the veil that barred the way ripped open by the hand of God, the road into the Most Holy Place flung wide forever. Sproul never tired of saying that the mercy seat is where the holiness of God and the mercy of God kiss. There, the blood covers the broken law beneath; there, justice and love embrace. And from the cross came the cry that ended all the sacrifices forever: "It is finished" (John 19:30). The scapegoat has carried our sin beyond the reach of memory; the blood is on the mercy seat; the veil is torn; the way is open. Holy, holy, holy — and we may come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — Before the Veil: How Aaron May Enter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The most solemn day of Israel's year opens not with ceremony but with a grave: "after the death of the two sons of Aaron" (v.1). Nadab and Abihu had rushed into God's presence with strange fire, and died. So the whole chapter is God's answer to a burning question — how may a sinful man come near a holy God and live? The answer is: not at any time, not any way he pleases, but only on this one day, only by blood, and only as God prescribes. Aaron lays aside his golden splendor and dresses in plain linen, bathes, and gathers a bull for his own sin and two goats for the people's. Before he touches anyone else's guilt, he must reckon with his own. Then the lots are cast over the two goats — one for the LORD, one for Azazel — the two halves of a single mercy about to unfold.
verseByVerse.theology: Access to God is God's gift, not man's right. The death of Nadab and Abihu stands at the door of this chapter as a warning written in blood: God will be treated as holy (Lev 10:3). Yet the same God who says "not at any time" opens "this way" (v.3) — grace hedged by holiness. And that the high priest must atone for himself first (v.6) exposes the flaw in every earthly mediator: he is himself a sinner. It makes us ache for a priest who needs no sacrifice for his own sin (Heb 7:26-27).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: no Israelite could stroll into God's presence; even the high priest entered trembling, once a year, by blood, or died.

Now: we have a High Priest "holy, innocent, unstained" who offered no sacrifice for Himself because He had no sin — and who bids us "draw near with confidence" (Heb 4:16). The linen Aaron put on, Christ was: perfect righteousness. We come clothed not in our splendor but in His.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron... Tell Aaron your brother not to come at any time into the Holy Place inside the veil, before the mercy seat... so that he may not die.
verseByVerse.commentary: The date-stamp is a grave. Nadab and Abihu had offered "unauthorized fire before the LORD" and were consumed (Lev 10:1-2); now their father is told plainly why the veil exists. It is not decoration but a barrier — a "keep out" sewn in blue and purple and scarlet, guarding the mercy seat where God said "I will appear in the cloud." The lesson lands hard on us who speak so casually of coming to God: the Holy One cannot be approached "at any time," on a whim, in a manner of our own choosing. The wonder of the gospel is not that God lowered the barrier but that He Himself passed through it — and then, at the cross, tore it from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). Feel both the terror and the tenderness here: the God who says "lest he die" is the God who would die that we might live.

verseByVerse.quote: But in this way Aaron shall come into the Holy Place: with a bull from the herd for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering... He shall put on the holy linen coat... He shall bathe his body in water and then put them on.
verseByVerse.commentary: "But in this way" — three words of pure grace. God does not only bar the door; He shows the way through it. Notice the change of clothes. On other days the high priest blazed with gold, blue, and precious stones, bells ringing as he moved (Ex 28). Today he strips it all off and puts on plain white linen, bathed and lowly, dressed like the humblest servant. The greater the day, the lower he stoops — a picture of our Lord, who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7), laying aside His glory to do the work of atonement. The goats and the ram come "from the congregation": the people supply the victims, for it is their sin being dealt with. Everything is provided; nothing is left to improvisation. Salvation is meticulous because holiness is not careless.

verseByVerse.quote: Aaron shall offer the bull as a sin offering for himself and shall make atonement for himself and for his house... And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats, one lot for the LORD and the other lot for Azazel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before Aaron can carry anyone else's sin, he must deal with his own. The mediator kneels as a sinner first — a quiet confession that no son of Aaron is clean enough to save. This is the crack in the old priesthood that makes us long for a better one: a priest who has "no need... to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins" (Heb 7:27). Then the two goats are set before the LORD and lots are cast. The meaning of Azazel is debated — perhaps a name for the place of removal, or simply "the goat that goes away," the scapegoat. But the picture is unmistakable: two goats, one atonement. One will be killed and its blood carried in; the other sent away alive, carrying sin out. Sin must be both paid for and carried away — and at Calvary both goats meet in one Lord: Jesus is the goat slain and the goat sent away at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-19 — Within the Veil: Blood on the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the high priest does what no one else in Israel may do, and what he himself may do only today: he passes through the veil into the Most Holy Place, into the immediate presence of God. He carries a censer of burning coals and sweet incense, so that a cloud will veil the mercy seat "that he may not die" (v.13) — even the mediator must be shielded from the unclouded glory. Then comes the blood: first the bull's, for himself; then the goat's, for the people; sprinkled on and before the mercy seat, seven times over. The very sanctuary is cleansed "because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel" (v.16). This is the beating heart of Leviticus, and Hebrews 9—10 is its inspired commentary.
verseByVerse.theology: This is propitiation — blood presented before the throne of God to turn away wrath and satisfy justice. The mercy seat (Hebrew kapporet, the "atonement cover") is where the blood meets the broken law kept in the ark beneath it. Here holiness and mercy meet without either being compromised: the law is honored, the sinner is spared. Paul reaches for this very object when he says God put Christ forward as a "propitiation by his blood" (Rom 3:25) — Jesus is the true mercy seat. And note: even the sanctuary needs cleansing, because sin defiles everything it touches, and "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb 9:22).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: once a year one man, alone, in a cloud of incense, sprinkled blood in the dark on a golden lid, and Israel's sins were covered for another year.

Now: Christ "entered once for all into the holy places... by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption" (Heb 9:12). He needed no incense-cloud to survive God's presence — He is that presence. He did not sprinkle and withdraw; He sat down (Heb 10:12). What Aaron repeated every year because it was never finished, Christ did once because it was.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall take a censer full of coals of fire from the altar... and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and he shall bring it inside the veil... that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat... And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger... seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary: Watch the high priest disappear behind the curtain. He carries fire and incense, and a cloud rises to shroud the mercy seat — for no man, not even Aaron, can gaze on the unveiled glory and live. The incense is a mercy: it hides him. Then he sprinkles the blood of his own bull "on the front of the mercy seat... seven times" — seven, the number of completeness, atonement fully made. Picture it: the ark below holds the tablets of the law Israel has broken; the blood falls above them, between the broken law and the God who gave it. That golden lid is the most important object in the world that day, because it is where wrath and mercy meet. Here is the gospel in shadow — the law accuses from beneath, the blood answers from above, and God looks down not on our sin but on the sprinkled blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people and bring its blood inside the veil... sprinkling it over the mercy seat and in front of the mercy seat. Thus he shall make atonement for the Holy Place, because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel...
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the people's goat. Its blood is carried where no Israelite could go, sprinkled where only God could see, "because of the uncleannesses of the people of Israel and... all their sins" (v.16). Notice what is being cleansed: not only the people but the place. Sin is so contaminating that it defiles even the tent where God consents to dwell "in the midst of their uncleannesses." Holiness and sin cannot share a room; either the sin is purged or the presence departs. So the blood goes everywhere — the Most Holy Place, the tent, the altar — each sprinkled seven times, each made clean. And while Aaron works, "no one may be in the tent of meeting" (v.17): atonement is a lonely labor. On the great Day of ours, too, the Mediator was utterly alone — "I have trodden the winepress alone" (Isa 63:3) — forsaken even by God, that we might never be.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-28 — Outside the Camp: Sin Carried Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blood has been presented; now sin must be removed. Aaron lays both hands on the head of the living goat and confesses over it "all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins" (v.21) — every category, nothing held back, pressed down onto the animal's head. Then the goat is led away by an appointed man into the wilderness, "to a remote area," and released where it can never find its way home. Israel watched it shrink to a dot on the horizon and vanish — and knew their sin was gone. Then the priest washes and reclothes, and the sin offerings are carried "outside the camp" and burned. Two movements, one atonement: sin paid for by blood, sin borne away by the goat.
verseByVerse.theology: This is expiation — the actual removal of guilt. The laying on of hands is a transfer: the sin of the people is reckoned to the substitute, and the substitute carries it away "to a remote area," never to return. It is Isaiah's gospel centuries early: "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6). And that the sin offerings are burned "outside the camp" is not lost on the New Testament: "So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood" (Heb 13:12). Our sin was carried out of the city, out of the camp, out of God's sight — as far as the east is from the west (Ps 103:12).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a nation stood in silence and watched a goat carry their sins over the horizon until it disappeared, and they believed it was gone.

Now: we look not at a vanishing goat but at an empty tomb. Christ carried our sins not into a wilderness we might one day stumble back into, but into death itself, and left them there. When guilt whispers that the old sins are still on file, faith answers with the horizon: it is gone, borne away, out of reach forever. "There is therefore now no condemnation" (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over it all the iniquities of the people of Israel, and all their transgressions, all their sins... The goat shall bear all their iniquities on itself to a remote area, and he shall let the goat go free in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is one of the most vivid pictures of salvation in all of Scripture. Aaron presses both hands on the goat's head — not a light touch but a leaning weight — and speaks aloud every kind of sin: iniquities (the crookedness of the heart), transgressions (deliberate rebellions), and sins (the failures and misses). Three words to leave nothing out; a whole year of a whole nation's guilt named over one head. Then the goat is led away and let go "in the wilderness," to a land cut off, never to return. Israel did not merely hear that their sin was forgiven; they watched it walk away. This is what your Savior did with your sin: He took it on His own head — "the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isa 53:6) — and carried it beyond recovery. It is not filed away. It is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and shall take off the linen garments... and shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments and come out and offer his burnt offering and the burnt offering of the people and make atonement for himself and for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary: With the sin borne away, the mood changes. Aaron washes, lays aside the plain linen, and puts his glorious garments back on — the servant's work done, the splendor restored. It is a small resurrection picture: humiliation, then glory; the linen of suffering exchanged for the robes of honor, as our Lord, having finished the work, was "crowned with glory and honor" (Heb 2:9). Now come the burnt offerings — whole animals given up entirely to God in the flames. Once sin has been dealt with, worship can rise. The order is everything and never changes: first atonement, then adoration; first the sin removed, then the life poured out in thankful surrender. We do not worship our way into acceptance; we are accepted, and so we worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he who lets the goat go to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water... And the bull for the sin offering and the goat for the sin offering... shall be carried outside the camp. Their skin and their flesh and their dung shall be burned up with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the man who handled the scapegoat, even the one who burns the carcasses, must wash before returning to the camp — sin's contamination clings to everything near it. And the bodies of the sin offerings are not eaten but carried "outside the camp" and burned to ash. The writer of Hebrews sees his Lord in that lonely fire beyond the gate: "So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured" (Heb 13:12-13). Golgotha was outside the city wall — the sin-bearer cast out as unclean, treated as sin itself, so that the unclean might be brought in. The place of shame became the place of cleansing. And the call to us is to go out to Him there, willing to share His reproach, because the camp of this world has nothing that compares.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-34 — A Statute Forever: The Sabbath of Atonement
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Finally God fixes the day in the calendar forever: the tenth day of the seventh month. On it Israel must "afflict yourselves and... do no work" (v.29) — the one day of the year commanded for fasting and self-denial, a Sabbath of solemn rest. The people do nothing; the priest does everything; and "on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you" (v.30). It is to be repeated "once in the year... forever" — and that very repetition preaches its own insufficiency. A finished work is never repeated. That the Day of Atonement came round every autumn was God's annual reminder that the true and final atonement had not yet come.
verseByVerse.theology: The command to "afflict yourselves" and yet "do no work" holds two truths together: we bring nothing to our cleansing but our need, and we rest while Another works. Atonement is received, not achieved. Yet its yearly return exposes the shadow: "it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins" (Heb 10:4). These sacrifices covered, deferred, and pointed forward; they could not finish. So the whole calendar leaned toward a cross, where One would cry "It is finished" (John 19:30) and the annual day would never be needed again.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: every autumn Israel fasted, rested, and watched their high priest secure another year's cleansing — and then waited, because it would all have to be done again.

Now: our Day of Atonement is behind us, done once by the true High Priest, and it will never come round again. The believer's whole life becomes the Sabbath rest these verses foreshadowed: "we who have believed enter that rest" (Heb 4:3). We grieve our sin no longer to earn cleansing, but because we already have it; we rest, because He has worked.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be a statute to you forever that in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and shall do no work... For on this day shall atonement be made for you to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins. It is a Sabbath of solemn rest...
verseByVerse.commentary: Notice the strange pairing: "afflict yourselves" and "do no work." Israel must feel the weight of sin — this was the one fast day in the law, a day to humble the soul — and yet must lift not a finger toward its own cleansing. Both are the gospel. We come empty-handed, mourning our sin, bringing nothing; and we rest, because the work is the priest's, not ours. "You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins" — not some, all; not partly, clean. What a word for a burdened conscience. And it is called "a Sabbath of solemn rest," the deepest rest of the year, because the deepest rest a soul can know is to be clean before God and to have contributed nothing but need. That rest has a name: "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: He shall make atonement for the holy sanctuary... for the tent of meeting and for the altar... for the priests and for all the people of the assembly. And this shall be a statute forever for you, that atonement may be made for the people of Israel once in the year because of all their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: The atonement is total in its reach — sanctuary, tent, altar, priests, and "all the people of the assembly" — nothing and no one left uncleansed. Yet listen to the two words that expose the whole system's limit: "once in the year." Every autumn it came again, because every autumn it wore off. A finished work is never repeated; the yearly return of this day was God's own admission that the real atonement was still to come (Heb 10:1-4). And so the chapter that is the summit of Leviticus is also a signpost, pointing past itself to a hill outside Jerusalem where the true High Priest would enter the true sanctuary with His own blood, "once for all" (Heb 9:12), and sit down. The book closes its holiest chapter with "once in the year"; the gospel answers with "once for all." And the veil that kept us out was torn in two, from top to bottom, forever.

16.theology:
Propitiation. The blood on the mercy seat turns away wrath and satisfies justice. Christ is our hilasterion, the propitiation by his blood (Rom 3:25; 1 John 2:2) — the place where holiness and mercy meet.

Expiation. The scapegoat bears confessed sin away into the wilderness. Christ carries our sin beyond recovery: 'the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all' (Isa 53:6).

Once for all. Aaron entered yearly with another's blood; Christ entered once with his own and sat down (Heb 9:12; 10:12). The torn veil (Matt 27:51) opens the way forever.
16.examples:
Then: Once a year all Israel waited in trembling silence as the high priest, in linen, passed alone through the veil with blood; one goat died and another was driven into the wilderness, and the nation was declared clean.

Now: Christ, our great High Priest, entered the true sanctuary with his own blood, once for all. He is both the goat slain and the goat sent away. The veil is torn; we draw near with confidence (Heb 10:19-22), resting in his cry: 'It is finished.'

17.title: The Sanctity of Blood: Life Given for Life
17.text: <sup>11</sup>For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.
17.overview:
With chapter 17 we cross into the second half of Leviticus, often called the Holiness Code (chs 17–27), where the focus shifts from the sanctuary to the life of the people — holiness lived out in the world. And it begins, fittingly, with blood. All slaughter must be brought to the tabernacle; no sacrificing in the open field to demons; and above all, no eating of blood. Why such reverence for blood? The chapter gives the answer in the single most important verse for understanding atonement in all of Scripture.

"For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life" (17:11). Here is the theological key that unlocks the whole sacrificial system. Blood is life; the wages of sin is death; therefore atonement requires the giving of a life in the place of the forfeit life. The blood on the altar is not magic; it is substituted life. God himself says, "I have given it" — atonement is God's gift, God's provision, God's gracious appointment.

The writer of Hebrews builds his entire argument on this verse: "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins" (Heb 9:22). There is no bloodless gospel. The cross is not an embarrassment to be explained away but the necessary outworking of this principle: life for life, blood for blood, the innocent for the guilty. To strip the blood from Christianity is to strip away the atonement, and with it all hope.

And the blood that once was forbidden to drink becomes, in Christ, the cup of the new covenant. "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins" (Matt 26:28). The blood of Christ "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24) — Abel's blood cried for vengeance; Christ's blood cries mercy, mercy, mercy. The sanctity of blood in Leviticus 17 finds its everlasting meaning at Calvary, where the life of the Son of God was poured out to make atonement for our souls.

sections.title: All Slaughter Brought to the LORD
sections.commentary:
Every animal killed for food must first be brought to the tabernacle, lest the people sacrifice "to goat demons, after whom they whore" (17:7). Calvin notes the pastoral wisdom: by centralizing slaughter, God guards his people from the idolatry that lurked in the open fields. Every meat-meal became an act of worship, a confession that life belongs to God.

The principle endures: there is no neutral territory. The God who claims the altar claims the field, the kitchen, the table. To take life, even for food, is to handle something sacred, and it must be done before the Lord.

sections.title: The Life Is in the Blood
sections.commentary:
This is the golden verse of Leviticus. "The life of the flesh is in the blood." Therefore blood, as life, is sacred — and therefore blood, as substituted life, can make atonement. Sproul called this the most concise statement of substitutionary atonement in the Old Testament. The penalty for sin is death; in the sacrificial blood, a life is given in the place of the sinner's life.

Note the divine initiative: "I have given it for you on the altar." Atonement is not something we achieve to placate an unwilling God; it is God's own gift, his gracious provision for our salvation. The cross is the Father's idea before it is the Son's obedience — "God so loved the world that he gave" (John 3:16). The blood does not change God's heart toward us; it flows from a heart already set on mercy.

sections.title: The Prohibition of Blood and Its Fulfillment
sections.commentary:
Twice the prohibition is pressed: no one shall eat blood, for the life is in it. The reverence is total. And this is what makes the words of Jesus at the Last Supper so staggering: "Drink of it, all of you, for this is my blood of the covenant" (Matt 26:27–28). The unthinkable command, the blood once utterly forbidden, now offered as the cup of salvation. In John 6 Jesus presses it to scandal: "unless you... drink his blood, you have no life in you" (John 6:53).

Begg observes the breathtaking reversal: the blood that meant death to consume now means life to receive — because it is the blood of the One whose life, poured out, becomes our life. "Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Heb 9:22), but the blood that has been shed now "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel" (Heb 12:24), crying not for vengeance but for mercy over all who trust in Christ.

sections.title: Holiness in the Handling of Life
sections.commentary:
Even eating an animal that died of itself, with its blood undrained, brings uncleanness requiring washing. The reverence for blood extends to the edges of ordinary life. The lesson is cumulative: life is God's, blood is sacred, and the people of God must handle the gift of life with reverence and care.

For the church, the enduring application is a profound reverence for the blood of Christ. We dare not treat lightly what cost the Son of God his life. To trifle with sin is to trample the blood (Heb 10:29); to receive grace is to be awed by the price.

17.theology:
Substitutionary atonement. 'It is the blood that makes atonement by the life' (17:11) — the giving of a life in place of the forfeit life is the heart of the sacrificial system and the cross.

Atonement as God's gift. 'I have given it for you' — atonement is God's gracious provision, flowing from a heart already set on mercy (John 3:16).

The blood that speaks mercy. The blood once forbidden becomes the cup of the new covenant; Christ's blood 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel' (Heb 12:24).
17.examples:
Then: Israel brought all slaughter to the LORD and drained the blood, reverencing life as God's and learning that atonement comes only through substituted life.

Now: We rest in the blood of Christ, shed for the forgiveness of sins, and receive the cup of the new covenant with awe — for without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, and that blood has been shed for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands that all sacrifices be brought to the one altar at the tent of meeting — no more slaughtering in the open field, no more offerings to the "goat demons" after whom Israel had played the harlot. Worship is not to be improvised wherever a person pleases; it comes to God's appointed place, in God's appointed way. There is one altar, because there is one way to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Centralizing sacrifice at the one altar guards against idolatry ("goat demons," v.7) and against worship on human terms. It teaches that access to God is not a free-for-all but comes his way, at his appointed place — ultimately fulfilled in the one altar, the cross, and the one mediator, Christ, for "there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men" (1 Tim 2:5). There are not many ways to God; there is one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: an Israelite could not set up his own altar wherever he liked; he brought his offering to the one place God appointed.

Now: we do not invent our own way to God; we come by the one way he has opened — "no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). One altar, one Mediator, one gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: If any one of the house of Israel kills an ox or a lamb or a goat... and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it as a gift to the LORD... that man shall be cut off from among his people... So they shall no more sacrifice their sacrifices to goat demons, after whom they whore.
verseByVerse.commentary: God commands that every sacrifice be brought to the one altar at the tent of meeting. No more killing sacrificial animals out in the open field, wherever one happened to be. Why such insistence on a single place? Two reasons surface. First, to guard against idolatry: scattered, private sacrifices had a way of drifting into offerings to "goat demons," the false gods of the field, "after whom they whore." Centralized worship kept Israel from slipping into the paganism all around them. Second, and deeper, to teach that worship comes to God on God's terms, at God's appointed place, in God's appointed way — never improvised to suit ourselves. There is one altar because there is one way to God. This truth runs straight through the Bible and lands at the cross, the one true altar, and at Christ, the one Mediator: "there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). The world imagines many roads up the mountain; God says there is one, and he has opened it himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-16 — The Life Is in the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now comes one of the most important verses in the entire Bible — the theological heart of the whole sacrificial system. God forbids the eating of blood, and tells them why: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life." Blood is sacred because life is sacred, and blood is the God-given means of atonement. Here, in one sentence, is why the cross had to be.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviticus 17:11 is the golden key to the whole book and to the gospel: "it is the blood that makes atonement by the life."
