Now: We live by Christ our light and bread, kept continually before the Father, and we hallow the Name we once dishonored — for Christ bore its curse and teaches us to pray, 'Hallowed be your name.'

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Lamp and the Bread of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two continual acts of worship are commanded: the pure oil to keep the lamp burning before the LORD "regularly, from evening to morning," and the twelve loaves of the bread of the Presence, set out fresh each Sabbath before God's face. Light and bread, kept perpetually in God's presence — one for each tribe — a standing sign that God's people are always before him, always provided for, always in his light.
verseByVerse.theology: The continual lamp (light) and the twelve loaves (bread, one per tribe) keep all Israel perpetually "before the LORD" (vv.3-4, 8). They picture God's people held constantly in his presence, provided for and illumined by him. Both point to Christ, "the light of the world" (John 8:12) and "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and to the fellowship he gives — a people kept before God's face and fed from his own hand.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the lamp burned and the bread lay before God's face without fail — a silent, standing sign that Israel was never out of his sight or beyond his care.

Now: in Christ we are kept perpetually before God, fed with the Bread of life and walking in his light. We are never forgotten, never out of his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Command the people of Israel to bring you pure oil from beaten olives for the lamp, that a light may be kept burning regularly... Aaron shall arrange it from evening to morning before the LORD regularly... You shall take fine flour and bake twelve loaves... And you shall set them in two piles... on the table of pure gold before the LORD... as a covenant forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two acts of continual worship frame the sanctuary: the ever-burning lamp and the ever-present bread. The people bring pure beaten olive oil so the lamp never goes dark, tended "from evening to morning before the LORD." And on the golden table sit twelve loaves of the bread of the Presence — literally the bread "of the face," one loaf for each of the twelve tribes, laid out fresh every Sabbath before God's face. Together they say something quietly wonderful. The light burning continually means God's people are never left in the dark; the bread standing perpetually means they are never out of his presence or beyond his provision. All twelve tribes, always, are kept before the face of God — remembered, illumined, and fed. And both point to Jesus. He is "the light of the world" (John 8:12), the lamp that never goes out; and he is "the bread of life" (John 6:35), the true bread of the Presence. To belong to him is to be kept eternally before the Father's face, walking in his light and fed at his table. You are never forgotten, never in the dark, never out of his sight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-23 — The Blasphemer, and Just Measure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A real incident interrupts the laws: a man of mixed parentage blasphemes "the Name" in a fight and is held in custody until God gives judgment — he is to be stoned. Woven into the ruling comes the principle of proportional justice: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" — a limit on vengeance, an equal standard for native and sojourner alike. God's name is holy and not to be dragged in the mud; and God's justice is exact, neither excessive nor slack.
verseByVerse.theology: The gravity of blaspheming "the Name" (vv.11, 16) shows how seriously God guards his own honor — the third commandment is no small thing (Ex 20:7). The lex talionis, "fracture for fracture, eye for eye" (v.20), is not license for revenge but the ceiling of just penalty, applied equally to "the sojourner and the native" (v.22) — one impartial standard of justice. Both truths meet at the cross, where the God whose name is holy bore, in the person of his Son, the exact penalty our sin deserved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God's name was guarded as holy, and his justice measured to the exact wrong, the same for foreigner and citizen alike.

Now: we "hallow" God's name (Matt 6:9) and trust his perfect justice. And we marvel that the holy Name we profaned was vindicated by the Son who bore our exact penalty in our place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an Israelite woman's son, whose father was an Egyptian... blasphemed the Name, and cursed. Then they brought him to Moses... And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying, Bring out of the camp the one who cursed... Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death... fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth... You shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native.
verseByVerse.commentary: Suddenly the flow of laws is broken by a real event: a man of mixed Egyptian and Israelite parentage, in the heat of a fight, blasphemes "the Name" — so sacred that the text will not even write it out — and curses. The people, unsure what to do, hold him in custody until God gives judgment, and the judgment is severe. This startles us, but it measures how seriously God guards his own holy name. The third commandment — "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain" (Ex 20:7) — is no minor rule. To drag God's name through the mud is to assault the holiest thing there is. Woven into the ruling comes the famous principle "eye for eye, tooth for tooth." As in Exodus 21, this is not a charter for revenge but a limit on it: the penalty may never exceed the crime, and — importantly — "you shall have the same rule for the sojourner and for the native." One law, one standard of justice, for foreigner and citizen alike; God's justice does not have one scale for the insider and another for the outsider. And here is the wonder the gospel adds: the holy Name that we have all profaned was vindicated not by our punishment but by the Son of God, who took the exact penalty our sin deserved, so that blasphemers might be forgiven and taught to pray, "Hallowed be your name" (Matt 6:9).

25.title: The Jubilee: The Year of the LORD's Favor
25.text: <sup>10</sup>And you shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 unveils one of the most radical and beautiful institutions in all of Scripture: the Sabbatical Year and, every fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Every seventh year the land rested and debts were eased; but every fiftieth year, the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement and liberty was proclaimed throughout the land — slaves set free, debts cancelled, ancestral lands restored to their original families. A whole society pressed the reset button. The poor were lifted, the enslaved were liberated, the dispossessed came home.

The theology beneath it is breathtaking: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (25:23). Israel did not ultimately own the land; God did. They were tenants of his grace. Therefore no debt could be permanent, no slavery perpetual, no family forever dispossessed — because everything belonged to God, and God is a Redeemer. The Jubilee was grace written into the economic order, a structural mercy, a society shaped by the character of a liberating God.

And then, in the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus stood up, opened the scroll of Isaiah, and read words steeped in the language of Jubilee: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to proclaim liberty to the captives... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" (Luke 4:18–19). Then he rolled up the scroll and said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). Jesus declared himself the true Jubilee. He is the liberty for the captives, the release for the debtors, the homecoming for the dispossessed. Every slave he frees, every debt he cancels, every exile he brings home.

Keller loved to preach that the gospel is the ultimate Jubilee: our debt of sin — which we could never repay — is cancelled entirely; our slavery to sin is broken; our lost inheritance is restored; and we who were strangers are brought home to the family of God. And the Jubilee that Christ inaugurated will be consummated in the new creation, the everlasting year of the Lord's favor, when all things are restored and the whole earth rests in the freedom of the children of God. The trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — for it is by the blood of the cross that our true Jubilee is bought. Liberty, at last, throughout the land.

sections.title: The Sabbath of the Land
sections.commentary:
Every seventh year the land itself was to rest — no sowing, no reaping, a Sabbath for the soil (25:1–7). The people had to trust God to provide. This taught radical dependence: the same lesson as the manna, that man does not live by his own labor alone but by the provision of God.

Calvin notes that the Sabbath year trained Israel to trust the LORD's provision over their own striving. It is a rebuke to the anxious, grasping, never-resting spirit of fallen humanity, and a call to the rest of faith that finds its fullness in Christ, who says, "Come to me... and I will give you rest" (Matt 11:28).

sections.title: The Year of Jubilee: Liberty Proclaimed
sections.commentary:
Every fiftieth year, on the Day of Atonement, the trumpet sounded and Jubilee was proclaimed: "proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants" (25:10). Slaves freed, debts released, ancestral lands returned. It is no accident that the Jubilee trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement — liberty flows from atonement; freedom is bought by blood.

This is the very text echoed in Isaiah 61 and read by Jesus at Nazareth (Luke 4:18–21). Keller called the gospel the ultimate Jubilee: the unpayable debt of sin cancelled, the chains of bondage struck off, the lost inheritance restored, the exile brought home. "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" — Jesus is the Jubilee in person.

sections.title: The Land Is Mine: A Theology of Redemption
sections.commentary:
The foundation is laid bare: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me" (25:23). Because everything belongs to God, no loss is permanent, and the figure of the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) emerges — the near relative who buys back lost land or frees an enslaved kinsman (25:25, 47–49). This is the role Boaz plays for Ruth, and the role, supremely, that Christ plays for us.

Carson observes that the kinsman-redeemer points unmistakably to Jesus, who took on our flesh to become our near kinsman (Heb 2:11–17) and redeemed us — bought us back — not with silver but with his own blood (1 Pet 1:18–19). The Jubilee theology of redemption finds its center in the Redeemer who restores our lost inheritance and brings us home. The whole chapter is a meditation on the God who will not let his people stay enslaved, indebted, or dispossessed forever.

25.theology:
The gospel as Jubilee. Liberty for captives, cancelled debts, restored inheritance — fulfilled in Christ who proclaimed 'the year of the Lord's favor' (Luke 4:18-21) as accomplished in himself.

'The land is mine.' All belongs to God (25:23); we are sojourners of his grace, which is why no debt or bondage is permanent under his rule.

The kinsman-redeemer. The go'el who buys back lost land and frees the enslaved points to Christ, our near kinsman who redeemed us with his blood (Heb 2:14-17; 1 Pet 1:18-19).
25.examples:
Then: Every fiftieth year the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, and across Israel slaves went free, debts were cancelled, and families returned to their lost lands — grace built into the social order.

Now: Jesus is our Jubilee. He cancels the unpayable debt of sin, breaks our slavery, restores our inheritance, and brings us home — and will consummate the everlasting year of the Lord's favor in the new creation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-22 — The Sabbath Year and the Year of Jubilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sabbath principle now expands to its grandest scale. Every seventh year the land itself rests. And every fiftieth year — after seven Sabbaths of years — comes the Jubilee: a trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement, and "liberty" is proclaimed "throughout the land to all its inhabitants." Debts are cancelled, slaves go free, and every family returns to its ancestral land. It is a national reset of grace, a year of release — and it is the very passage Jesus opened to announce his mission.
verseByVerse.theology: The Jubilee ("proclaim liberty throughout the land," v.10 — the words on the Liberty Bell) is the Sabbath principle applied to society: a God-ordained release of debts, slaves, and land, so that poverty could never become permanent and no family was locked forever out of its inheritance. It required extraordinary faith — God promised to provide a triple harvest in the sixth year (vv.20-22). And it points unmistakably to Christ, who opened Isaiah's Jubilee prophecy in Nazareth and said, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:18-21) — proclaiming liberty to captives and "the year of the Lord's favor." He is the true Jubilee.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: when the Jubilee trumpet sounded, the debtor was freed, the slave went home, the lost family land was restored — a whole society released by grace.

Now: Jesus is our Jubilee. He "proclaims liberty to the captives" (Luke 4:18), cancels the debt we could never pay (Col 2:14), and restores our lost inheritance (1 Pet 1:4). The trumpet has sounded; the year of favor has come.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath to the LORD. For six years you shall sow your field... but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of solemn rest for the land, a Sabbath to the LORD. You shall not sow your field or prune your vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sabbath rhythm, which governed the day and the week, now governs the years. Every seventh year the land itself must rest — no sowing, no pruning, no organized harvest — "a Sabbath to the LORD." Whatever grows on its own is left for the poor and the animals to eat freely. This was a remarkable act of trust. To let your fields lie fallow an entire year meant staking your survival on the faithfulness of God to provide. It taught Israel, on a grand scale, the same lesson the weekly Sabbath taught on a small one: the world does not depend on your ceaseless labor; God is the one who provides. The land, too, belongs to him and lives by his rhythm, not our greed. There is wisdom here even for creation care — God builds rest into the very soil — but the heart of it is faith. A people who could trust God enough to stop working for a whole year had learned the deepest lesson of the gospel: that our life and provision rest not in our striving but in the hands of a faithful God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall consecrate the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee for you, when each of you shall return to his property and each of you shall return to his clan... For it is a jubilee. It shall be holy to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the mountaintop of the whole system: the Year of Jubilee. After seven Sabbaths of years, in the fiftieth year, on the Day of Atonement, a trumpet sounds across the whole nation, and "liberty" is proclaimed "throughout the land to all its inhabitants" — the very words later cast onto the Liberty Bell. And what liberty it was: debts cancelled, slaves set free, and every family restored to its ancestral land. Whatever a man had lost through poverty or misfortune over the decades was given back. It was a national reset of grace, ensuring that in Israel poverty could never become a permanent, inescapable prison, and no family could be locked out of its inheritance forever. It required staggering faith — but God promised to send a triple harvest in the sixth year to carry them through (vv.20-22). And every fiftieth-year trumpet was pointing forward. When Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, he opened the scroll to Isaiah's Jubilee prophecy — "to proclaim liberty to the captives... to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor" — and said, "Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:18-21). He is the true Jubilee. He cancels the debt we could never pay (Col 2:14), sets the captives free (John 8:36), and restores the inheritance we had forfeited (1 Pet 1:4). The trumpet has sounded, and his name is Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-55 — Redemption of Land and of People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Jubilee rests on a stunning truth: "The land is mine," says the LORD; Israel are only tenants, "strangers and sojourners with me" (v.23). So land could never be sold permanently, only leased until the Jubilee, and a kinsman could always redeem it. The same mercy extends to people: care for the poor brother, lend without interest, and if he is sold into servitude, a redeemer may buy him back. Here the great biblical word "redeem" fills the page — and points to the Redeemer who bought us back.
verseByVerse.theology: "The land is mine... you are strangers and sojourners with me" (v.23) grounds everything: we own nothing absolutely; all is God's, held in trust. The kinsman-redeemer (go'el) who buys back lost land or an enslaved relative (vv.25, 47-49) is one of Scripture's clearest pictures of Christ, our near Kinsman who took our flesh to redeem us (Heb 2:11-14; Ruth 4). The care commanded for the poor — no interest, no harsh rule, release at Jubilee — flows from grace: "for they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt" (v.42). Redeemed people redeem.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a ruined man was not abandoned; a kinsman could step in, pay the price, and buy back his land or his freedom.

Now: we had lost everything and sold ourselves to sin, but our near Kinsman came — "you were bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20). Christ is the Redeemer who paid what we could not, and brought us home.

verseByVerse.quote: The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me... If your brother becomes poor and sells part of his property, then his nearest redeemer shall come and redeem what his brother has sold... If your brother becomes poor... you shall support him... You shall not lend him your money at interest.
verseByVerse.commentary: Beneath the whole Jubilee lies one earth-shaking sentence: "The land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me." Israel did not ultimately own the land at all; God did, and they were his tenants, holding it in trust. That is why land could never be sold off forever, only leased until the next Jubilee — and why a "nearest redeemer" could always step in to buy it back for a ruined relative. Here that great biblical word appears: redeem. The kinsman-redeemer (the go'el) is a relative near enough and able enough to pay the price and restore what his brother has lost — the role Boaz would play for Ruth (Ruth 4). And the same tender mercy governs how the poor are treated: support your struggling brother, lend without grinding interest, never rule over him harshly. Why such kindness? "For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt" (v.42). Grace received becomes grace given. And the kinsman-redeemer points straight to Christ, our near Kinsman, who took our very flesh and blood (Heb 2:14) so that he might pay the price and buy back everything we had lost.

verseByVerse.quote: If your brother becomes poor beside you and sells himself to you, you shall not make him serve as a slave... For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt... he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him... For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends by extending redemption from land to people. If an Israelite fell so deep into poverty that he had to sell himself into servitude, he was not to be treated as a slave but as a hired worker, and he was to go free at the Jubilee. And crucially, he could always be redeemed — a brother, an uncle, any near kinsman with the means could come and pay the price to buy him back before the Jubilee arrived. The reason God gives is the ground of everything: "For it is to me that the people of Israel are servants... whom I brought out of the land of Egypt." They already belonged to God, who had redeemed them from Egyptian bondage; they could never be the permanent property of another master. Do you see how the whole chapter has been preparing us for the gospel? We were the ones who sold ourselves — sold under sin (Rom 7:14), enslaved, our inheritance forfeited, no way back on our own. And then our Kinsman-Redeemer came. He did not send money by another hand; he came in person, took our flesh, and paid the price with his own blood. "You were bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20); "you were ransomed... with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:18-19). The Jubilee trumpet finds its final, joyful blast at the cross, where the true Redeemer proclaimed liberty to the captives forever.

26.title: Blessings and Curses: The Covenant's Heart
26.text: <sup>3</sup>If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them... <sup>12</sup>And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people... <sup>44</sup>Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them... <sup>45</sup>But I will for their sake remember the covenant with their forefathers.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 brings the covenant to its solemn climax with the great recital of blessings and curses — the two roads that lie before the covenant people. Covenant faithfulness brings blessing: rain in season, fruitful harvests, peace in the land, victory over enemies, and above all the crowning promise: "I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people" (26:12). Covenant unfaithfulness brings curse: in escalating waves, disease, drought, defeat, famine, and finally exile from the land. The structure mirrors the covenant treaties of the ancient world, but the heart of it is the presence or absence of God himself.

The escalating judgments are sobering — "sevenfold" again and again (26:18, 21, 24, 28), as God patiently, repeatedly disciplines a stubborn people. Yet even the curses are not vindictive; they are the disciplines of a covenant Father designed to bring his people to repentance. And here lies the chapter's astonishing grace: even when Israel is exiled in the land of their enemies, broken and scattered, God says, "if they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant" (26:40–42). "Yet for all that... I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44).

This is the heart of the matter: God's covenant faithfulness outlasts his people's faithlessness. Even in the deepest judgment, mercy has the last word, because the covenant rests finally not on Israel's obedience but on God's character. "I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:45). The God who threatens curse is the God who will not let his people go.

And the cross is where the curses and the blessings meet. For the dreadful truth is that Israel — and we — chose the road of unfaithfulness and earned every curse. But "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree'" (Gal 3:13). On the cross, Jesus drank the full cup of covenant curse, every sevenfold judgment, the ultimate exile of God-forsakenness — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" — so that the covenant blessing might come to us: "so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles" (Gal 3:14). He bore the curse; we receive the blessing. And the crowning promise of verse 12 finds its everlasting fulfillment: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God" (Rev 21:3).

sections.title: The Blessings of Obedience
sections.commentary:
God promises rich blessing for covenant faithfulness — rain, harvest, peace, security, fruitfulness (26:3–10). But the summit of all blessing is relational: "I will make my dwelling among you... And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people" (26:11–12). The greatest blessing is not the gifts but the Giver, not the land but the LORD walking in their midst.

Ferguson notes that this is the refrain of the whole covenant — "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" — the heartbeat of redemption from Eden to the New Jerusalem. God's deepest desire is to dwell with his people, and our deepest blessing is to have him.

sections.title: The Curses of Disobedience
sections.commentary:
The curses unfold in escalating waves, each introduced by God's patient warning to discipline "sevenfold" if they will not turn (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Disease, drought, wild beasts, the sword, famine so severe it leads to horror, and finally exile and scattering among the nations (26:33). The land itself will keep its Sabbaths while the people are away (26:34–35).

Sproul observed that these curses are not the rage of a capricious deity but the covenant discipline of a holy God, designed to break a hardened people and drive them to repentance. The escalation reveals divine patience as much as divine justice — God warns and warns again before the final judgment of exile. Yet the curses are real, and they fell: the exile to Babylon was Leviticus 26 coming to pass.

sections.title: Mercy Has the Last Word
sections.commentary:
And then, astonishingly, grace breaks through the curses. "If they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant with Jacob" (26:40–42). Even in exile, the door of repentance stands open. And the ground of hope is not Israel's worthiness but God's faithfulness: "Yet for all that... I will not spurn them... I will for their sake remember the covenant" (26:44–45).

This is the gospel's foundation: the covenant rests on God's character, not ours. Keller pressed that God's faithfulness outlasts our faithlessness, that mercy triumphs over judgment for all who confess. And the cross is where it all converges: Christ bore the full covenant curse (Gal 3:13) — the disease, the sword, the famine, the exile of God-forsakenness — so that we might inherit the covenant blessing and that God might dwell with us forever (Rev 21:3). The chapter that ends in mercy points to the cross where mercy was bought with blood.

26.theology:
The covenant's two roads. Blessing for faithfulness, curse for unfaithfulness — with the crowning blessing being God's own presence: 'I will walk among you... you shall be my people' (26:12).

Mercy outlasts judgment. Even in exile, confession reopens the door, for the covenant rests on God's faithfulness, not ours: 'I will for their sake remember the covenant' (26:45).

Christ bore the curse. Jesus 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us' (Gal 3:13), drinking the full covenant judgment so the blessing might come to us (Gal 3:14).
26.examples:
Then: Israel stood before two roads — blessing or curse — and was warned that unfaithfulness would bring escalating discipline and finally exile, yet promised that confession would meet a faithful, remembering God.

Now: We who earned every curse find that Christ drank it all on the cross, bearing even the exile of God-forsakenness, so that the covenant blessing is ours and God dwells with us forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-46 — Blessing, Discipline, and Covenant Faithfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book comes to its great covenant climax: the blessings that follow obedience and the disciplines that follow rebellion. If Israel walks with God, he promises rain, harvest, peace, fruitfulness, and — best of all — his own presence: "I will make my dwelling among you... and I will walk among you and will be your God." If they turn away, he warns of escalating discipline, "seven times" over, ending in exile. Yet the chapter does not end in wrath. It ends in astonishing grace: even in exile, if they confess, "I will remember my covenant." God's faithfulness outlasts his people's failure.
verseByVerse.theology: The covenant blessings and curses (echoed in Deut 28) set before Israel life and death — and the crown of blessing is not prosperity but Presence: "I will walk among you and will be your God" (v.12), a promise Paul applies to the church (2 Cor 6:16). The disciplines are not vengeance but a Father's chastening, escalating precisely to bring his people back (cf. Heb 12:6). And the climax is grace: "Yet for all that... I will not spurn them... I will remember... the covenant" (vv.44-45). God's covenant love rests finally on his own faithfulness, not ours — the very foundation of the new covenant secured in Christ (Rom 11:29; 2 Tim 2:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Israel was set before blessing and discipline — and assured that even if they failed all the way to exile, God would remember his covenant and not cast them off forever.

Now: our hope rests not on our faithfulness but on his: "if we are faithless, he remains faithful" (2 Tim 2:13). The covenant in Christ's blood cannot finally fail, because it rests on God's remembering, not ours.

verseByVerse.quote: If you walk in my statutes and observe my commandments and do them, then I will give you your rains in their season... I will give peace in the land... And I will make my dwelling among you... And I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: God sets before his people the blessings of obedience, and they are rich: rain in season, abundant harvests, peace in the land, safety from enemies, fruitfulness. But do not miss where the list climbs to its summit. The greatest blessing is not the crops or the peace or the security; it is God himself: "I will make my dwelling among you... and I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people." There it is again — the golden thread of the whole Bible, the promise that God will dwell with his people and walk among them, as once he walked with Adam in the garden in the cool of the day. Every other blessing is just the setting for this jewel. And this is the promise Paul lifts straight onto the church: "I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people" (2 Cor 6:16). The whole aim of redemption, from Exodus to Revelation, is God with us. Prosperity is not the prize; Presence is. The soul that has God has everything, and the soul that has everything but God has nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you will not listen to me and will not do all these commandments... then I will do this to you: I will visit you with panic... And if in spite of this you will not listen to me, then I will discipline you again sevenfold for your sins... And I will scatter you among the nations, and I will unsheathe the sword after you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Then comes the hard word: the discipline that will follow if Israel turns away. It escalates in waves, each introduced by a chilling refrain — "if in spite of this you will not listen... I will discipline you again sevenfold." Disease, defeat, drought, wild beasts, the sword, siege so terrible that the passage names unspeakable horrors, and finally exile, the land itself resting while its people are scattered among the nations. It is sobering to read, and it is meant to be. But we must understand what kind of word this is. This is not the raw vengeance of a cruel tyrant; it is the escalating discipline of a Father who will not let his children destroy themselves in silence. Notice that at every stage the door stands open — the discipline intensifies only "if" they still will not turn back. Each blow is aimed at the heart, designed to break through Israel's stubbornness and bring them home. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves" (Heb 12:6). Every one of these judgments is, in its own severe way, an act of covenant love — God refusing to let go of a people bent on ruin, striking not to destroy but to recover.

verseByVerse.quote: But if they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant with Jacob, and I will remember my covenant with Isaac and my covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land... Yet for all that, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them, for I am the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary: And now the chapter turns, and grace has the last word. After all the warnings, after the exile, when Israel has fallen as far as they can fall, God speaks the sweetest promise of all: "if they confess their iniquity... then I will remember my covenant." Even in the land of their enemies, even after every discipline has run its course, God says, "I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly." Why not? Not because they deserve it — they have earned only judgment. The reason is entirely in God: "for I am the LORD their God," and he will remember the covenant he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Here is the deepest comfort in the whole book. The covenant does not finally rest on Israel's faithfulness — which fails and fails again — but on God's. Their sin is real, their discipline is real, but his covenant love is deeper still. "If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself" (2 Tim 2:13). This is the granite foundation beneath the new covenant sealed in Christ's blood: our salvation is kept safe not by our fragile grip on God, but by his unbreakable grip on us. God remembers his covenant. And that is why we are not consumed.

27.title: Vows and Dedications: All Things Are His
27.text: <sup>28</sup>...every devoted thing is most holy to the LORD. <sup>30</sup>Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD. <sup>34</sup>These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
27.overview:
Leviticus closes not with the thunder of Sinai but with the quiet, voluntary devotion of the heart — laws about vows and dedications, the freewill consecration of persons, animals, houses, and land to the LORD. After all the commanded offerings, the book ends with the offerings that no one commands: the spontaneous overflow of a grateful heart that says, "All I have is yours, and I give it gladly."

The chapter provides a careful valuation system for redeeming what has been vowed (27:1–25), and reaffirms that the firstborn, the devoted thing, and the tithe already belong to the LORD (27:26–33). "Every tithe of the land... is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD" (27:30). The principle beneath it all is the great truth that crowns the whole book: everything belongs to God. "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof" (Ps 24:1). What we vow to him, we give back from what was already his.

Some have wondered why Leviticus, having reached its glorious heights in the Day of Atonement and the Jubilee, should end on such an administrative note. But there is a deep fittingness. The book that began with God calling sinners to draw near through sacrifice ends with redeemed sinners drawing near with their whole lives, voluntarily, joyfully consecrated. The proper response to all the grace of Leviticus — the offerings, the priesthood, the atonement, the holiness, the Jubilee — is the glad surrender of everything to God. Worship that begins with God's gift to us ends with our gift to God.

And it all points to Christ, who is both the One devoted wholly to God and the price of our redemption. He is the true tithe, the firstborn given to the Father, the One who could say, "I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7), holding nothing back. And he is the ransom by which we, who could never pay our own valuation, are redeemed — "you were bought with a price" (1 Cor 6:20). The book that opened with the burnt offering — total consecration — closes with the same call, now turned toward us: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (Rom 12:1). Holy, holy, holy is the LORD — and all that we are and have is his.

sections.title: The Valuation of Persons
sections.commentary:
When someone vows a person to the LORD, a monetary valuation is set for redeeming the vow (27:1–8). Strikingly, provision is made for the poor: "if someone is too poor to pay the valuation, then he shall be made to stand before the priest, and the priest shall value him" (27:8). No one is shut out of devotion by poverty; the priest adjusts the price to what the person can afford.

Calvin notes the dignity this confers: every person has worth before God, and even the poorest may consecrate themselves. And the deeper truth presses in — we could never pay our own true valuation before God. The price of our redemption was beyond all silver and gold; it was "the precious blood of Christ" (1 Pet 1:19). We are valued not by what we can pay but by what Christ paid for us.

sections.title: Devoting Animals, Houses, and Land
sections.commentary:
Detailed regulations govern the dedication and redemption of animals, houses, and fields (27:9–25), with the recurring option to redeem a vowed thing by adding a fifth (27:13, 15, 19) — the same generous overpayment we saw in the guilt offering. The system protects against rash vows while honoring genuine devotion.

Begg notes the seriousness with which God treats our promises to him: a vow is not to be made lightly, for "it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay" (Eccl 5:5). Yet the heart of the chapter is the gladness of giving back to God what is his, the joyful consecration of the things of ordinary life — our property, our possessions, our place — to the Lord who gave them all.

sections.title: The Tithe Belongs to the LORD
sections.commentary:
The chapter, and the book, close by reaffirming what already belongs to God: the firstborn (27:26), the devoted thing which is "most holy to the LORD" (27:28), and the tithe — "every tithe of the land... is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD" (27:30). We do not give God a tithe as if the other ninety percent were ours; the tithe simply confesses that all of it is his.

So Leviticus ends where true worship always lands: "All things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (1 Chr 29:14). The book that began with sinners drawing near through blood ends with redeemed sinners consecrating their whole lives in glad surrender. And it all points to Christ, the firstborn devoted wholly to the Father (Heb 10:7), the ransom that redeemed us when we could not redeem ourselves (1 Cor 6:20). The final word of Leviticus calls us to present ourselves, body and soul, a living sacrifice to the holy God who has made us his own.

27.theology:
All things belong to God. The tithe and the devoted thing confess that everything is the LORD's (27:30; Ps 24:1); what we give, we give back from what was already his.

Voluntary consecration. The book ends with freewill devotion — the glad surrender of a redeemed heart, the fitting response to all the grace of Leviticus (Rom 12:1).

Christ our ransom. We could never pay our own valuation; we were redeemed by 'the precious blood of Christ' (1 Pet 1:19), the firstborn devoted wholly to the Father (Heb 10:7).
27.examples:
Then: An Israelite, moved by gratitude, might vow himself, his animals, his house, or his field to the LORD, and bring his tithe — confessing that all he had belonged to God.

Now: Having received all the grace of Leviticus, we present our whole selves to God as a living sacrifice. We give gladly because all is his, and because Christ first gave himself wholly for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-34 — Vows, the Devoted Thing, and the Tithe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book ends, perhaps surprisingly, with laws about vows — the freewill promises by which a person could dedicate himself, an animal, a house, or a field to the LORD — and about the tithe. God sets fair values for redeeming what is vowed, and declares the tithe and the firstborn already his. It seems a quiet ending, but it is exactly right: the book about how to draw near to a holy God closes with the whole of life — persons, possessions, produce — freely consecrated to him.
verseByVerse.theology: Vows were voluntary (no one was required to make one), but once made, binding (cf. Deut 23:21-23; Eccl 5:4-5) — a lesson in the seriousness of promises to God. The tithe "is the LORD's; it is holy" (v.30) — already his before we give it, so tithing is not gift but acknowledgment. That the book closes on consecration — everything given over to God — matches its whole aim: a people wholly the LORD's. It anticipates the New Testament call to present "your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Rom 12:1), the truest vow of all.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: an Israelite could dedicate his most precious things — even himself — to God by vow, and give the tithe that was already the LORD's.

Now: we give not to earn God's favor but because we are already his, bought by Christ. The truest response to grace is to present our whole selves — a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God (Rom 12:1).

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone makes a special vow to the LORD involving the valuation of persons, then the valuation of a male from twenty years old up to sixty years old shall be fifty shekels of silver... And if it is an animal such as men offer as an offering to the LORD, all that anyone gives to the LORD is holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final chapter deals with vows — the voluntary promises by which an Israelite could dedicate something precious to the LORD: himself or a family member, an animal, a house, a field. God sets fair, graded valuations so that what was vowed could, if needed, be redeemed at a set price, with compassionate provision for the poor who could not afford the standard amount (v.8). Two lessons rise from this. First, vows were entirely voluntary — no one had to make one — but once made, they were binding and holy. God takes our promises to him seriously; "when you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it... It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay" (Eccl 5:4-5). Our word to God is not to be given lightly or broken casually. Second, notice the beautiful principle: "all that anyone gives to the LORD is holy." Whatever is truly given over to God is set apart, sacred, no longer common. When we dedicate something — our money, our time, our children, ourselves — to God, it enters a new category. It becomes holy, because it now belongs to the Holy One.

verseByVerse.quote: Every tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD... These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai.
verseByVerse.commentary: The book closes with the firstborn, the devoted thing, and the tithe — and a quietly profound truth about the tithe: it "is the LORD's; it is holy to the LORD." The tenth was not, strictly speaking, the Israelite's to give; it was already God's. To bring the tithe was not to make a gift so much as to acknowledge a fact — that everything belongs to God, and the tithe simply confesses it. And so Leviticus ends. Think about where it began: with a sinner bringing a sacrifice, longing to draw near to a holy God (ch. 1). And here at the end, the whole of life — persons, animals, houses, fields, harvests, flocks — is being consecrated, given over, declared holy to the LORD. That is the perfect ending, because that is the whole point of the book. God did not give all these laws to keep his people at a distance, but to make a way for them to come near and belong to him wholly. "These are the commandments that the LORD commanded Moses for the people of Israel on Mount Sinai." From the first drop of sacrificial blood to the last consecrated tithe, Leviticus has been teaching one glorious lesson: how a holy God can dwell with an unholy people, and how that people can be wholly his. It all points to the Lamb who fulfilled every sacrifice, the Priest who fulfilled every priesthood, and the Redeemer in whom we are made holy and brought near forever. The only fitting response is to give him everything: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (Rom 12:1).
